Its rung one and seed plan are site control, interconnection and flipping shovel-ready projects for developer fees, the same execution-moat developer category as powered brownfields/land promotion; its own write-up flags the developer-moat resemblance and a contested rung (Broad Reach, Engie, Jupiter, Spearmint, Eolian).

Rewind: robot-assisted distribution-transformer remanufacturing plant: merged into Rewind Transformer Works.
Rewound: data-graded distribution transformer remanufacturing: merged into Rewind Transformer Works.

Breakerline (second entry, re-certified MV switchgear integrator): merged with the first Breakerline entry.

scored.name: Brightfield Rescue (buy underperforming and orphaned C&I and community solar)
scored.industry: Energy: distributed solar, 0.5-7 MW C&I and community solar
scored.rung_one: Buy one 1-5 MW community or C&I solar project running 15-40% below P50 (failed inverters, broken trackers, soiling, vegetation, dead monitoring) from bankrupt EPCs/installers (SunPower 2024, Sunnova and installer failures 2025), broken sales (PowerBank's 16.9 MW NY projects returned in 2026), or exiting tax-equity sponsors, at a 30-60% discount (about $0.4-1.0M/MW). Revenue is the existing PPA or subscriber book plus SRECs, about $100-250k a year per MW. Greenbacker, Altus Power/TPG and Sol Systems buy healthy portfolios; rescue buyers are fragmented.
scored.ladder: 1) Single rescued project. 2) Fleet of 100-500 MW mixed-vintage DG solar. 3) Owner-operated robotics for module swap, cleaning and vegetation plus a tracker/inverter repair depot at fleet density. 4) Batteries and repowering on existing interconnection. 5) Subscriber management and retail supply across community-solar states. 6) Distributed IPP and community energy retailer.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: finding underperformers from state incentive production reports (NY-Sun, IL Shines, MA SMART), satellite soiling/vegetation imagery and bankruptcy dockets, and pricing the fix. Rung 2: fleet fault detection against a physics twin. Rung 3: robot routing and automatic work orders. Rung 4: storage and repower sizing on measured output. Rung 5: subscriber churn and credit ML.
scored.seed_plan: Run the model over IL Shines and NY-Sun data for 50 projects under 75% of nameplate, buy two with $1.5M equity plus green-bank back-leverage (NY Green Bank, CT Green Bank), restore output within 6 months, refinance at the restored value and recycle equity. Kills: subscriber defaults, module warranty voids; weakest on L3 since robotic O&M is copyable. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 2, L4 3, L5 4, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: My estimates, built from the sources below. Healthy operating DG/community solar trades at roughly $1.0-1.5/W. A vendor composite puts a new 2 MW community project at $1.43/W capex and 8.2% IRR (surgepv; weak source). A distressed purchase at $0.4-1.0/W is plausible, but no transaction found discloses $/W. The only data point on distressed pricing is Sunnova: it went as a whole platform to its DIP lenders (credit bid plus $25M cash). That suggests big bankrupt fleets clear as portfolios to creditors, not as single projects at a discount. Revenue: about 1,200-1,400 MWh/MWdc per year at roughly $0.09-0.15/kWh, plus SRECs/RECs, gives about $110-220k per MW per year. That is consistent with the candidate's $100-250k (one Illinois Shines disclosure shows $0.11/kWh fixed, or subscriptions priced at 70% of bill credits). Fix cost (estimate): $0.05-0.15/W for inverters, trackers, vegetation and monitoring. Restoring 25% of lost output on a 2 MW project adds about $90k a year. At an 8-10x EBITDA/cap-rate exit that is about $0.7-0.9M of value created per project. Capital (estimate): two 2 MW projects at about $0.7M/MW comes to $2.8M plus about $0.3M of repairs. That fits $1.5M of equity plus green-bank or back-leverage debt. Hidden costs that can erase the discount: ITC recapture inside the 5-year window, tax-equity and offtaker consents, liens, transferring subscriber contracts, and module warranties voided because the manufacturer went bankrupt. A two-project company earns roughly $0.3-0.5M a year, which keeps it alive but is not venture scale.
scored.buyers: For exit or refinance of the restored rung there are well-capitalised buyers of operating DG solar. Altus Power was taken private by TPG Rise Climate at about $2.2B EV, owns over 1.3 GW and bought 234 MW from Greenbacker in Dec 2025. Other buyers: CleanCapital (bought 22.7 MW from Kendall in Dec 2024), Standard Solar (28.8 MW from AC Power, 2026), Aspen Power, Dispatch Energy (208.9 MW Green Lantern), Greenbacker, Sol Systems, Spruce Power and SunStrong/GoodFinch. So rung one is clearly sellable. These buyers pay healthy-asset multiples, and that gap is the arbitrage.
scored.incumbents: The rescue niche is partly held, not empty. CleanCapital is a secondary-market aggregator of small operating DG assets and markets underperformer buys, backed by hundreds of $M of institutional capital. Spruce Power (public) and SunStrong/GoodFinch (Sunnova's DIP-lender buyer) do distressed residential. Altus/TPG, Greenbacker, Standard Solar, Aspen Power, Dispatch Energy, Sol Systems, Summit Ridge and New Leaf buy operating C&I and community solar and can bid on fixable assets. The fix-and-monitor layer (rung 2-3 software) is held by Omnidian (oversees 1.3 GW of DG after buying PV Pros), MaxGen, Raptor Maps (raised about $45M+), Power Factors and Heliolytics. Robotic O&M is held by AES Atlas and several cleaning-robot vendors. Single 1-5 MW broken projects are fragmented and get little attention from big buyers, which is the real opening, but anyone with a balance sheet can copy it.
scored.end_state: US solar was about 279 GWdc cumulative at YE2025, forecast to reach 769 GWdc by 2036 (SEIA/WoodMac). Community solar was about 10.1 GWdc cumulative at YE2025, with over 8 GW in development and a forecast of 15 GWdc by 2029. Estimate: non-residential DG (C&I plus community) is about 40-50 GW, producing about 55-65 TWh a year at about $100-130/MWh. That is a revenue pool of about $6-8B a year, plus O&M (about $1B) and storage/repower adders. A "distributed IPP plus community retailer" reaches multi-$10B only if retail supply is counted, and that step is not credible from this base. The proof-point end state is Altus Power at about $2.2B EV, a good outcome but a yieldco multiple, not a software one.
scored.killer: The returns are financial arbitrage and execution, not ML, so cap rates and access to deals decide them. Main risks: (1) deal flow is lumpy, and large bankruptcies clear as portfolios to DIP lenders and credit bidders (Sunnova), not as cheap single projects. (2) ITC recapture plus tax-equity and offtaker consents block or delay transfers. (3) Subscriber churn and defaults in community solar, and voided module warranties from bankrupt OEMs. (4) Interest rates squeeze the refinance-and-recycle loop. (5) Detecting underperformance from NY-Sun, IL Shines and satellite data is copyable, and CleanCapital, Omnidian or Raptor Maps-style players already do it. (6) The policy cliff after the OBBBA ITC phase-down reduces new supply but also changes buyer appetite. This is the same failure mode as powered brownfields: an execution-moat asset roll-up dressed as an ML company.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is winnable and sellable (a rescued operating solar project with real buyers like Altus/TPG and CleanCapital), but the edge is distressed-asset arbitrage, which capitalised secondary buyers and O&M platforms already partly hold. ML does not compound past finding the targets, and the end state is a roughly $2B yieldco rather than a multi-$10B chain: about 19/30.

scored.name: Armature (MV motor and generator repair roll-up climbing to motor OEM and drive-train-as-a-service)
scored.industry: Machines / industrial electric motors, generators, pumps and drives
scored.rung_one: Acquire one or two of the roughly 1,500-3,000 independent North American (EASA) motor and pump repair shops handling motors and generators from 200 hp to 10,000 hp, typically $2-10M revenue with 15-30 staff and a 60+ owner, at 3-5x EBITDA ($1.5-8M) financed by seed equity (about $1-2.5M) plus SBA 7(a) and seller notes. Mills, water utilities, mines, refineries, pipelines, food plants and data-center cooling plants pay $2k-500k per rewind or overhaul plus emergency premiums, and $50-500k a year per plant for service and predictive-maintenance route contracts. Cash-flowing from day one. Competitors: Integrated Power Services (PE roll-up), Hupp, Koontz-Wagner, Shermco, Sulzer, OEM services (ABB, WEG, TECO), and sensor-only startups Augury (over $250M raised) and Tractian, which own no physical rung.
scored.ladder: 1) Repair and rewind shop. 2) Regional cluster of 5-10 acquired shops with wireless vibration/current sensors on customer fleets sold as condition monitoring and guaranteed-uptime contracts. 3) Owned exchange pool of remanufactured large motors and generators as rotating spares. 4) Remanufactured and new high-efficiency IE4/IE5 motors and motor-plus-VFD packages (synchronous reluctance, PM, axial flux) on own designs, displacing OEM replacement purchases. 5) Owning drive-train assets (pumps, fans, compressors) at customer sites under energy-savings-as-a-service contracts (motors use about 45% of global electricity). End state: an industrial motor-systems OEM and lifecycle owner in a $150B+ motor, pump and drive pool.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: every teardown digitised (winding data, failure mode, test results, CV on windings and bearings) into a structured failure database, with automated quoting, rewind design (copper and insulation optimisation) and shop scheduling that lift throughput. Rung 2: condition-monitoring models labelled by the shop's own teardown outcomes, the ground truth sensor-only vendors lack; each acquired shop adds historical records and installed base and gets the software, so integration gets cheaper. Rung 3: cross-customer failure statistics decide which spares to pool and where and price exchange contracts. Rung 4: motor design trained on the largest proprietary dataset of real-world duty cycles and failures. Rung 5: efficiency and load data from the metered installed base underwrite energy-savings contracts.
scored.seed_plan: About $1-2.5M equity plus SBA 7(a) and a seller note to buy one profitable MV shop at 3-5x EBITDA. Keep the foreman and technicians; founders ship the quoting/diagnosis tool and a sensor retrofit within 6 months and sign the shop's top 20 customers to monitoring contracts; first exchange-pool contracts by month 9-12, then buy shop two. Kills: technician scarcity, thin margins, integration risk, industrial downturns, and looking like a PE/search-fund roll-up to YC. Rubric estimate about 24/30: L1 5, L2 5, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Rung one is a real, cash-flowing business, but a small and slow-growing one. Comparable listing: a Louisville industrial motor and pump repair shop shows about $3.08M trailing revenue and about $538k SDE (BizQuest). That is roughly 17% SDE margin, and EBITDA after a paid manager would be roughly 10-15% (estimate). At the candidate's 3-5x EBITDA a $3-8M revenue MV shop costs about $1.5-5M (estimate). Brokers do not publish multiples for these deals, and good MV shops with 200 hp+ rewind capability, balancing and VPI tanks command more because PE platforms bid for them. Capital: 10-20% equity under SBA 7(a), which caps at $5M and needs a personal guarantee, plus a seller note. So $0.5-1.5M equity buys one shop, leaving about $1M for the sensor and software build. Margin per job: rewinds run about 25-40% gross (estimate), and emergency premiums lift that. Monitoring contracts at $50-500k per plant are aspirational: a typical sensor SaaS contract is $5-50k per site per year (Augury/Tractian pricing class, estimate). Market: rewind/repair services are estimated at $5-13B globally (Trendlogic $5.2B 2022, FMI $9.1B 2025, DataHorizzon $10.5B 2024). Broader repair and maintenance is about $33.6B (IMARC 2025), growing 1-6% a year. North America is probably 25-30% of that (estimate).
scored.buyers: Pulp and paper mills, steel, mining, cement, water and wastewater utilities, refineries, pipelines and midstream, chemicals, food plants, power generators, and data-center chiller and cooling plants. All of them are capitalised and already pay for repair. Exit buyers for the shops themselves: Searchlight's IPS, Blackstone's Shermco, Sulzer, distributors such as E&I Sales and Motion Control Enterprises, and many PE platforms. So rung one is clearly sellable on its own.
scored.incumbents:
Rung one is fragmented but heavily contested by PE capital.
- Integrated Power Services: Searchlight Capital majority since Oct 2021, 33+ service centers, 5,000+ customer locations. It keeps adding shops: ABB's US industrial services unit (2024, 5 centers), Demaria Electric (Feb 2025), three Western shops (2022).
- Shermco: Blackstone bought it for about $1.6B in Aug 2025, with Hitachi Energy taking a minority stake. It roughly doubled revenue under Gryphon through add-ons.
- Other shops and service arms: Hupp, Koontz-Wagner, Sulzer service centers, L&S Electric (6 EASA-accredited centers).
- Distributors buying shops: E&I Sales (bought Industrial Motor Services), Motion Control Enterprises (bought Piedmont Electric, 2024).
- OEM service arms: ABB, WEG, TECO-Westinghouse, Siemens.
- Sensor-only players: Augury (about $369M raised, $75M in Feb 2025, per CB Insights) and Tractian ($120M Series C Dec 2024, about $183M total, per CB Insights) already hold the condition-monitoring layer at rung two.
- Search funds routinely target exactly this kind of shop.
scored.end_state: The headline $150B+ motor, pump and drive pool is real in aggregate (estimate: industrial motors about $20-25B, pumps about $60-70B, drives about $25B). The climbable chain is much smaller. Repair is $5-13B global (narrow) or about $34B (IMARC, broad). Rungs 4-5 mean competing as a motor OEM against ABB, Siemens, WEG and Nidec, all with scale, distribution and IE4/IE5 SynRM/PM products already shipping, and against ESCOs such as Ameresco, Johnson Controls and Siemens in energy-savings contracts. The path from a repair-shop roll-up to an OEM is not credible inside a venture timeline. IPS and Shermco show the realistic end state is a $1-2B-EV services platform sold to PE. That is a good outcome, but not a venture-scale chain.
scored.killer:
The main killer is weak software compounding plus a PE-dominated buyer market, which together make this a search-fund roll-up dressed as a startup.
1. The teardown dataset is small. A shop does hundreds to low thousands of jobs a year across heterogeneous machines, far too few to train condition-monitoring models that beat Augury and Tractian, who have hundreds of thousands of sensored assets. Teardown labels are a nice edge, not a moat.
2. Deal flow is contested. Shop multiples get bid up by IPS (Searchlight), Shermco (Blackstone), distributors and search funds, so the roll-up has no pricing edge.
3. Technician scarcity caps throughput. Winders and machinists retire faster than they can be trained, and the founders cannot software their way around it.
4. Rung four requires OEM-scale R&D, certification and channels against ABB, Siemens and WEG.
5. Revenue is cyclical and concentrated in heavy industry. Thin margins plus SBA leverage under a personal guarantee make a downturn dangerous.
6. YC optics: it reads as a levered roll-up with software sprinkled on top.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is winnable and cash-flowing, but a levered roll-up in a PE-contested $5-13B repair niche. ML gains little at shop data volumes against the sensor incumbents, and the climb to OEM against ABB, Siemens and WEG is not credible, so it scores about 19/30.

scored.name: Fluidline (transformer fluid and DGA lab climbing to remanufactured transformers)
scored.industry: Grid / power: transformer diagnostics, service and lifecycle
scored.rung_one: An owned ISO 17025 dielectric-fluid and DGA lab plus a mobile oil-processing truck, sold as annual fleet sampling contracts to utilities, IPPs, data-centre owners and industrial plants at about $150-400 per sample and $40-120k per site per year once field oil processing and diagnostics are added. Incumbents SDMyers, Doble/ESCO, Weidmann and TJ|H2b sell tests, not rebuilt units; Ayr Energy, Heron and Amperesand build new units; FluxCo is a sourcing marketplace. Nobody runs lab-to-reman with ML.
scored.ladder: 1) Fluid/DGA lab and field oil service. 2) Field repair: bushings, tap changers, gaskets, dry-outs. 3) Owned rewind/rebuild shop taking failed or retired units from customers' fleets (a rebuilt 20-100 MVA unit sells close to new price amid 2-4 year lead times). 4) A certified-rebuilt transformer product line plus a leased spare fleet. 5) New-build core/coil manufacturing from the teardown corpus. End state: a vertically integrated transformer lifecycle company in a $70B+ global transformer and service pool.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML on DGA, furan and moisture time series predicts failure and remaining life across every customer fleet. Rung 2: predictions schedule field work before failure, and the work history labels the data. Rung 3: teardown findings give ground-truth labels test-only competitors cannot get, and remaining-life scores pick which retired units are worth buying cheaply to rebuild. Rung 4: lease fleet dispatched by failure-probability forecasts. Rung 5: design rules from a failure-mode corpus of thousands of units.
scored.seed_plan: Buy or set up one accredited fluid lab in Texas or the Southeast (about $0.8-1.5M, or buy a retiring owner's lab). Sign 3-5 data-centre/IPP fleet contracts by giving away the remaining-life dashboard. Add one oil-processing truck in month 9. Fund the rebuild shop (about $10-20M) at Series A with revenue in hand. Kills: rung-3 capex and the shortage softening after 2029. Rubric estimate 23/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 5, L4 4, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Pricing: the only list price I found is DEWA's (Dubai utility lab): DGA at 1,850 AED (about $500), moisture at 310 AED, furans at 1,110 AED per sample. My estimate, not sourced: US commercial contract DGA runs about $50-150 per sample, well below the candidate's $150-400, because fleet contracts are bundled and SDMyers, Weidmann and TJ|H2b price on volume. Capital: setting up an accredited lab costs about $0.8-1.5M (estimate: GC headspace DGA rigs, Karl Fischer, furan HPLC, ISO 17025 accreditation, 2-4 chemists). An oil-processing (degasifier/dehydration) truck adds about $0.5-1M (estimate). A single lab clears maybe $1-3M revenue a year at 20-35% EBITDA once full (estimate). Field oil processing and repair is where the $40-120k per site figure becomes realistic. Rung 3 (a rewind/rebuild shop for 20-100 MVA units) needs about $10-20M plus a skilled winding workforce. Seed money gets you a small, profitable lab and service business, not a technology wedge.
scored.buyers: Utilities, IPPs and solar/wind/BESS owners (big transformer fleets at their collection substations), data-centre developers and colos, and heavy industry (steel, chemicals, mining, pulp). All are well funded, and the shortage makes them care about remaining life. But large IOUs often run oil labs in-house or hold long-standing SDMyers/Doble contracts. The most open buyers are renewables IPPs and data-centre owners with young, fast-growing fleets, and young fleets produce few failures to learn from.
scored.incumbents:
Rung one (fluid/DGA lab and field oil service) is crowded and mature:
- SDMyers (private, Ohio; kept its oil-testing core when GE bought three of its units in 2004)
- Doble Engineering (owned by ESCO Technologies; holds a decades-long DGA and test database plus analytics)
- Weidmann (Swiss, global labs)
- TJ|H2b Analytical
- SGS, Intertek and other testing majors
- Utility in-house labs

Rung 3 (repair/reman) is being consolidated by private equity:
- CORE Transformers, Seneca SC (new and reconditioned units for data-centre and industrial customers); Emerald Lake Capital invested in Sept 2025 and plans add-on acquisitions
- B&B Transformer, bought by Integrated Power Services in Aug 2024
- Sunbelt Transformer, merged with Solomon Corporation
- OTC Services, Cam Tran (PE-backed repair/reman)
- OEM service arms: Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova/Prolec

New-build startups (adjacent): Ayr Energy (~$25M raised, order book over $500M), Heron Power ($140M Series B, Feb 2026, a16z/Breakthrough), FluxCo ($26M, July 2026, sourcing marketplace). The claim that nobody runs lab-to-reman is roughly right for the ML part, but CORE and the Solomon/Sunbelt group already join testing, repair and reconditioned stock without ML.
scored.end_state:
The full transformer pool is roughly $60-70B+ a year worldwide (new units, estimate consistent with common industry figures), so the end state is genuinely large. The rungs one to three are actually reachable for a startup are small:
- Transformer services overall: about $5.5B in 2024, rising to about $8.2B by 2031 (Insight Partners, via GII)
- Rebuild services: about $1.83B in 2025, growing only 3.1% a year (Global Growth Insights)
- Oil testing alone: under $1B (estimate)

Getting from rung 3 to rung 5 (new core/coil manufacturing) means going head to head with Hitachi, Siemens, HD Hyundai, Prolec GE and Ayr, and building plants that cost $100M+. That end-to-end path is possible but unlikely.
scored.killer: 1) Rung one is commoditised and taken: DGA is a low-margin, relationship-driven test, and incumbents (Doble/ESCO, SDMyers, Weidmann) already have much larger historical DGA datasets and analytics, under IEEE C57.104-2019 and Duval methods. A new lab starts with the smallest dataset, which inverts the flywheel claim. 2) The valuable ground truth comes from teardowns, and that sits at rung 3, behind a $10-20M capex wall and a scarce workforce of skilled winders. Meanwhile PE roll-ups (CORE/Emerald Lake, Solomon/Sunbelt, IPS) are buying the same shops and their fleets of used units. 3) Demand for reman depends on the shortage. As Ayr, Hyundai, Hitachi and Siemens capacity arrives from 2028-2030, rebuilt units stop selling near new price. 4) Liability and certification: rebuilt units in utility or data-centre duty need OEM-equivalent warranties and insurance acceptance. 5) It is not the asymmetric "cheap right that jumps in value" pattern. It is a services roll-up with ML on top, so the moat is in execution and acquisitions more than in data.
scored.one_line_reason: A real, well-funded buyer base and a large end state, but rung one is a commoditised test lab, incumbents hold bigger DGA datasets, and PE firms are already rolling up the rung-3 reman shops. That makes it an execution-heavy services roll-up with weak ML leverage (18/30), not a 23.

scored.name: Recast (reverse-engineered obsolete spares for power plants, grid, rail and transit)
scored.industry: Machines / advanced manufacturing: industrial and energy aftermarket spare parts
scored.rung_one: Owned production of qualified replacement parts for obsolete or long-lead machinery: gas-turbine, hydro and steam-plant components, pump impellers, valve internals, seals, gearbox gears, breaker mechanisms, rail and transit parts. Parts are CT/blue-light scanned, reverse engineered and made via certified AM, printed-mold sand casting and CNC. Buyers are IPPs, utilities, munis, refiners, paper mills, transit agencies and DLA/DoD sustainment, paying $2k-500k per part (mostly emergency-outage budgets) when the OEM quotes 12-24 months or 'no longer supported', at 50%+ gross margin. Competitors: OEM aftermarket arms (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi), PSM (Hanwha), EthosEnergy and Sulzer for big frames, Re:Build, digital-inventory software (Replique, Ivaldi) that does not own production, and AM shops without the qualification layer. The owned-production, cross-fleet library rung is fairly open.
scored.ladder: 1) Part-by-part reverse-engineering and fulfilment. 2) A pre-qualified digital inventory catalogue of owned part files and qualification packages, sold repeatedly to every fleet with the same equipment. 3) Component remanufacture and repair (blades, vanes, bearings, pumps, valves, gearboxes, breakers). 4) Outage services and long-term parts-supply and sustainment agreements competing with OEM CSAs, becoming the de facto aftermarket OEM for orphaned equipment families. 5) Own whole-assembly designs (replacement combustor kits, retrofit breakers) and acquisition of orphaned product lines and IP from defunct OEMs. 6) An independent OEM-equivalent aftermarket player and roll-up of legacy machine brands across the legacy thermal, hydro and transit fleet.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: scan-to-CAD ML inferring geometry, material (with spectroscopy), tolerances and design intent from scans, wear patterns and similar parts, plus automated process planning and quote/lead-time prediction, cutting reverse engineering from weeks to days. Rung 2: a cross-fleet part-identity knowledge graph (shared parts across equipment families, failure rates, fits, qualified suppliers) from customer maintenance records that quotes instantly and forecasts which part files to pre-qualify and stock. Rung 3: repair-vs-replace models from inspection imagery and wear analytics across returned parts that make parts better than OEM originals. Rung 4: fleet-level outage scheduling and risk models to price long-term supply agreements. Rung 5: the library and installed-base map choose which orphaned OEM lines to buy. The qualified-design library compounds and is hard to copy.
scored.seed_plan: About $2.5M: a metrology lab with CT and blue-light scanners, a 5-axis CNC, and casting and AM partners (or a metal printer), ISO 9001 then AS9100/utility vendor qualification. Start with one tractable, acute vertical: hydro and small gas-turbine (aeroderivative/industrial) owners and municipal utilities underserved by OEMs, or transit agencies with publicly posted obsolete-part bids, plus DLA sustainment solicitations. Kills: OEM IP litigation (mitigate with discontinued parts and clean-room reverse engineering), slow qualification, and a lumpy per-part business that can stay services-like. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 3, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Unit price: about $2k-500k per part, mostly emergency-outage pricing (candidate's figure; the high end is gas-turbine hot-section parts, where buyers expect a discount to OEM list). Cost (ESTIMATE): an industrial CT scanner is about $0.5-1.5M (or rent time from a service bureau); blue-light scanners about $50-150k; a 5-axis CNC about $0.3-0.8M; a metal printer about $0.5-1M or outsource it. A $2.5M seed covers a lab plus 8-12 months of runway, but not much inventory. Gross margin (ESTIMATE): 40-60% on one-off emergency parts, but engineering hours per part (scan, CAD, material ID, first-article inspection, customer qualification) eat much of it at first. Realistic year-one revenue (ESTIMATE): $1-3M across dozens of jobs. Capital to climb: rung 3 (hot-section coating and repair, which needs vacuum furnaces and coating lines) is $10-50M+. Rung 5 (buying orphaned OEM lines) is M&A capital. Rung one itself is light; the later rungs are not.
scored.buyers: IPPs and utilities: gas-turbine fleet owners after their OEM service agreements expire. Turbomachinery Magazine reports the F-class market "has begun to open up" for independents as OEM contracts lapse, and Chromalloy itself advises buying OEM parts for engines under about 10 years old. Also hydro owners, municipal utilities, refiners and pulp mills, transit agencies (posted bids for obsolete parts), and DLA/DoD sustainment through its reverse-engineering and DMSMS programs. These buyers have money, but their purchasing is conservative: each utility runs its own vendor qualification, and spend is lumpy and driven by outages.
scored.incumbents: Gas turbines: the OEM aftermarket arms (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Power) dominate through long-term service agreements. Independents: PSM (owned by Hanwha), EthosEnergy (formerly Wood Group GTS), Chromalloy (owned by Veritas; PMA/reverse-engineered turbine parts), MD&A, Sulzer. Nuclear: Curtiss-Wright Nuclear already sells reverse-engineered replacement parts and commercial-grade dedication. Startups or venture-backed: Re:Build Manufacturing ($120M round from General Catalyst in Aug 2024, about $233M total); AddParts (digitizes, stores and makes obsolete spares; pre-seed Apr 2026); Intropy (AI for spare-parts management, about $11M seed Jul 2026); Novineer (AI photo-to-CAD for defense sustainment, built on federally funded research); DISCUS Software (AFWERX AI reverse engineering and technical data packages); Elevate Systems (DoD reverse engineering); digital-inventory platforms Replique and Ivaldi; plus thousands of local reverse-engineering, AM and machine shops. The specific "owned production plus cross-fleet library" combination is open-ish, but rung one as an activity (reverse-engineer and make a part) is crowded and fragmented.
scored.end_state: Gas turbine services alone are about $24-27B (2025): GMI puts it at $27.1B growing to $78.7B by 2035; Spherical Insights at $23.67B. Chromalloy's president put it at $16-20B. Add hydro, steam, grid switchgear, rail/transit and DoD sustainment parts and the pool is multi-$10B+ (ESTIMATE $50B+). But most gas-turbine value sits in OEM long-term service agreements and hot-section parts for recent frames, which independents have attacked for 30 years and hold only a minority of. The end state (an independent OEM-equivalent across legacy fleets) amounts to building PSM, EthosEnergy and Chromalloy combined, which took decades and big M&A balance sheets.
scored.killer: 1) It is a job shop. Each part needs its own scan, material ID, tolerancing, first-article inspection and a qualification at each customer, so revenue scales with engineering headcount and gross margin looks like services. The library compounds weakly because parts are not reused much across sites (different frames, revisions and wear). 2) Qualification and liability: a failed reverse-engineered rotating part causes an outage or safety incident, so utilities default to the OEM or to established independents like PSM and EthosEnergy. One failure can end the company. 3) OEM IP and contracts: long-term service agreements often penalise non-OEM parts, and parts for current frames bring litigation risk. That pushes the company toward genuinely orphaned, low-volume parts, which are the smallest part of the pool. 4) The ML is not the moat. Scan-to-CAD is being commoditised (Novineer, DISCUS, CAD vendors' tools), and the defensible assets are qualification records and customer trust, which build slowly. 5) Climbing to repair and hot-section rungs needs a $10-50M+ capex wall.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is a real, fundable and sellable reverse-engineering job shop, but the software does not compound much across sites, rung one is crowded with independents and startups (Re:Build, AddParts, Novineer, Curtiss-Wright, Chromalloy, PSM, EthosEnergy), and the end state means fighting OEM service agreements in a $24-27B gas-turbine service market already contested for decades, so it is a solid services business rather than an ML-compounding ladder (about 18/30, below the candidate's own 21).

scored.name: Dedicate (obsolete-parts house for operating reactors)
scored.industry: Nuclear components / qualified manufacturing (operating-fleet spares)
scored.rung_one: An NQA-1 / 10 CFR 50 App. B qualified commercial-grade dedication and reverse-engineering cell, bought as a small existing App. B shop (about $1-2M with SBA/seller note, keeping NUPIC audits and approved-vendor status), owning an inventory of dedicated safety-related spares (relays, breakers, transmitters, valve internals, pump seals, obsolete I&C cards) sold to utilities running the 94 US units and the CANDU fleet (Constellation, Duke, Southern, TVA, Vistra, Bruce, OPG) at $5-80k per part, a 3-10x markup, with outage premiums. Incumbents: Curtiss-Wright, Paragon Energy Solutions, Framatome, Westinghouse spares, Nuclear Logistics/AZZ, Ultra Energy; fragmented, slow and not software-driven.
scored.ladder: 1) CGD and obsolete-part dedication cell. 2) Owned consigned spares inventory and a pooled cross-fleet spares programme. 3) In-house component line for chronically obsolete families under an ASME N/NPT stamp. 4) Qualified supplier to SMR and advanced-reactor builders (X-energy, TerraPower, GE BWRX-300, Kairos). 5) Module/skid fabricator and full safety-related BOP supply, a 'Hadrian for nuclear'.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: an LLM/ML pipeline turning parts histories, NRC Part 21 reports, LERs and obsolescence notices into a dedication-package generator, cutting engineering hours per package about 70%. Rung 2: cross-fleet demand forecasting from outage schedules and failures decides what to pre-dedicate and stock. Rung 3: a reverse-engineering corpus makes each new obsolete design cheaper. Rung 4+: digital quality records and CV on CMM/NDE data lower NQA-1 traceability cost for new-build components.
scored.seed_plan: Buy a retiring owner's App. B shop or CGD house ($3-10M revenue), build the dedication software in-house to push throughput 2-3x on the same staff, target the 30 most-requested obsolete families from public Part 21 and LER data, and win 3-5 utility blanket POs in 12 months to fund stocking. Kills: utility procurement conservatism and acquisition availability. Rubric estimate about 23/30: L1 4, L2 5, L3 4, L4 4, L5 4, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Strong comparable at scale: Mirion bought Paragon Energy Solutions (engineered components, obsolescence, reverse engineering and CGD for every operating North American reactor) for about $585M cash, closed Dec 2025. That is about 18x projected 2026 adjusted EBITDA, on about $150M revenue at 20-22% EBITDA margin (Mirion/BusinessWire, D Magazine). So the rung earns money and has buyers. Curtiss-Wright QualTech NP says it has dedicated more than 50,000 items. It runs reverse engineering and seven categories of 'OBSOLUTIONs', and its RAPID parts database is effectively a software layer already. Per-part pricing of $5-80k and a 3-10x markup are the candidate's numbers. I found no source for them; EPRI and the NRC do not publish per-package cost (ESTIMATE, unverified). Acquisition cost is ESTIMATE. A healthy App. B/NUPIC-audited shop with $3-10M revenue at about 15-20% EBITDA would sell at 4-7x EBITDA, so about $2.5-14M, more than the $1-2M claimed. The 18x strategic multiple also pushes up small-shop asking prices. A shop selling for $1-2M is probably distressed or depends on one key person. Change of ownership can trigger NUPIC re-audit and utility approved-vendor review. Stocking inventory ahead of blanket POs needs about $1-3M of working capital more (ESTIMATE). Example of a price anchor: Duke spent $27M replacing Oconee computer systems after spares became unobtainable and custom manufacture became prohibitive.
scored.buyers: About 20 operating-fleet utilities and owners: Constellation, Duke, Southern, TVA, Vistra, Dominion, Entergy, NextEra, Xcel, plus Bruce Power and OPG for CANDU. Also the OEMs and integrators that resell (Westinghouse, Framatome). Exit acquirers have a proven appetite: Mirion, Curtiss-Wright, BWXT, AMETEK, and PE firms (Windjammer, Argosy).
scored.incumbents: This is not an open, fragmented field. Mirion/Paragon ($585M deal; Paragon came out of AZZ's Nuclear Logistics Inc., so the candidate counts NLI/AZZ twice) and Curtiss-Wright Nuclear/QualTech NP (public, multi-$B parent, more than 50k items dedicated, RAPID database) are the big players. Westinghouse (Brookfield/Cameco) runs third-party CGD and generic dedication plans for product families, and Framatome does the same. Ultra Energy and smaller App. B houses fill the rest. AI-for-nuclear software startups could move into dedication-package automation: Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, Sept 2025, at more than 65 reactors) and Atomic Canyon ($7M seed, 2025, nuclear document AI). I found no startup that owns a dedication cell and uses AI to generate packages.
scored.end_state: Operating-fleet spares, obsolescence and CGD look like a few $B/yr at most (ESTIMATE). The anchor is Paragon at about $150M as a leading player, with US nuclear O&M at roughly $15-20B/yr, mostly labour and fuel. Rungs 4-5 (qualified supplier and module/BOP fabricator for SMRs) only reach a multi-$10B pool if new nuclear build actually happens at scale (ESTIMATE, depends on orders). Those rungs are contested by BWXT, Doosan, IHI, Curtiss-Wright, and the reactor vendors' own supply chains, and need ASME N/NPT stamps and plant-scale capex. The path from end to end is plausible but not credible from a $3M start.
scored.killer: 1) Moat comes from incumbents and procurement. Utilities buy from an approved-vendor list built over decades, and Curtiss-Wright, Mirion/Paragon and Westinghouse already have the parts databases and dedication history. Software alone does not dislodge them. 2) Regulators cap how much AI can do. Every package still needs a responsible engineer's signature, and the NRC and NUPIC treat AI-generated technical evaluations conservatively, so the 70% hours cut is optimistic. 3) Quality escape is fatal: a single Part 21, counterfeit or fraudulent-item event can end a small shop. 4) Acquisition availability and price. Shops are scarce, being bid up after an 18x strategic print, and depend on key QA people. 5) About 20 utility customers, with a fleet that grows only if SMRs arrive.
scored.one_line_reason: It is a real, profitable, sellable rung: Paragon has about $150M revenue at 20%+ EBITDA and sold to Mirion for $585M. But rung one is held by Curtiss-Wright, Mirion/Paragon and Westinghouse, who already own parts databases. A seed-funded App. B acquisition costs more than claimed, AI dedication runs into signature and NUPIC conservatism, and the multi-$10B end-state depends on SMR new build. Score about 18/30, not 23.

scored.name: Ringforge (AI-run open-die and ring-rolled forgings)
scored.industry: Machines and energy components: large open-die forgings and seamless rolled rings
scored.rung_one: An acquired small open-die and ring-rolling forge ($5-15M revenue, retiring owner, 4-6x EBITDA financed mostly by SBA 7(a) and seller notes, founder equity under $1.5M) selling rings, shafts and blocks to GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, valve and pump OEMs and navy shipyard subtiers at $5-20/kg with $20-500k jobs; large forgings are a known defense and energy bottleneck. Incumbents: Scot Forge, PCC Wyman-Gordon, Ellwood, Frisa; startups target machining (Hadrian), sheet forming (Machina Labs) and castings (Foundry Lab, Rangeview), so ML-native forging is open.
scored.ladder: 1) One re-instrumented forge. 2) Roll-up of 3-5 forges with heat treat and machining shipping finished rings. 3) Greenfield large ring mill and heavy press for gas-turbine casings, SMR vessels and naval shafting (DoD-funded). 4) Own VIM/ESR specialty-alloy melt. 5) Complete rotating components (discs, races, flanges); a $40B+ forging market at shortage pricing.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: press and furnace sensors and FEM-surrogate forging-sequence planning cutting passes, reheats and the 20-40% excess machining stock. Rung 2: a cross-plant quoting engine learning cost and yield from every job, making each acquired shop more profitable. Rung 3: microstructure and property prediction for qualification. Rung 4: melt-to-forge genealogy cutting coupon testing. Rung 5: design-for-forging services winning whole-part contracts.
scored.seed_plan: $2.5M: about $1.2M equity into an SBA/seller-financed buyout of a $6-10M ring roller plus $1M for instrumentation, ML and heat-treat upgrade; keep operators and customers, cut material input 10%+ and quote time from weeks to hours within 12 months, then buy forge two with cash flow plus Series A. Kills: acquisition and labour execution, oil and gas cyclicality, two-OEM concentration. Rubric estimate about 22/30: L1 5, L2 5, L3 3, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: NOTE: the shared web-search budget ran out before this run made any query, so every figure below is an estimate from prior knowledge and has not been checked against live sources. Target: a $6-10M revenue ring roller or open-die shop. Small job-shop forges typically earn 10-18% EBITDA (est.), so about $0.8-1.5M EBITDA. At 4-6x that is a $4-8M price. SBA 7(a) caps at $5M per borrower. Anyone owning 20% or more must give a personal guarantee, and lenders usually want the buyer to have run a similar operation. Two ML founders with no plant history and VC-held equity are a hard fit for SBA, so the gap probably needs a seller note of 10-20% plus mezzanine debt. Realistic equity is $1-2M, plus $0.5-1M of working capital (steel inventory is a large share of COGS) plus about $1M for instrumentation and heat-treat upgrades. That is roughly $3-4M all in, not $2.5M. Pricing: carbon and alloy rings sell for about $4-10/kg and nickel and stainless for $15-40/kg (est.). Material is 40-60% of COGS. A 10% cut in input material is therefore worth about 4-6 points of margin, which is the main ML value lever. Debt service on 70-80% leverage takes most of the free cash flow in years 1-3. Buying forge two from cash flow inside 18 months is optimistic.
scored.buyers: GE Vernova and Siemens Energy (gas and wind turbine rings, flanges, casings), Baker Hughes, Flowserve, Emerson and other valve and pump OEMs, bearing makers (Timken, SKF, Schaeffler), mining and heavy equipment OEMs, and Navy shipbuilding subtiers (HII, General Dynamics Electric Boat and BWXT supply chains). These buyers are well capitalised but run long qualification cycles (first-article inspection, source approval, often 6-24 months), so an acquired shop mostly keeps its existing approved part numbers and is slow to win new ones.
scored.incumbents: Not checked because search was unavailable; drawn from prior knowledge. Large forgings: PCC Wyman-Gordon and Shultz (Berkshire Hathaway), Howmet, ATI, Scot Forge (employee-owned, est. $400M+ revenue), Ellwood Group (private), Frisa (Mexico), Bharat Forge, Japan Steel Works and Doosan (very large forgings), Forged Solutions Group, Patriot Forge, Canton Drop Forge and McInnes rolled rings. There are no venture-backed startups in open-die or ring forging that I know of, so the startup slot is open. Nearby startups: Hadrian (precision machining, raised about $200M+), Machina Labs (robotic sheet forming, about $100M+), Foundry Lab and Rangeview (castings), and Re:Build Manufacturing (an industrial roll-up that has raised hundreds of millions). The real competition for the rung-one acquisition is lower-mid-market private equity, search funds and strategic roll-ups (for example Forged Solutions and Doncasters-type platforms) bidding for the same retiring-owner forges. DoD Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment and Navy Maritime Industrial Base programs fund capacity at incumbents.
scored.end_state: Global forgings are roughly $80-100B (est.) and open-die plus seamless rolled rings roughly $15-25B (est.). The candidate's $40B figure is plausible only when closed-die aerospace forgings are counted. Shortage pricing does exist in very large forgings (naval shafting, reactor vessels, large gas-turbine casings), but that segment is a few billion dollars and is held by PCC, JSW, Doosan and Scot Forge. Going end to end requires a heavy press (10-50 kt) at about $100-500M, VIM/ESR/VAR melt at about $100M+ per line, and multi-year nuclear and naval qualification. Rungs 3-4 are capital-intensive, DoD-dependent bets that put the company in direct competition with Berkshire-owned PCC. The path exists only with large government co-funding.
scored.killer: 1) Execution: two technical founders without plant experience taking on a highly levered union or blue-collar shop, where losing key hammer and press operators or the plant manager kills throughput. SBA lenders will push back on this team. 2) Data poverty: a $8M shop runs a few thousand jobs a year on a handful of old presses. FEM-surrogate planning and quoting ML have little data to compound on, and the main gains (pass planning, stock allowance) can be done with off-the-shelf DEFORM/QForm simulation, which is not a moat. 3) Cyclicality and concentration: oil and gas, mining and wind rings swing 30-50%, and two OEMs often make up 40%+ of revenue. 4) Capex wall at rungs 3-4. 5) The business looks like a PE roll-up with a software story, so the VC and YC return profile is weak until rung 2-3. The likely outcome is a good 3-5x leveraged-buyout return, not a venture-scale ML company.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is a real, cash-flowing, sellable business and the startup slot in forging is open. But the ML layer is thin (small job-shop data, simulation tools already sold commercially), the acquisition is harder to finance than shown for founders with no operating history, and the end state hits a $100M+ press and melt capex wall against Berkshire-owned PCC. It reads as a levered industrial roll-up rather than a compounding ML ladder: about 18/30 versus the self-estimate of 22.
sources: No live web sources: the shared WebSearch budget (200 per turn) was used up before this run made any query, so all figures are prior-knowledge estimates and are marked (est.)
SBA 7(a) program terms ($5M cap, personal guarantee for owners of 20% or more), https://www.sba.gov/funding-programs/loans/7a-loans (prior knowledge, not fetched)
Hadrian, Machina Labs and Re:Build Manufacturing funding are public press-reported figures from prior knowledge, not fetched this session
Berkshire Hathaway ownership of Precision Castparts (Wyman-Gordon) since 2016, prior knowledge

scored.name: Breakerline (reconditioned MV/HV switchgear and breakers climbing to prefab power blocks)
scored.industry: Grid / power: switchgear, circuit breakers, protection and e-houses
scored.rung_one: An owned test shop (15-30k sq ft with high-current and hipot bay) plus inventory of reconditioned and retrofit-certified LV and MV circuit breakers (480V-38kV vacuum/SF6), full metal-clad lineups and HV dead-tank breakers, sourced from plant retrofits, mill and data-center decommissioning and utility change-outs, recertified to ANSI/UL. Buyers are data-center and industrial electrical contractors (Rosendin, Cupertino Electric), utilities replacing obsolete breakers, IPP collector substations and AI/crypto sites needing gear now (new MV lead times 40-120 weeks). Breakers sell for $5-60k, lineups $150k-1.5M; one shop is $30-60M a year at maturity. Rivals are fragmented reconditioners and resellers (Circuit Breaker Sales/CBS group, Southwest Electric, Electric Power Systems, Electrical Reliability Services under Vertiv, Powell service) plus OEM aftermarket arms (Eaton, ABB, Siemens); none software-native.
scored.ladder: 1) Reconditioned breakers and roll-in retrofill kits (new vacuum bottles, digital relays) for obsolete cubicles. 2) Complete lineups mixing reconditioned and new components, tested to UL/ANSI. 3) Own-design SF6-free MV switchgear built to stock in standard data-center configurations. 4) E-house and skid integration for 5-100 MW sites (switchgear, transformers, protection) and prefab substation/power-block products, sold or leased. 5) Own and operate electrical balance-of-plant for power islands as an energized-capacity service ($/kW-month), linking to substation-as-a-service. End state: a challenger switchgear OEM in a roughly $100B global market dominated by ABB, Schneider, Siemens and Eaton.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: a parts interchange graph covering decades of obsolete breaker models (Westinghouse DHP, GE Magne-Blast, ITE) built from manuals, nameplates and teardowns, matching a legacy cubicle to a retrofit or reconditioned unit instantly; CV plus test-data grading (contact resistance, timing, insulation); and a spec-to-inventory matcher that parses buyers' submittal PDFs and one-lines, the illegible-data edge. Rung 2-3: retrofill design generator per cubicle family and automated SLD-to-BOM and layout generation that turns a data-center one-line into a quoted lineup in hours, salvaged inventory first. Rung 4-5: auto-generated protection-coordination and arc-flash studies, plus fleet monitoring (partial discharge, thermal) for uptime contracts. Every quote and test enriches the interchange graph, demand forecast and design library.
scored.seed_plan: About $2M: lease the shop with about $0.5M of test equipment, hire one NETA-certified test lead and two techs (or acquire a small reconditioner), buy lots from industrial demolition firms and liquidators, and launch an 'upload your nameplate photo, get a retrofit quote' tool plus the spec matcher as the funnel to plant managers and data-center electrical contractors. First revenue month 4-6. Kills: UL/listing and insurer acceptance of reconditioned gear on data centers (NEMA guidance), and OEM channel retaliation. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 5, L3 3, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Prices are the candidate's figures (estimates, in line with what resellers list): reconditioned LV/MV breakers $5-60k, lineups $150k-1.5M. Typical reconditioning gross margin is about 35-55% (estimate), driven by cheap salvage lots and scarcity pricing for obsolete frames. Seed of about $2M covers roughly $0.5M of test gear, a shop lease, and a NETA lead plus 2 techs. The binding cost is inventory working capital. A credible stock of MV lineups and HV dead-tank breakers costs several $M on its own, so $2M only works on a consignment or brokered model (estimate). The demand tailwind is real. MV switchgear lead times are typically 40-60+ weeks, data-center-spec gear runs 2-3 years at the busiest OEMs, and the pre-COVID baseline was 12-16 weeks (T&D World, IPS, Giga Energy). The model is proven by RESA Power, a services, retrofit-switchgear and obsolete-parts roll-up. It grew revenue and EBITDA more than 4x in 2021-2025 and sold to Kohlberg in 2025, reportedly for $825M+ (PE Hub, unconfirmed). Power-services comps trade at about 11-13x EBITDA. A $30-60M/yr shop is plausible but would take years, not 18 months (estimate).
scored.buyers: Buyers with money: industrial plant reliability managers and utilities replacing obsolete breakers like-for-like. This is the best early fit, because they care less about listings and need the part to fit an existing cubicle. Also data-center and industrial electrical contractors (Rosendin, Cupertino Electric), IPP collector substations, and crypto/AI behind-the-meter sites. Hyperscale and colo data centers are the buyers the pitch leans on, but they are the least likely to accept reconditioned MV gear in critical paths, because of NEMA guidance against reconditioned breakers, insurer and Uptime-style requirements, and owner specs calling for new UL-listed gear.
scored.incumbents:
Rung one is held by consolidated, PE-backed roll-ups.
- RESA Power: Kohlberg-owned after a reported $825M+ exit by Investcorp. It has acquired Switchgear Unlimited and West Coast Switchgear and keeps a large inventory of obsolete parts plus custom retrofit switchgear.
- Integrated Power Services (IPS): acquired National Switchgear in 2021.
- Group CBS / Circuit Breaker Sales: an acquirer, including Berthold Electric in 2018.
- Others: Midwest Switchgear Group, Southwest Electric, Electric Power Systems, ERS (Vertiv), Powell service, and OEM aftermarket and retrofill arms (Eaton, ABB, Siemens, Schneider).
On the new-build, fast-delivery side, Giga Energy (Houston) makes stock transformers and UL 891 switchboards for data centers, including CoreWeave. It has raised about $3.4M equity per The Information, and some sources say up to $10-30M. It is the closest software and speed-native startup analogue to rungs 3-4. Not software-native is true of the reconditioners, but their moat is inventory, NETA techs and relationships, not software.
scored.end_state: The global switchgear market was about $93-169B in 2025 depending on the source: Meticulous $92.8B, Roots $123B, Straits $135.5B, GII $141B, GMI $168.9B, growing about 7% a year. The prefab e-house and power-block plus energy-as-a-service rungs add more. The pool is large, but the path to a challenger OEM means facing ABB, Schneider, Siemens, Eaton and Hitachi, which are all adding US capacity (Eaton's 370k sq ft switchgear plant). It also needs UL/IEEE type-testing and a new design lab for SF6-free MV gear, which costs tens of $M. Rungs 1-2 (reconditioning) do not naturally lead to rung 3 (new-design OEM). They are different businesses with different moats. The credible end state is a large services and retrofit roll-up like RESA (about $1B EV), not a $10B OEM.
scored.killer: 1) Data-center acceptance. NEMA guidance and insurers or owners refuse reconditioned MV gear in critical paths, so the headline AI buyer mostly buys new. 2) Supply is the constraint. Good salvage MV and HV inventory is scarce and contested by RESA, IPS and CBS, so you cannot scale on demand. 3) Lead-time normalisation. OEM capacity expansions from Eaton, Siemens, Hitachi and others collapse the scarcity premium within 2-4 years. 4) The software edge is thin. Interchange graphs and spec matching are a nice front end, but incumbents already have the inventory and the cross-reference knowledge in their techs' heads. The data flywheel does not carry into rungs 3-5, where type-testing, manufacturing and EPC execution are the moat. 5) Working capital, plus liability for failures of recertified gear.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is real, profitable and winnable, but it is held by PE roll-ups (RESA reportedly sold for $825M+ in 2025). The data-center buyer largely rejects reconditioned MV gear, and the software barely compounds past the parts-interchange layer into the OEM and EPC rungs. This is a good services roll-up, not a compounding ML ladder: about 17/30.

scored.name: Bayline (fast-turn switchboard and MV switchgear line)
scored.industry: Electrical machines / power distribution for AI data centres
scored.rung_one: A UL 891/1558 assembly line building LV switchboards and power-distribution skids from licensed or bought breakers for data-centre electrical contractors and modular DC integrators. Each section is $80-400k and a full hall's lineup about $2-6M, with 12-16 week lead times against 40-60 weeks at the majors. Incumbents: Eaton, Schneider, ABB, Siemens and fragmented regional panel shops; software-native entrants are rare (only configurator SaaS).
scored.ladder: 1) LV switchboards and PDU skids. 2) MV (15-38 kV) metal-clad switchgear under licence, then own designs. 3) Integrated prefabricated eHouse power blocks (switchgear, UPS, transformers). 4) Own breaker and protection-relay component manufacture. 5) Operating power blocks under lease to neoclouds as electrical capacity-as-a-service.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: an LLM plus rules-engine configurator turns one-lines and spec PDFs into BOMs, drawings and bus-bar cut files, cutting engineering hours per order about 70%; every order improves the parser. Rung 2: arc-flash and coordination study automation in the quote. Rung 3: reusable digital-twin power-block designs. Rung 4: component-scarcity forecasting from the order book. Rung 5: fleet telemetry feeds failure prediction and protection tuning back into designs.
scored.seed_plan: About $1.5M for a 25k sq ft shop, third-party UL listing and bus-bar CNC punch/bend equipment; recruit a retired panel-shop GM; win first orders from lead-time-desperate modular DC integrators and EPCs via 2-3 electrical contractors. Founders write the spec-to-BOM automation as the margin engine. Kills: breaker supply allocation from the majors (hence rung 4) and a cyclical DC capex downturn. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 4, L2 5, L3 3, L4 4, L5 2, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Unit: an LV switchboard section is roughly $80-400k and a full hall lineup roughly $2-6M (these are the candidate's figures; they look plausible but I could not verify them). Margin benchmark: Fibrebond, a builder of pre-integrated modular power enclosures, had about $378M of trailing revenue and about $110M of expected 2025 adjusted EBITDA (around 29%). Eaton bought it for $1.4B, about 12.7x EBITDA, which is a good sign for exit value and for margin in a supply-short market. A new shop should expect much less, around 15-22% gross margin (estimate), because breakers and bus copper are pass-through cost bought from the same majors it competes with. Lead-time gap: MV switchgear is quoted at 44-65 weeks, and one source says more than 60 weeks by May 2026, up from about 44 in late 2025. That is the real wedge. Capital: about $1.5M for a 25k sq ft shop, CNC bus punch/bend equipment and a third-party UL 891 listing is plausible (estimate). The binding constraint is working capital, not the shop. A $2-6M lineup ties up roughly 50-70% of its price in breakers and copper for 3-4 months, so 3-4 lineups in flight need $5-15M of working capital or customer deposits (estimate). That pushes the real seed need past $3M unless buyers pay 30-50% up front.
scored.buyers: Electrical contractors (e.g. Rosendin, Cupertino Electric, Faith Technologies), modular DC integrators, neocloud and colo developers building fast (crypto-to-AI conversions, CoreWeave-style tenants), EPCs. These buyers are well funded and desperate on schedule, but they buy on a proven track record and on warranty and bonding capacity, and the first $2-6M PO to an unproven shop is hard to land.
scored.incumbents: Majors: Eaton (now owns Fibrebond, $1.4B, 2025, plus a new 370k sq ft switchgear plant), Schneider, ABB, Siemens (more than $500M of recent switchgear capacity investment across the US and Germany), Vertiv, and LS Electric (won a $64M contract for 38 kV data centre switchgear in 2026). Closest to this exact ladder is Giga Energy (Houston/Austin; bootstrapped, reportedly profitable). It already builds UL 891 switchboards (200+ built), GigaBase 24.9/34.5 kV MV switchgear modules and transformers, and it operates data centres and power-market software (Giga Power Systems, launched Jan 2026). In other words Giga already runs rungs 1, 2, 3 and 5 of this ladder with the same fast-delivery pitch. Below them sit hundreds of regional UL 891/508A panel shops that already have the listing and the breaker-distributor relationships. Rung one is held, and the 'software-native fast-turn' angle is not novel.
scored.end_state: Global switchgear is about $93-104B (2025), rising to about $137B by 2030 (MarketsandMarkets, Meticulous). Data-centre-specific switchgear is $2.4-8.8B in 2025 depending on the source (P&S, Stratview, Meticulous). Adding eHouses, UPS, transformers and power-as-a-service makes the DC electrical chain a multi-$10B pool. The end-state is large, but climbing to rung 4 (own breakers and relays) means competing head-on with Eaton/Schneider/ABB/Siemens on century-old certified component lines. Credible end to end only on a 10+ year horizon with billions of capital.
scored.killer: Breaker supply allocation. The switchboard is basically an enclosure plus bus around Eaton/Schneider/ABB/Siemens breakers, and those majors allocate scarce breakers to their own assembly lines first. A shop whose pitch is 'beat the majors' lead time' depends on them for its critical-path parts, and LS/Hyundai alternatives carry spec-acceptance friction with engineers of record. The other killers are working capital and bonding for multi-million-dollar lineups, an AI DC capex downturn (the lead-time wedge closes once major capacity expansions land around 2027-28), and Giga Energy already running the same playbook. The ML layer (spec-to-BOM configurator) is a cost saver but not a moat: engineering is a small share of COGS next to breakers and copper, and the parser data does not compound into anything a competitor cannot copy.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is real, sellable and supply-short, but Giga Energy already holds this exact ladder, breakers come from the competitors, working capital pushes past seed, and the software is a margin helper rather than a compounding moat: about 17/30.

scored.name: Acceptance (NETA testing crews climbing to substation-as-a-service for data centres)
scored.industry: Energy / electrical infrastructure
scored.rung_one: A NETA-accredited acceptance and maintenance testing company (relay testing, breaker timing, transformer turns ratio, cable VLF, IR thermography) with owned test sets and crews, sold to EPCs and hyperscale/colo developers at $150k-1.5M per electrical-room or substation commissioning package, plus recurring NFPA 70B maintenance contracts. Incumbents: Shermco (Gryphon), IPS, RESA Power, Hampton Tedder and Vertiv/Schneider service arms, PE roll-ups with no software compounding; the rung is crowded.
scored.ladder: 1) Commissioning and maintenance testing crews. 2) Engineering studies (arc flash, coordination, power quality) from data crews already capture. 3) Owned spare-gear depot and emergency repair (breakers, switchgear refurb, mobile substations). 4) Design-build-own customer substations and MV yards behind the meter as interconnection or power-as-a-service. 5) Own and operate behind-the-meter power islands (storage plus switchgear) under long-term contracts.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: auto-generated NETA reports from instrument logs (halving paperwork) and anomaly detection across every test, forming a cross-OEM gear-failure dataset. Rung 2: models calibrated on the field corpus make studies near-free. Rung 3: failure predictions decide spare stocking and price emergency SLAs. Rung 4: design reuse and a reliability model underwrite uptime guarantees. Rung 5: fleet-level dispatch and maintenance optimisation.
scored.seed_plan: Hire or acquire-hire two NETA Level 4 leads, buy about $600k of test sets, target data-centre commissioning in one hub (Dallas, Columbus or Phoenix) where crews are booked out; $2-3M seed covers 3 crews, with $4-6M year-1 revenue. Kills: labour scarcity, DC capex cycle, concentration on 2-3 hyperscalers. Rubric estimate 22/30: L1 5, L2 5, L3 3, L4 4, L5 2, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Commissioning packages of $150k-1.5M per electrical room or substation are plausible but are the candidate's own figure, not verified. ESTIMATES: a NETA crew bills about $150-250/hr per tech, so a 3-4 person crew brings in about $1.2-2M a year. With 3 crews, year-1 revenue is $4-6M at 25-35% gross margin (normal for field services; EBITDA 10-18%). A full set of test equipment (relay test set, breaker analyser, TTR, VLF, Megger, thermal camera) costs about $400-700k for 3 crews, so the $600k figure holds. The real constraint is NETA Level 3/4 technicians: scarce, $120-180k fully loaded, and poached constantly. The $2-3M seed covers about 12 months of payroll float, because EPC payment terms run 60-90 days, so working capital eats much of the seed. For scale, Shermco sold to Blackstone for about $1.6B (Aug 2025) with 600+ NETA techs, 200 engineers and 40 service centres. That is about $2.7M of enterprise value per tech, so rung one exits at services multiples (roughly 1.5-2.5x revenue).
scored.buyers: EPCs and electrical contractors (Rosendin, Cupertino Electric, MMR, Faith Technologies), hyperscale and colo developers (Microsoft, Meta, AWS, QTS, Vantage, Aligned, CyrusOne), and commissioning agents who subcontract the testing. They have plenty of capital and pay quickly enough at commissioning, but few buyers dominate each hub. Recurring NFPA 70B maintenance goes to facility operators. Exit buyers are PE platforms (Blackstone/Shermco, Kohlberg/RESA) or strategics (Vertiv, Schneider, Eaton services).
scored.incumbents: Shermco: Blackstone is acquiring it from Gryphon for about $1.6B (announced Aug 2025), with 600+ NETA techs and 40 service centres, and it is headquartered in Dallas, one of the target hubs. RESA Power: Investcorp bought it in 2021, Kohlberg took a majority stake in Apr 2025, and it keeps rolling up NETA firms (HEET, HVES, PTS in 2024; 3MD Power and SGE in Jan 2026). Also IPS (Integrated Power Services, PE-backed), Hampton Tedder, Vertiv, Schneider Electric Services, Eaton EESS, ABB, Siemens field services, and hundreds of regional NETA firms. Software for the paperwork layer already exists in Megger PowerDB, Doble and commissioning tools (CxPlanner, Bluerithm, Facility Grid). Rung five has its own capitalised players: VoltaGrid raised $1B from Blackstone and Halliburton (May 2026, 7.5 GW order book), plus Bloom, Enchanted Rock and others. No venture-backed software-first NETA testing company was found. That is open space, but it is open mostly because PE roll-ups already win this rung on labour and footprint.
scored.end_state: The revenue pool is large but split across separate markets that do not compound into one another. Data-centre commissioning and testing services are about $2.2B (2025), possibly about $10B by 2035 (Astute Analytica, a single analyst estimate). US electrical testing and maintenance services overall are an ESTIMATED $8-15B. Switchgear and substation design-build and behind-the-meter power for data centres reach $10s of billions (ESTIMATE, from roughly $300B+ a year of data-centre capex, of which 10-15% is electrical). Rungs 4-5 (owning substations and power islands under contract) are infrastructure-finance businesses needing $100M-$1B+ of project capital (compare VoltaGrid's $1B). Testing-crew data barely lowers that capital cost, so the path from end to end is not credible.
scored.killer: The rung is crowded and decided by labour. Blackstone's Shermco and Kohlberg's RESA have deep technician benches, nationwide footprints and existing EPC master service agreements, and they are buying regional NETA shops right now, so they will outbid a seed startup for Level 3/4 techs. The software layer is weak. NETA report automation already exists (PowerDB, Doble), so it is a feature, not a moat. Acceptance tests on new gear mostly pass, so the failure dataset is thin and spread across OEMs. ML does not make the next rung cheaper in a way that matters, because rungs 4-5 are limited by capital and interconnection, not by data. Other risks are the data-centre capex cycle and concentration on 2-3 hyperscalers or EPCs per hub. In practice this is a services roll-up that would exit to PE at services multiples, not an ML company.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one wins revenue and sells easily, but Blackstone's $1.6B Shermco and Kohlberg's RESA are already rolling it up, the software is thin, existing report-automation tools cover it, and the upper rungs are capex-heavy infrastructure that testing data does not unlock. It scores 17/30, not the claimed 22.

scored.name: Quiet Fleet (zero-emission temporary power rental fleet)
scored.industry: Energy storage / machines: mobile battery-generator rental
scored.rung_one: An owned fleet of 20-40 trailer-mounted batteries (250 kWh-2 MWh, built from bought LFP and power conversion) rented instead of diesel gensets to film/TV productions, festivals, construction sites under noise and emissions rules (California, NYC, London, Netherlands) and utility crews, at $1.5-6k per unit per week; a well-utilised $150-400k unit pays back in 2-3 years. Incumbents: Aggreko, Sunbelt and United Rentals (small battery lines), Moxion (bankrupt 2024), Power Edison, Volta Energy, Polarium.
scored.ladder: 1) Rental fleet in one metro. 2) Multi-metro power-as-a-service contracts with GCs and studios. 3) Idle units aggregated as a VPP (CAISO DSGS, NYISO, ERCOT ERS) and leased to utilities for PSPS and disaster response. 4) In-house trailer design and build line sold to rental majors. 5) Charging-as-a-service and permanent microgrids at served sites. 6) Firm-power company for temporary-to-permanent construction and industrial energy.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: telemetry load profiling right-sizes each rental, and route and swap optimisation cuts truck rolls. Rung 2: demand forecasting by job type for pricing and positioning. Rung 3: aggregation and bidding on real fleet availability. Rung 4: field load and degradation data drive hardware revisions. Rung 5: site load histories size permanent systems.
scored.seed_plan: About $2M on 8-12 units built from integrator cabinets plus custom trailers, launched in LA with productions; cash-flow positive per unit inside 12 months. Kills: utilisation risk, per-unit capex, rental majors copying. Self-score about 21/30: L1 5, L2 5, L3 3, L4 3, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Real price point: a 30-40 kVA / 60 kWh trailer battery rents for $377 a day, $1,234 a week or $3,011 for four weeks (Whiting-Turner equipment hub). That is about $20 per kWh per week, falling to about $12.5 per kWh per week on monthly terms. Monthly terms are the norm on construction jobs. At those rates a 250 kWh unit brings in about $3-5k a week at list price. Build cost (my estimate): about $150-250 per kWh for LFP cabinets plus a PCS, plus $30-60k for the trailer, enclosure, telematics and certification. That puts a 250 kWh unit at roughly $90-120k and a 1 MWh unit at roughly $250-350k, in line with the candidate's figure. At a realistic 40-55% time utilisation (rental industry norm, estimate), payback is about 2.5-4 years. That is before delivery trucks, recharge logistics (most units need a generator or grid top-up on site, which erodes the 'zero-emission' pitch) and battery degradation. A $2M seed buys about 10-15 units, or about $1.5-2.5M a year of revenue at full use. It is cash-flow positive per unit, but the company only grows by raising asset-backed debt. Gross margin before overhead is likely 45-60% (estimate). It is a sound small rental business, not a venture-scale margin structure.
scored.buyers: The rung-one buyers are renters rather than acquirers. They are film/TV productions (LA, NYC, London), festivals, general contractors under jobsite emissions rules (e.g. Turner, Swinerton, Webcor and DPR all piloted Moxion units), utilities (PSPS and storm response) and telecom. A fleet that is used well is a sellable asset: rental majors (United Rentals, Sunbelt, Herc, Aggreko) buy regional fleets as tuck-ins, so there is an exit floor. Buyers of the later rungs (in-house trailer line, VPP) are the same rental majors, who already source from OEMs.
scored.incumbents: The rung is crowded. Moxion Power raised more than $110M, including a $100M Series B in 2022 with Sunbelt as an investor and buyer, then went into Chapter 7 in July 2024. Anode Technology was started by Moxion's founders Huelskamp and Hanson and came out of stealth in Sept 2025 with a $9M seed led by Eclipse; it does mobile BESS plus charging-as-a-service for construction, events, data centers and EV fleets. That is almost exactly this ladder, already funded. Ampd Energy (about $43.4M raised, aggregator figure; Ampd Silo) has a reported 2026 distribution deal with United Rentals (unverified). Other players: Aggreko (battery and hybrid fleet), Atlas Copco ZenergiZe, Sunbelt, United Rentals, Herc, Power Edison (utility mobile storage), and EU players Polarium and Pramac.
scored.end_state: Temporary power rental is about $6-14B globally in 2025, depending on the definition. MarketsandMarkets puts the power rental market at $11.44B in 2025, growing to $15.05B by 2030 at a 5.6% CAGR, with North America the largest region. Market Intelo gives $14.2B in 2025, rising to $27.1B by 2034. The battery share is a fraction of that today. 'Firm power for temporary-to-permanent construction and industrial energy' would be multi-$10B only if it grows into distributed energy and microgrids generally. That is a different and crowded business, and the path to it is not credible from a rental fleet. A realistic end state is a $1-3B-revenue specialty rental company.
scored.killer: Capex and utilisation. Every dollar of growth is a balance-sheet dollar, and seasonal or lumpy demand (film strikes, construction cycles) leaves assets idle. Moxion's $110M Chapter 7 is the reference failure. Other threats: rental majors with cheaper capital and existing customer relationships can buy the same LFP cabinets from Ampd, Atlas Copco and others and price below a startup. Anode, run by the same founders with Eclipse money, is already climbing this exact ladder. Battery hardware is commoditising, so there is no defensible product. Recharge logistics often reintroduce a diesel genset. VPP revenue on mobile, often-deployed units is small and unreliable.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but capital-hungry rental business: the rung is winnable and sellable, but it is crowded (Anode, Ampd, Aggreko, Atlas Copco, the rental majors), the software layer is commodity telematics rather than compounding ML, and Moxion's $110M collapse shows the capex and utilisation killer. About 17/30.

scored.name: Fieldmark (field-evaluation body to NRTL for chargers, robots and power gear)
scored.industry: Deeptech / product safety certification (TIC)
scored.rung_one: An IAS-accredited Field Evaluation Body with owned accreditation, inspectors and a bench lab, applying field labels to unlisted or modified electrical equipment (custom switchgear, imported EV chargers, robot cells, BESS skids, data-centre power gear) so AHJs pass it, at $3-20k per unit or site. Incumbents: UL, Intertek, CSA, TUV SUD, QPS, Eurofins MET, with weeks-long turnaround.
scored.ladder: 1) Field-evaluation body. 2) OSHA NRTL recognition for listing and recurring factory inspections. 3) Own test lab for EVSE, robotics safety (ISO 10218/UL 3300) and power electronics. 4) International schemes (CB/IECEE, UKCA, CE notified body). 5) Field monitoring and recall management. Electrical product safety is a multi-$10B slice of a roughly $250B TIC market.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: a standards graph (UL/IEC/NEC clauses linked to component data) auto-drafts evaluation plans from BOMs and photos, cutting inspector hours about 50%. Rung 2: every listing adds labelled pass/fail evidence, improving pre-compliance predictions sold as a design-time funnel. Rung 3: test data trains predictors that skip redundant tests. Rung 4: one dossier mapped across schemes. Rung 5: field-failure data feeds the standards graph.
scored.seed_plan: Hire 2-3 ex-UL/Intertek engineers, get IAS accreditation (6-12 months, under $500k), sell field labelling to EV-charger importers and data-centre power integrators facing AHJ red tags; $2-4M revenue in year 2. Kills: NRTL recognition taking 1-3 years and independence rules limiting moves into making products. Est. 21/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 2, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: ALL ESTIMATES. The web search budget ran out before any query returned, so these figures come from prior knowledge and none are freshly sourced. Unit price: one field evaluation typically costs about $2.5-10k for a single unit (an EV charger or a panel), and $15-30k+ for a multi-unit site, a BESS skid or a robot cell, plus inspector travel. That is consistent with the candidate's $3-20k. Cost: the work is mostly senior inspector hours (loaded cost about $150-250k a year per engineer) plus travel. Gross margin is probably 40-55%, like other TIC field services. Capital: IAS accreditation (IAS AC354/ISO 17020 or 17065) costs well under $500k including staff and quality system, so seed money can cover it. A bench lab for EVSE and power electronics adds roughly $0.5-2M. NRTL recognition (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.7) takes 1-3 years. Revenue per inspector is maybe $300-600k a year, so $2-4M in year 2 needs about 6-10 billable inspectors. That is a services business that scales roughly with headcount. The ML saving (about 50% fewer drafting hours) cuts cost but does not change the slope: the label still has to be signed by a person who carries liability.
scored.buyers: Importers and distributors of EV chargers that are not UL-listed, often Chinese or EU units. Data-centre power integrators and custom switchgear/PDU shops. BESS integrators facing AHJ red tags, and robot-cell and machine integrators (NFPA 79). Owners or contractors who need a certificate of occupancy. The pain is real, and the buyers are capitalised but fragmented. Demand is lumpy and project-driven. AHJ acceptance of a new field evaluation body (FEB) is decided by each jurisdiction separately.
scored.incumbents: These are estimates from prior knowledge, not checked in this run. UL Solutions is public, with about $2.9B revenue in 2024. Intertek (about GBP 3.4B), CSA Group, TUV SUD, TUV Rheinland, SGS and Bureau Veritas all run field-labelling programmes. Field-evaluation specialists include QPS Evaluation Services, Eurofins MET Labs, Field Evaluation Services and many small IAS-accredited FEBs. OSHA's list has about 20 NRTLs, including smaller ones such as ETL (Intertek), NTS, TUV America, SGS North America and Element. I know of no venture-funded operator taking this rung. Funded startups in this space sell compliance software rather than accredited labelling. The rung is fragmented, but plenty of capable players already hold it.
scored.end_state: ESTIMATE. The whole TIC market is roughly $250B (common industry figure, about EUR 230-250B). Electrical and electronic product safety testing and certification is perhaps $15-25B of that. The end-to-end chain (FEB, NRTL, lab, CB/notified body, post-market surveillance) is still a TIC services chain. There is no vertical integration into making or running the physical product, because independence rules (ISO 17065 impartiality, OSHA NRTL independence) forbid it. The pool is large enough, but each step up is slow, needs accreditation, and moves revenue roughly with headcount.
scored.killer: The moat is accreditation and execution, not ML. The standards are public, inspectors can move to competitors, and the label's value comes from signed liability and AHJ trust that the incumbents built over decades. NRTL recognition takes 1-3 years and is gated by OSHA. Independence rules block integration into products. Product-liability and E&O exposure from a failed charger or BESS is serious. Gross margins look like services, and incumbents can simply speed up turnaround. Regulatory change is a risk too: UL 2594/2202 listings becoming common, or chargers shipping already listed, would shrink the field-label market.
scored.one_line_reason: The pain is real and rung one is cheap to win, but this is a headcount-bound, liability-bearing TIC services roll-up. Independence rules block real vertical integration, and the ML layer only cuts costs. The rung is crowded with UL, Intertek, CSA, TUV, QPS, MET and dozens of small FEBs, so it reads as an execution-moat services business rather than a compounding ML ladder (17/30 against the self-scored 21).
