scored.name: Halcyon Motor Works (NDAA-compliant drone propulsion line)
scored.industry: Sovereign defense manufacturing / machines (brushless motors, ESCs, magnets)
scored.rung_one: An owned US/allied cell making Blue-UAS/NDAA-compliant brushless outrunner motors and matched ESCs for Group 1-2 drones at about $60-400 per motor, 10-50k units a year to start, sold to US and European drone OEMs (Neros, Skydio, Teal/Red Cat, Performance Drone Works, Auterion partners, Quantum, Tekever, Ukrainian and Taiwanese NATO suppliers) that depend on T-Motor and other Chinese suppliers excluded by NDAA 848 and FY25 bans. Competition: ePropelled, KDE Direct, Orbital/Unusual Machines, OEMs in-house; contested but fragmented and capacity-starved.
scored.ladder: 1) Motor assembly from imported compliant magnets and laminations. 2) ESC and flight-power electronics sold as a propulsion module. 3) In-house lamination stamping and winding automation. 4) Owned NdFeB or ferrite/MnBi magnet line. 5) Group 3 and loitering-munition propulsion, then actuators for robotics and humanoids.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: end-of-line dyno logging thrust, efficiency and thermal curves for every unit, building a performance-vs-design-vs-process dataset. Rung 2: ESC firmware auto-tuned per airframe from field flight logs. Rung 3: ML surrogate EM-plus-thermal motor design trained on the proprietary test corpus, cutting design cycles from months to days. Rung 4: magnet-process quality prediction.
scored.seed_plan: About $2.5M: lease a 15k sq ft unit, buy semi-automatic winding, balancing and dyno equipment ($1.2M), source compliant magnets from Japan, Korea or Vietnam, get two OEM design-wins on 2-3 SKUs by month 9 matching T-Motor at 1.5-2x price; target $3-8M revenue in 18 months. Kills: OEM vertical integration and price pressure if bans soften. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 5, L2 4, L3 3, L4 4, L5 2, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: ALL NUMBERS ARE ESTIMATES FROM PRIOR KNOWLEDGE; the shared web-search budget was used up, so no live figures were checked this round. Unit price: Group 1 FPV and quad motors from T-Motor or similar cost about $20-60 retail. NDAA-compliant US equivalents (KDE Direct, Lumenier/Unusual Machines) list at about $80-250. Group 2 motors run $150-600. The candidate's $60-400 ASP is plausible. COGS for an assembly-only cell using imported Japanese or Korean NdFeB magnets and laminations: magnets and copper are about 30-45% of COGS, and compliant magnets cost 1.5-3x Chinese ones. At 10-50k units, gross margin is likely 25-40%, not the software-like 50%+. Revenue math: 30k units x ~$150 ASP is about $4.5M per year, so $3-8M in 18 months needs about 2 design wins of real volume. Capital: about $1-1.5M for winding, balancing, dyno and test equipment plus a lease is realistic, so rung one fits a $2.5M seed. The binding constraint is OEM qualification time (6-12 months per SKU), not capex. Volume risk is high: one FPV/attritable program such as Neros Archer (thousands per month) can be the whole business, or none of it.
scored.buyers: US drone OEMs: Neros, Skydio, Red Cat/Teal, Performance Drone Works, ModalAI-based integrators, Anduril (small UAS and loitering munitions), AeroVironment (Switchblade), Shield AI. European and Ukrainian suppliers: Tekever, Quantum Systems, Helsing (HX-2), Auterion partners. Demand drivers are FY25 NDAA Sec. 848 and the follow-on bans on Chinese components, the June 2025 'Unleashing American Drone Dominance' EO, and FY26 small-UAS procurement (Army's goal of about 1M drones and the Replicator/Drone Dominance funds). Buyers are well capitalised, but they are prime-driven and lumpy.
scored.incumbents: From prior knowledge, not re-verified. Unusual Machines (NYSE: UMAC) owns Fat Shark/Lumenier and raised tens of millions in 2025 (about $40M+ through several offerings) to build an Orlando NDAA motor factory explicitly aimed at this rung. KDE Direct (Oregon) is an established US maker of compliant motors and ESCs. ePropelled (NH) does UAS propulsion and power systems, with DoD contracts. Vertiq (NC) makes integrated motor+ESC modules and is VC-backed. Neros (about $75M+ raised, Series B 2025) builds motors in-house for Archer. Orqa (Croatia) does in-house FPV motors and electronics for the EU/Ukraine. Ukrainian domestic motor makers are scaling with state support. ModalAI and ARK Electronics cover ESC/flight power. Magnet rung: MP Materials (DoD equity and offtake deal, July 2025, 10X magnet plant), Vulcan Elements ($65M raise plus about $620M DoD loan, late 2025), Noveon, USA Rare Earth, Niron (iron nitride). So rungs 1 and 4 are both being funded heavily.
scored.end_state: Estimate. Small-UAS propulsion (motors + ESCs) for Group 1-3 is probably about $1-3B a year globally by 2030, assuming 10M+ attritable drones a year at $50-300 of propulsion content each, and it is very volume-sensitive to the war in Ukraine. The adjacent chain is larger. NdFeB magnets are about $15-20B a year globally. Electric motors for robotics and humanoid actuators are a multi-$10B projection, but owned by Harmonic Drive, Nidec, Maxon, Kollmorgen and Tesla/Figure in-house. Full chain from magnet to motor to actuator clears $10B+ only if it reaches robotics/industrial actuators, where Halcyon has no edge. End-to-end execution needs a rare-earth magnet plant ($100M-1B, which is the MP/Vulcan scale), so the path is not credible for a seed-stage team.
scored.killer: 1) OEM vertical integration: Neros, Orqa and the Ukrainian producers already wind their own motors, because motor assembly is low-barrier, so the best-volume customers make rung one themselves. 2) Unusual Machines is publicly funded, building the same factory, and politically connected. 3) Magnet dependency: 'compliant' magnets and laminations still trace to Chinese rare-earth supply, and rung 4 needs a $100M+ plant against DoD-backed MP/Vulcan. 4) Demand is lumpy and concentrated in a few programs, and it is exposed to ceasefires or softer bans. 5) The software layer is weak. Motor EM and thermal design is mature (Motor-CAD, JMAG, Ansys), dyno data gives a modest process-QC advantage rather than a flywheel, and ESC auto-tuning is commoditised in open firmware (AM32, BLHeli, PX4).
scored.one_line_reason: A real, winnable and sellable rung riding the NDAA tailwind, but it is low-barrier hardware assembly where the best customers integrate in-house and UMAC/KDE/Vertiq are already funded. The ML layer is a QC nicety rather than a compounding moat, and the magnet rung is owned by DoD-backed giants. About 17/30, below the candidate's own 21.

scored.name: Continuum Energetics (continuous-flow energetic materials line)
scored.industry: Sovereign defense manufacturing / deeptech chemistry (explosives, propellant ingredients)
scored.rung_one: An owned small-footprint continuous-flow (microreactor) line for one bottlenecked energetic or precursor (NTO, TATB, HMX/RDX substitutes, nitrocellulose-free binders) at 20-200 tonnes a year and $50-400/kg, sold to DoD (Army JPEO A&A, Navy), primes (Northrop, L3Harris/Aerojet, GD-OTS, Nammo) and SRM startups (X-Bow, Ursa Major, Anduril) facing single-source Holston/Radford supply. Incumbents: BAE Holston and Radford (GOCO), Nammo, Chemring, Firehawk, Repkon USA, X-Bow in-house; few in flow-chemistry ingredients, so partly open.
scored.ladder: 1) One molecule from one licensed site. 2) Second and third molecules on the same modular platform plus qualification packages. 3) Load, assemble and pack of warheads and motor grain casting. 4) Full energetics-to-round or energetics-to-motor production for loitering munitions and interceptors. 5) Replicated sovereign plants for allies (Europe, AUKUS, Japan) on licence.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: closed-loop process control and ML yield/safety models on inline PAT spectroscopy, raising yield and shortening qualification. Rung 2: Bayesian/active-learning reaction optimisation where each molecule's data cuts the next molecule's development. Rung 3: CV on CT/X-ray for loaded-item and grain defects. Rung 4: digital lot genealogy. Replicated plants ship with trained models.
scored.seed_plan: Pick one molecule with documented sole-source or foreign-only supply, prove a bench flow route at 1-5 kg/day in 9 months in a licensed lab or university partner (Purdue, NMT/EMRTC, Picatinny), win a DPA Title III / IBAS or Army ManTech award ($2-10M non-dilutive) plus a prime offtake LOI; $3M seed covers team, lab and pilot skid. Kills: ATF and DoD siting and licensing timelines, 2-4 year qualification, single government buyer. Rubric estimate about 19/30: L1 3, L2 3, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: ALL ESTIMATES. The shared web-search budget was already used up when this agent ran, so none of these numbers were checked live; they come from prior knowledge and need verifying before use. Unit price: the candidate's own $50-400/kg range. HMX/RDX-class and IM ingredients (NTO, DNAN) run roughly $50-250/kg (est.); TATB can be higher. Revenue: 50 t/yr at $150/kg is about $7.5M/yr; 200 t/yr at $200/kg is about $40M/yr (est.). Gross margin: maybe 30-50% once qualified, if continuous flow really cuts labour and solvent cost; nothing is proven at tonnage (est.). Capital: a bench and pilot skid of 1-5 kg/day fits in $1-3M. A production line at 20-200 t/yr on an explosives-sited facility (ATF manufacturer licence, DoD 6055.09 quantity-distance siting, magazines, PSM/OSHA 1910.119) is more like $15-60M (est.), so it needs DPA Title III / IBAS / OSC money or a prime to pay for it. Time to first production revenue: 3-5 years, because qualification under NAVSEA/Army IM and lot acceptance takes 2-4 years. Before that, revenue is SBIR/OTA R&D ($0.25-2M per award, est.). Technical risk: microreactors handle liquid-phase nitrations well, but HMX, TATB and NTO crystallise as solids and need crystal morphology and particle-size control. That makes it hard to scale microflow to hundreds of tonnes, and is why the incumbents still use batch or semi-continuous processes.
scored.buyers: Army JPEO Armaments & Ammunition and the Army Contracting Command at Picatinny/Rock Island. Navy (NSWC Indian Head, NAVSEA). Missile primes and motor makers: Northrop Grumman, L3Harris/Aerojet Rocketdyne, General Dynamics OTS, Nammo, Rheinmetall. New solid-rocket-motor and munitions entrants (X-Bow, Ursa Major, Anduril). Allied MoDs later. The buyer is well funded, but in practice there is one demand signal, the DoD budget, and buyers only purchase qualified lots.
scored.incumbents: From prior knowledge, not checked live (search budget exhausted); funding figures are approximate. GOCO incumbents: BAE Systems runs Holston AAP (RDX/HMX, IMX) and Radford AAP (nitrocellulose, propellants), with multi-billion-dollar Army modernisation money behind them. Chemring (US: Chemring Energetic Devices, Ensign-Bickford), Nammo, Northrop Grumman (Allegany Ballistics Lab, captive energetics), GD-OTS, Rheinmetall/American Rheinmetall. Repkon USA has an Army award of roughly $435M for a TNT plant in Kentucky (approx., memory). Funded startups: Firehawk Aerospace (energetics and motors, roughly $60M Series C in 2025, approx.), X-Bow Systems (SRMs and in-house energetics, Series B around $70M plus Army and Navy contracts, approx.), Ursa Major (over $100M raised, approx.), and Anduril (in-house SRM production, multi-billion-dollar balance sheet). Few of these do continuous-flow ingredient chemistry specifically, so a molecule niche is still open, but defense hard-tech capital is now crowding the space.
scored.end_state: ESTIMATES. US DoD munitions and missile procurement is roughly $30-40B/yr after FY24-26 replenishment (est.). The global military ammunition and energetics market is roughly $25-35B/yr, and the wider missile market is much larger. Energetics-to-round and energetics-to-motor is a multi-$10B pool, and allies (EU ASAP, AUKUS) want sovereign capacity. The path to doing it end to end exists in principle; Anduril and Nammo are vertically integrated examples. But each rung needs its own sited, licensed and qualified facility, so climbing the ladder is capex-gated, not software-gated.
scored.killer: Time to qualification and the capex wall. Rung one does not earn production revenue for 3-5 years, and the line costs $15-60M on explosives-sited land. On top of that: a single sovereign buyer, budget whiplash once the replenishment cycle ends, fierce competition for the same OSC/IBAS money from Firehawk, X-Bow, Anduril and Repkon, the safety-incident tail risk, and the fact that solids-forming energetics resist microreactor scale-up. Software is real at rung two (reaction optimisation), but it does not shorten the qualification clock, and that clock is what decides who wins.
scored.one_line_reason: Real sovereign bottleneck and big end-state, but rung one is a 3-5 year, $15-60M qualified-plant problem with one buyer and a crowding field, so ML is a nice-to-have rather than the moat; about 17/30.

scored.name: Fouling Rights (licensed robotic hull-cleaning concessions turning into fleet-performance contracts)
scored.industry: Robotics / maritime energy efficiency (shipping fuel, about $150B+ a year)
scored.rung_one: An approved in-water cleaning permit plus a robot fleet with capture and treatment at 1-3 ports where capture-of-debris cleaning is mandatory or newly allowed (Singapore MPA, Australia/NZ biosecurity, US West Coast, Rotterdam). Ship operators and charterers (Maersk, MSC, bulk pools) pay about $15-40k per clean; clean hulls save 5-15% fuel ($0.5-1.5M a year per large vessel) and help CII/FuelEU compliance. Scarce permits make the rung defensible. Competitors: Hullbot (A$16M Series A Nov 2025), HullWiper, Jotun HullSkater, Fleet Cleaner, Neptune Robotics and SEAHI (Singapore MPA trial winners April 2026), diver companies; competitive in Singapore, thin at many ports.
scored.ladder: 1) Port concession and per-clean jobs. 2) Multi-port network with proactive in-voyage or anchorage grooming. 3) Fleet-performance contracts paid as a share of fuel saved, plus inspection-class reports replacing diver surveys. 4) Combined coating-and-cleaning package with robot-friendly foul-release coatings. 5) Hull, propeller and energy-saving retrofit EPC. 6) Owning or chartering efficiency-optimised tonnage selling verified low-carbon freight.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: vision SLAM hull mapping and fouling segmentation feeding compliance logs. Rung 2: a fouling-growth model (water temperature, salinity, idle days, AIS route, coating) predicting when each ship needs cleaning and booking robots ahead. Rung 3: speed-power regression on noon reports and AIS attributing billable fuel savings. Rung 4: independent coating-performance data across thousands of hull-cycles. Rung 5: retrofit ROI models.
scored.seed_plan: Pick one jurisdiction with mandatory biofouling rules and few approved operators (Australia/NZ, or Singapore's post-trial framework); spend $1.5M on 3-4 robots built on modified commercial ROV crawlers with capture and filtration and $1M on permit approval and the first hub; sign 2-3 charter pools on per-clean contracts. Kills: per-clean price competition, permit politics, shipping cycles. Scores 23/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 5, L4 4, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Live web searches were not available for this call: the workflow's shared search budget was already used up, so every number here is an ESTIMATE from prior knowledge and none was checked against a source. Price per clean: about $10-40k for a large vessel, depending on hull area and whether debris is captured. Diver and robot cleans in competitive ports sit at the low end; in Australia/NZ and Singapore, where capture is mandatory, they sit higher (ESTIMATE). Cost per clean: a 3-5 person crew, a support boat or barge, filtration and waste disposal come to about $4-10k, which gives a 40-60% gross margin per job once robots are utilised (ESTIMATE). Capital: a capture-capable robot built on a modified ROV/crawler costs about $250-600k with its filtration skid; a port hub with a boat costs about $0.5-1M. The bigger cost is time and money on approval: biofouling and effluent testing (for example Australia's DAFF/state EPA approvals, NZ MPI, Singapore MPA's post-trial accreditation) can take 12-24 months and $0.3-1M (ESTIMATE). Revenue per port: about 150-400 cleans a year at a busy hub gives $3-10M a year (ESTIMATE). Fuel saving: the 5-15% figure is real for a badly fouled hull versus a clean one, but on a well-coated ship the marginal saving per extra clean is closer to 2-5%.
scored.buyers: Ship managers and technical superintendents (V.Ships, Anglo-Eastern, Synergy, Wilhelmsen), container lines (Maersk, MSC, CMA CGM, Hapag-Lloyd), bulk and tanker pools, and time charterers who pay for fuel. Charterers capture the fuel saving, but owners pay for hull care: the split-incentive problem. These buyers are well capitalised but buy hull cleaning as a commodity port service through agents (GAC, Wilhelmsen Ships Service, Inchcape), mostly on price and availability.
scored.incumbents: All from prior knowledge; none of the funding figures were checked in this pass. Neptune Robotics (Hong Kong): large Series B in 2025 of roughly US$50M, an ESTIMATE; Singapore MPA trial winner; operating in several Asian ports. Hullbot (Australia): A$16M Series A, Nov 2025, per the brief. HullWiper (UAE, GAC-linked): diver-free capture cleaning in dozens of ports. ECOsubsea (Norway): approved in multiple EU ports. Fleet Cleaner (Netherlands): Rotterdam and the Netherlands. Jotun HullSkater: an onboard robot sold with Jotun's coating as its Hull Skating Solutions offer, backed by a multi-billion-dollar coatings major. Also SEAHI (MPA trial), C-Leanship (Denmark), Shipshave (Norway, crew-operated ITCH), SeaRobotics/Armach, Notilo Plus (inspection), and diver majors (Subsea Global Solutions, Franmarine in Australia). Rung one is crowded in exactly the ports the brief targets, and coating majors (Jotun, Hempel, AkzoNobel International, PPG, Chugoku) already bundle coating with cleaning and fuel-saving guarantees.
scored.end_state: Shipping fuel spend is about $150-200B a year (ESTIMATE; about 300 Mt of fuel at roughly $550-650/t). Hull and propeller performance: hull fouling is often cited as adding about 5-10% to fleet fuel, a value pool of roughly $10-20B a year. The services actually bought are much smaller. In-water cleaning and inspection is roughly $1-3B a year (ESTIMATE). Marine coatings are about $4-5B a year in newbuild plus drydock (ESTIMATE), held by a Jotun/Hempel/AkzoNobel/PPG/Chugoku oligopoly. Energy-saving retrofit EPC is about $2-5B (ESTIMATE). Rung 6, owning or chartering efficient tonnage, is the multi-$100B freight market, but it is a capital-heavy commodity business where software gives little edge. Doing the chain end to end means taking on the coating oligopoly and becoming a shipowner, which is not a credible path for this company.
scored.killer: 1) Commodity per-clean pricing in a crowded field (well-funded Neptune, HullWiper, ECOsubsea, Hullbot, plus divers), with agents choosing on price. 2) Coating majors bundling (Jotun HullSkater plus hull-performance guarantees) and onboard crew-run robots (Shipshave, HullSkater) take the job out of the port-service model entirely. 3) Permit politics: approvals are port by port, slow and revocable, and can be granted to many operators, so scarcity is not durable. 4) Split incentives and the shipping cycle cap fuel-share contracts. Weather routing and performance software (ZeroNorth, DeepSea, Kongsberg, Danelec/StormGeo) already does the speed-power attribution, and the counterparty to a shared-savings deal can read the result off its own noon reports.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is real and sellable but already crowded in exactly the target ports. The software layer (fouling prediction, speed-power attribution) is already sold by performance-software firms. The upper rungs run into a coatings oligopoly and capital-heavy shipowning, so this is about 17/30 rather than the brief's 23.
sources: No web sources: WebSearch was blocked because the workflow's shared per-turn search budget (200 calls) was already used up. All figures are estimates from prior knowledge and should be checked.
Brief-supplied: Hullbot A$16M Series A (Nov 2025); Neptune Robotics and SEAHI as Singapore MPA trial winners (Apr 2026)

To verify: Neptune Robotics 2025 Series B size; Singapore MPA in-water cleaning approved-operator list; Australian DAFF anti-fouling and in-water cleaning guidelines; Jotun Hull Skating Solutions pricing; IMO 2023 biofouling guidelines

scored.name: Rewind Transformer Works (data-graded distribution and pad-mount transformer remanufacturing)
scored.industry: Grid / power: distribution, pad-mount and small substation transformers
scored.rung_one: One owned remanufacturing plant (leased 20-60k sq ft in Texas, the Southeast or the Midwest, with a vacuum oven, winding machines, robotic winding/blast/paint cells, oil processing and a test bay). It buys retired, failed or surplus pole, pad-mount and small substation transformers (25 kVA to about 30 MVA, core focus 25-2,500 kVA) from utilities, co-ops, demolition contractors, recyclers and surplus auctions at scrap-plus prices. Units are graded, rewound or re-cored, re-tanked, retested to IEEE C57 and DOE 2027 efficiency, and sold with warranty to solar/BESS/EV-charging EPCs, data-center builders, co-ops, munis and industrials. Prices run $8k-60k for distribution units and up to $1.5M for larger units, 10-50% below new, with delivery in 1-12 weeks against 60-120 weeks (2-4 years) for new. Gross margin 40-55%; one plant at 1,500-3,000 units a year is about $40-90M revenue at maturity. Incumbents are fragmented regional shops and resellers: Maddox (PE-backed), T&R Electric, Solomon/Sunbelt Solomon, ELSCO, Virginia Transformer service arms, Pacific Crest. None is robotic or data-led.
scored.ladder: 1) Remanufacture and resell distribution units. 2) Take-back and fleet-swap contracts with utilities (owning reverse-logistics core supply), plus a leasing and spares-as-a-service pool with guaranteed 72-hour swap. 3) Build-to-stock hybrid units (new windings on salvaged cores and tanks), then new-build distribution transformers on the same robotic line with GOES or amorphous cores and standard data-center/solar step-up SKUs. 4) Substation power transformers (5-100 MVA) refurbishment, then new build. 5) Upstream core cutting/stacking and GOES supply partnerships, plus a transformer-as-a-service fleet that reclaims cores and copper in a closed loop. End state: a vertically integrated US transformer OEM in a $60B+ global market where roughly 80% of large US units are imported.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: an ML triage and grading model on incoming cores (nameplate OCR, DGA, oil, FRA, winding resistance, insulation tests, teardown and tank photos) predicts remanufacture cost, yield, residual life and achievable loss class before purchase, deciding buy, part-out or scrap, so the company outbids scrap brokers precisely. Demand forecasting by kVA and voltage from interconnection-queue and permit data, and robot path planning for winding and inspection. Rung 2: a failure-cause dataset across thousands of units by utility, climate and loading (which no OEM gets, since utilities scrap without analysis) prices the spares and swap product. Rung 3: generative core/coil design that fits new windings to legacy cores at minimum copper against DOE loss rules, trained on the company's own failure data, plus test-floor ML that shortens acceptance testing. Rung 4: the same DGA/FRA models scale to large units. Rung 5: sensors shipped in every unit give field-life data that feeds back into grading, design and lease residual underwriting.
scored.seed_plan: About $2.5M: lease the building, buy used oven, winding, test and oil equipment plus 1-2 robotic cells (about $0.8-1.2M), hire 2-3 senior rewind technicians from retiring shops (or acquire a small rewind shop and build the grading model from its historic test records), and get third-party test certification. Buy inventory at utility surplus auctions (GovDeals, co-op surplus) and from recyclers. Pre-sell with deposits to 3-10 solar/BESS EPCs and co-ops already paying brokers for anything in stock. Revenue from month 4-6, break-even near 40 units a month. Kills: lead-time normalisation as new OEM capacity arrives 2027-30, used-core supply tightening within 2-3 years, GOES supply, thin margins without good triage ML; hedged by climbing to hybrid and new build by rung 2-3. Rubric estimate about 24/30: L1 4, L2 5, L3 4, L4 5, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Demand is real. Wood Mackenzie (2025, as reported by POWER) puts the shortfall at about 30% for power transformers and about 10% for distribution units. Distribution demand is up 34% since 2019, and some distribution classes cost 78-95% more than in 2019. About 40M US distribution units are past their design life. Wood Mackenzie also says distribution availability has already improved, while large units still take more than 2 years. The 60-120 week figure in the pitch fits large units, not the 25-2,500 kVA core range. Refurbishment saves up to about 30% versus new (WEG, a vendor claim). That matches the pitch's 10-50% discount. Rung-one numbers (my estimates, not verified): reman pole and pad-mount units sell for about $4k-60k. Cores bought at scrap-plus cost about $0.5-5k, and rewind labour plus copper, oil and test add about 30-50% of the sale price, so gross margin is plausibly 30-45%. The pitch's 40-55% assumes the shortage premium lasts. Capital: about $2-3M for a leased plant, used oven, winding gear, oil processing and test bay. Buying an existing rewind shop is likely cheaper and faster than robotic cells, which pay off poorly in low-volume, high-mix rewinding. Working capital for core inventory is the hidden draw, likely another $1-2M at 40 units a month. Reaching $40-90M revenue per plant needs 1,500-3,000 units a year of good cores, and incumbents with 18+ yards already compete for that supply.
scored.buyers: Solar and BESS EPCs, EV-charging developers, data-center builders, co-ops, munis and industrials needing units in stock now. These buyers are capitalised and buy in a fragmented way. Utilities buy spares and emergency replacements. Brokers and resellers already sell to all of these.
scored.incumbents: The rung is fragmented but held. Sunbelt Solomon is Trilantic North America-backed: Trilantic invested in Sunbelt in 2018, and Sunbelt merged with Solomon (formerly Oaktree GFI) in 2020. Pre-merger it had 7+11 locations, sells new, reman and rental units, claims one of the industry's largest REMAN inventories, and offers a 3-year warranty. CORE Transformers (founded 2020; Emerald Lake Capital equity stake in Sep 2025, terms undisclosed) is building a PE-funded North American platform for new and reconditioned units aimed at data-center and renewables buyers, with money for technology, inventory and roll-up M&A. Maddox (privately held) is a large in-stock new and reman reseller. Also T&R Electric, ELSCO, Pacific Crest and Virginia Transformer service arms, plus many regional rewind shops. Wind Point (Central Moloney, 2023) and Mill Point (Pioneer/Power Partners) show PE rolling up the adjacent new-build distribution space. None is visibly ML-led, but PE platforms with inventory capital are already chasing the same scarce cores.
scored.end_state: Global transformer market is about $60B+ (pitch's figure, plausible). US distribution plus power transformers is about $15-25B a year (estimate). Wood Mackenzie says about 80% of US large power transformers and about 50% of distribution units are imported. The path to a vertically integrated US OEM is credible on paper but means competing head-on with much larger capital spenders. Hitachi Energy is building a $528M Mississippi plant (Sep 2026) as part of about $1.5B in US expansion. Cleveland-Cliffs is building a $150M distribution transformer plant in Weirton and owns its own GOES supply, which a startup would lack. Industrial Info tracks about $2B in US transformer-plant projects. Rungs 4-5 (new-build substation units, core cutting, GOES) are capex walls of hundreds of millions, owned by incumbents with steel supply.
scored.killer: The main killer is the shortage itself. The margin depends on a lead-time premium that is already easing for distribution units (Wood Mackenzie) as new US capacity (Cliffs, Hitachi, Eaton and others) arrives in 2026-28. Without the premium, reman becomes a 25-35% margin regional service business. Second killer: core supply. PE platforms (CORE, Sunbelt Solomon) already have yards, utility relationships and inventory capital, and will bid up retired cores. Third: the climb to new build needs GOES access (Cliffs is effectively the sole US supplier) and capex far beyond venture scale. Fourth: warranty and liability risk on rebuilt units sold into data centers. Finally, the ML triage edge is thin, because incumbents have decades of teardown experience and the yield-prediction gain is a few margin points, not a moat.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is real and sells (a profitable reman business), but it is a PE roll-up category (Sunbelt Solomon/Trilantic, CORE/Emerald Lake 2025) living on a distribution shortage that is already easing. The ML compounds weakly, and the climb to OEM hits GOES and capex walls held by Cliffs and Hitachi, so about 16/30, not 24.

scored.name: Orphan Grid (buy back C&I battery fleets orphaned by vendor exits)
scored.industry: Energy: behind-the-meter commercial battery storage and VPPs
scored.rung_one: Buy C&I BTM batteries (100 kW-2 MWh) left without an operator after Enel X North America exited C&I storage, Stem pivoted to software and smaller developers went bankrupt, at $0.05-0.2 per dollar of original capex (about $20-150k per site). Revenue is shared demand-charge savings with the host (hospital, warehouse, school) plus DR and capacity payments (NY, CA, MA, PJM), about $30-150k a year per site. Stem, Enel X, Voltus and CPower run vendor software or aggregate customer load; none buys stranded hardware.
scored.ladder: 1) Single rescued site. 2) Fleet of 100-1,000 sites run as one VPP (FERC 2222). 3) New-build BTM storage and solar plus storage on fleet-informed hardware. 4) Battery refurbishment and second-life line. 5) Aggregated capacity sold as non-wires alternatives. 6) Distributed energy retailer and IPP.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: a model finding orphaned systems from interconnection queues, SGIP and NY-Sun records and bankruptcy schedules, estimating revived value. Rung 2: a vendor-agnostic control stack reverse-engineering dead BMS/EMS APIs (each integration makes the next acquisition cheaper), plus fleet forecasting and bidding. Rung 3: mixed-vendor degradation data guides hardware choice and warranty pricing. Rung 4: SoH grading for refurbishment. Rung 5: track record underwriting firm capacity.
scored.seed_plan: Pick NYISO or CAISO, scrape SGIP and NYSERDA records for 2016-2021 installs by exited vendors, make offers to tax-equity funds, trustees and hosts, buy 20-40 sites for under $2M and bring 10 back online on the own controller within 9 months. Kills: firmware lock-in and demand-charge reform. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 4, L4 3, L5 4, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Unit: one 100 kW-2 MWh C&I battery, mostly installed 2016-2021. The $20-150k purchase price (5-20 cents per dollar of original capex) is the candidate's assumption and I found no market evidence for it. Revenue of $30-150k a year per site is also an estimate. A 500 kW system in high-demand-charge areas like ConEd or SCE plausibly makes $40-100k a year from shared demand-charge savings plus DR or capacity payments, but the host takes a share. Small sites make far less. Each revival costs extra, roughly $15-60k per site (estimate): a new controller or EMS, reverse-engineering the BMS, recommissioning, fire-code re-inspection (FDNY in NYC), insurance, and often replacing modules on packs past warranty. The seed plan's under $2M for 20-40 sites is arithmetically possible. But net per-site margin after host share, O&M, insurance and degradation is probably $15-50k a year (estimate). So 10 live sites give roughly $0.2-0.5M a year of revenue, a small cash-yield business. Precedent: in about 2020, owners SUSI Partners and SK E&S hired Stem to operate the 87-battery, 345 MWh AMS fleet in SCE territory when AMS left (GTM). The owner of an "orphaned" fleet usually keeps it and hires a new operator, so it does not sell at a distressed price.
scored.buyers: Rung one sells to hosts (shared demand-charge savings), ISO/utility DR and capacity programs (NYISO SCR, ConEd DLM, CA ELRP/DSGS, MA ConnectedSolutions, PJM) and VPP aggregators. A fleet of revived assets with yield could later go to infrastructure or DG funds as a portfolio. The buyers are capitalised, but each site is small and payments depend on programs.
scored.incumbents: Replacement operators already pick up orphaned fleets. Stem/PowerTrack took over the 87-site AMS portfolio for SUSI and SK E&S, and in Dec 2025 signed an operating deal for a third-party owner's 4-site SoCal portfolio. Stem is public and raised more than $1B in total, though it is now distressed and software-focused. Other operators and aggregators: Voltus (about $200M+ raised), CPower (owned by LS Power), Enel X DR (still active), GridBeyond, Generac Concerto/Enbala, Uplight/AutoGrid, Power Factors, NRG/Sunrun VPP. Nobody seems to run a dedicated "buy stranded hardware" strategy. That rung is open, but mostly because owners rarely sell at distressed prices. Correction: I found no evidence that Enel X North America exited C&I storage. The documented Oct 2024 exit was Enel X Way's EV charging business (JuiceBox). The main supply thesis is therefore unverified.
scored.end_state: The rungs that look like this business (BTM C&I storage) are small. Wood Mackenzie puts 2025 US community-scale plus C&I storage at only 95.6 MW, against 18.9 GW / 51 GWh for all US storage, with 39% segment growth forecast to 2030. The US installed C&I base is probably low single-digit GW (estimate), so the pool of orphaned stock is likely a few hundred sites at most. The large end-state (distributed energy retailer/IPP, non-wires alternatives) is a multi-$10B pool, but it is crowded and won with capital, not software. The path from salvaged 2018 batteries to an IPP is not credible as a moat.
scored.killer: Thin, unverified supply: the Enel X storage exit was not confirmed, and owners (tax-equity funds, SPVs) rehire operators like Stem instead of selling cheap, so deal flow may be a handful of sites a year. The assets are aging 2016-2021 NMC/LFP packs near or past warranty end, carrying fire-code and liability exposure and firmware lock-in. Revenue depends on demand-charge tariffs and DR program rules, which are being reformed. The C&I BTM segment is under 100 MW a year in new installs, which caps every later rung.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a scrappy distressed-asset play with no verified supply (Enel X's documented exit was EV charging, not storage), and owners usually rehire Stem-type operators rather than sell. The C&I BTM segment adds under 100 MW a year, so rung one is a small yield business and the ladder tops out in a crowded, capital-driven IPP market; about 16/30, not the claimed 21.

scored.name: Second Wind (buy and life-extend end-of-PPA wind farms with an in-house reman line)
scored.industry: Energy / machines: legacy onshore wind (1999-2010 turbines, 0.6-1.65 MW)
scored.rung_one: Buy one 5-30 MW farm (e.g., Vestas V47 or GE 1.5 turbines in Iowa, Minnesota, Texas or California) whose PPA and PTC have ended and whose small owner (community or farmer co-op, small IPP) faces decommissioning or uneconomic repower, at near-scrap $50-150k/MW. Sell merchant energy plus RECs or a short-term PPA to a co-op or muni; life-extension with refurbished parts gives 10+ years at $25-45/MWh opex. NextEra and Invenergy repower their own large fleets; Gearbox Express, ZF and Global Wind Service sell services without owning turbines; nobody buys small legacy farms.
scored.ladder: 1) Single life-extended farm. 2) Fleet of 300-1,000 MW of legacy wind. 3) Owned reman line for gearboxes, generators, blades and pitch bearings harvested from decommissioned turbines, supplying its fleet then selling exchange units. 4) Repowering on existing interconnection (requalifying for 45Y where the 80/20 rule allows). 5) Batteries at the same POI. 6) Brownfield-wind IPP plus parts remanufacturer, the 'Copart of wind components'.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML over EIA-860/923, USWTDB and PPA expiry dates ranks farms by remaining life value. Rung 2: SCADA anomaly detection and RUL models across a mixed old fleet OEMs no longer support. Rung 3: CV and acoustic grading of harvested parts for keep/rebuild/scrap; failure history sets exchange inventory and pricing. Rung 4: per-turbine repower-vs-extend optimiser. Rung 5: storage dispatch on shared interconnection.
scored.seed_plan: About $1M to buy one 5-10 MW farm of 600-750 kW turbines from a co-op, using neighbouring decommissioned turbines as a spare pool; contract tower climbing while founders build SCADA and RUL; sell to a muni or merchant into MISO/SPP. Within 18 months: one operating farm and a teardown bay. Kills: low merchant prices at negative-price nodes, blade and crane cost spikes, US wind policy. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 4, L4 3, L5 4, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Buying the farm is cheap and doable. Juhl Wind bought a controlling 99.9% stake in the 10.2 MW Woodstock Hills farm in Minnesota for $400k, about $40k/MW (nsenergybusiness; undated, likely around 2010). Broker asking prices for used GE 1.5s run EUR 95-150k per turbine, about EUR 63-100k/MW. V47 gearboxes are listed at about GBP 12k and generators at about GBP 12.5k (MWPS listings). So the farm plus a spare pool fits inside $1M (confirmed). The problem is operations. Example, all estimates: a 10 MW farm of 660 kW V47s at 25-28% capacity factor makes about 22-24 GWh/yr. At SPP North wind capture prices of about $20/MWh (S&P Global 2022; still roughly $15-25 at negative-price wind nodes) plus $1-3/MWh for voluntary RECs, revenue is about $0.45-0.6M/yr. Opex runs about $0.55-1.0M/yr: the pitch's own $25-45/MWh, or roughly $45-60/kW-yr for 2000s-vintage fleets with no OEM support, plus land lease, property tax and insurance. LBNL warns that its life-extension LCOE gains assume flat O&M and no degradation, so they overstate the benefit. Rung-one gross margin is therefore about zero to negative under merchant pricing. A short muni or co-op PPA at $35-45/MWh would make it positive, but only by $0.2-0.5M/yr per 10 MW (estimate). Capital: about $0.5-1M purchase plus $0.3-0.8M for crane-heavy major-component swaps (estimate).
scored.buyers: Rung one sells energy, not a unit. Buyers would be munis and co-ops on short PPAs, merchant sales into MISO/SPP/ERCOT, and voluntary REC buyers. The farm itself would sell to a yieldco or infra fund only if it produces cash, which at these economics is unlikely. The reman exchange units at rung 3 have better buyers: ISPs and owners running orphan GE 1.5, V47/V82 and Suzlon fleets. But Gearbox Express, ZF, Moventas and Global Wind Service already serve that market without owning farms.
scored.incumbents: For buying old farms: NeXtWind in Germany buys 'teenage' end-of-FIT farms to life-extend or repower and raised large private-equity funding (IREI, PE Wire). Juhl Wind did exactly this in Minnesota and stayed tiny. NextEra, MidAmerican (whose GE retrofit added about 20 years), Allete and Invenergy repower their own GE 1.5 fleets. For reman and spares: Gearbox Express, ZF Wind Power, Moventas, Global Wind Service, the MWPS used-turbine marketplace, and the OEM aftermarket arms (Vestas, GE Vernova). For RUL and SCADA analytics: ONYX Insight, Clir and others. In the US, the small-farm acquisition rung itself is open, mainly because the cash flow is poor, not because nobody has noticed it.
scored.end_state: The addressable fleet is small. The US had about 40 GW of wind installed by 2010 (estimate from the LBNL market reports), and most of it sits with utilities and big IPPs who repowered it for PTCs during 2017-2023. The small-owner, non-repowered slice is probably 2-5 GW (estimate). At about $20-30/MWh that is roughly $0.2-0.4B/yr of energy revenue. The broader US wind O&M and aftermarket pool is about $5-7B/yr (estimate), and the global one about $15-20B/yr (estimate), but those are the markets of the service incumbents. Repowering credits at rung 4 are largely cut off by the 2025 OBBBA phase-out of wind credits under 45Y. 'Copart of wind components' is a real but niche business, likely around $1B revenue at most (estimate), not a multi-$10B chain.
scored.killer: Merchant price below opex. At SPP/MISO wind nodes, capture prices of about $15-25/MWh with rising negative-price hours sit below the $25-45/MWh opex of unsupported 20-year-old turbines, so the farm only works with a subsidised short PPA. The remaining killers: crane and blade cost spikes on a few small turbines, OBBBA removing the wind tax-credit path for repowering, and a fleet of the target vintage that keeps shrinking as it is scrapped. The ML layer is thin: a few hundred mixed obsolete turbines give little training data, and ONYX Insight and Clir already sell RUL tools.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is cheap to win (about $40k/MW precedent) but loses money or runs near break-even at merchant prices, the pool of legacy small farms is a few GW, the repowering credit is mostly gone, and the reman rung competes with established service firms. About 16/30, not 21.
sources: https://www.nsenergybusiness.com/?p=1737 (Juhl Wind bought 10.2 MW Woodstock Hills for $400k)
https://emp.lbl.gov/news/new-study-finds-expected-useful-life-wind (LBNL lifetime and LCOE study, flat-O&M caveat)

https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/electric-power/042622-growth-of-wind-is-contributing-to-key-challenges-in-spp-market-mmu-report (SPP North wind capture of about $19.75/MWh, rising negative prices)

scored.name: Sunfield Ops (robot-operated utility solar O&M that buys distressed solar assets)
scored.industry: Energy / utility-scale solar operations
scored.rung_one: Fixed-price vegetation, cleaning and module-swap O&M contracts on 50-300 MW solar farms using an owned fleet of autonomous mowers, cleaning robots and a module-replacement robot, at about $3-6/kW-yr ($0.6-1.2M a year for 200 MW), sold to NextEra, AES, Lightsource bp, Arevon and Silicon Ranch. Competitors: Renu Robotics, Ecoppia, NovaSource, Clearway O&M; semi-crowded and low-margin.
scored.ladder: 1) Robot vegetation and cleaning contracts. 2) Full-wrap O&M with guaranteed availability. 3) Buying underperforming or distressed solar assets and fixing them. 4) Repowering and adding storage on owned sites. 5) Solar-plus-storage IPP with the lowest O&M cost per MWh.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: vegetation-growth forecasting (weather, species, NDVI) and soiling models. Rung 2: string-level fault detection from inverter data and drone thermal imaging, tracker-failure prediction. Rung 3: acquisition model comparing expected yield to actual EIA/ISO output and pricing the fix on real O&M cost. Rung 4: repower and storage sizing.
scored.seed_plan: $2M on 15-20 autonomous mowers and 2 trucks; win 3-5 sites in Texas and Georgia on 2-year contracts for $2-3M ARR in 18 months; the case rests on reaching rung 3. Kills: price-shopped low-margin service, IPP insourcing, acquisition capex. Scores 22/30: L1 5, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 2, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Price: the pitch's $3-6/kW-yr for vegetation, cleaning and module swaps alone is too high. Berkeley Lab's industry survey puts total O&M (all scopes, not just vegetation) at about $5-8/kWDC-yr on many US utility projects, inside about $17/kWDC-yr of total opex once you add tax, land lease, insurance and asset management (LBNL via pv magazine; the LBNL 2025 Data Update has current figures). Vendor sources say $8-20/kW-yr for full-service O&M (SurgePV, a weaker source). A realistic scope price for vegetation plus cleaning is more like $1.5-3/kW-yr (estimate), or $0.3-0.6M a year for a 200 MW site, not $0.6-1.2M. Hitting $2-3M ARR in 18 months would then take about 5-10 sites, not 3-5. Cost: autonomous mowers run roughly $80-150k each (estimate, not verified). 15-20 units is $1.5-2.5M, which uses up most of the $2M seed before trucks, crews and working capital. Gross margin for robot mowing is maybe 25-40% at scale (estimate). Vegetation contracts get competitively bid against human mowing crews and sheep grazing, which pushes margins toward 15-25%. Capital: rung one fits in about $2-3M only if you buy mowers from Renu or Swap. That makes the company a fleet operator on someone else's robot, with no hardware moat. Building your own robots costs much more. Rung three (buying distressed assets) is a different capital class altogether: a 100 MW operating site costs about $40-90M (estimate), so it needs tax-equity or infrastructure-fund partners.
scored.buyers: The buyers are capitalised: NextEra, AES, Lightsource bp, Arevon, Silicon Ranch, Clearway, Invenergy, plus third-party O&M primes that subcontract vegetation work. But vegetation and cleaning are a procurement line item that gets bid out every 1-3 years against local mowing crews and grazing contractors. The largest IPPs (NextEra, AES) keep moving O&M in-house and run their own robot pilots, for example AES with its own robotics work. A startup with no track record will struggle to win a 200 MW site from a top-five IPP inside 12 months. Mid-size independent owners and funds are the realistic first buyers.
scored.incumbents: Robot vegetation: Renu Robotics (US, founded 2018, about $6-7.5M raised across several rounds per CB Insights and Crustdata, figures conflict; new CEO June 2025; 3rd-generation robot). Swap Robotics (Canada, autonomous vegetation cutting plus module handling; reported $16M Series A in June 2025, unverified; aggregators also list about $3M). Robot cleaning: Ecoppia (Israel, well funded, large Middle East and US fleet), Aegeus (India, 8 GW installed, IPO August 2026), Sunpure (China, Series A over RMB 100M). Robot construction and module work: Gritt ($32M, July 2026), Cosmic Robotics (seed), AES's in-house install robot, Sarcos and Terabase-type players. Full-wrap O&M: NovaSource, Clearway O&M, SOLV/Swinerton, Qcells/REC services. Owner-operators of aging or underperforming assets: REC Power, and the secondary-market funds (Greenbacker, Foresight, the Sunnova/GoodFinch-style distressed buyers). Rung one is semi-crowded on robots and very crowded on O&M services.
scored.end_state: The US has roughly 150-200+ GWac of operating utility solar (estimate, EIA/LBNL). At $5-8/kW-yr that is a US utility O&M pool of only about $1-2B a year (estimate). The real end state is a solar-plus-storage IPP: US utility solar plus storage wholesale and PPA revenue is a pool of tens of billions a year (estimate), so it passes the multi-$10B test. But that end state is a capital and financing business (cost of capital, tax equity, interconnection). O&M cost per MWh is a minor lever: O&M is about 5-8 of about 17 $/kW-yr of opex, and a small share of LCOE next to capex and financing. Being the lowest-O&M-cost IPP is not a decisive advantage against NextEra's cost of capital.
scored.killer: Three things. 1) Rung one is commoditised, price-shopped service work. Robots get bought from Renu or Swap, so there is no hardware moat, and bids compete with sheep and human crews, giving thin margins and churn every 1-3 years. 2) There is a capex and financing wall between rung two and rung three. Buying distressed assets needs $40-90M per site plus tax-equity structuring, and that rung is won by funds with cheap capital (REC Power, infrastructure funds, distressed lenders like the Oaktree/GoodFinch group on Sunnova), not by an ML yield model. EIA plant-level output is public, and every secondary buyer already runs the same expected-versus-actual comparison. 3) Big IPPs are moving vegetation and cleaning robotics in-house, so customers concentrate and eventually compete with you. Also, the 2025 federal credit cuts and tariffs reshape new-build and repower economics in ways outside the company's control. The ML is weak at rungs one and two: vegetation forecasting and string fault detection are already sold by Raptor Maps, Heliolytics and inverter OEMs. The data does not compound into a proprietary acquisition edge.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is a crowded, low-margin service run on someone else's robots. The ladder only pays off at rung three, distressed-asset buying, which is won by cost of capital rather than ML, so the pitch's 22/30 is too high: realistically about 16/30.
sources: https://pv-magazine-usa.com/?p=6169 (LBNL survey: O&M $5-8/kWDC-yr, total opex about $17/kWDC-yr)

scored.name: Stackforge (quick-turn SiC power-module line climbing to grid power conversion)
scored.industry: Power electronics / energy
scored.rung_one: A low-volume, high-mix SiC power-module packaging line (silver-sinter die attach, wire/clip bonding, transfer molding or gel fill, power-cycling test) building custom half- and full-bridge modules in lots of 50-5,000 at $300-3,000 each with 4-6 week turns, for low-volume OEMs underserved by Infineon, Wolfspeed, onsemi and Semikron-Danfoss: eVTOL, mining and haul trucks, SST and solid-state breaker startups, data-centre 800 VDC rack power, defense. Competitors: Semikron-Danfoss, Infineon, Wolfspeed modules, Amber Semiconductor, Cissoid, Chinese contract packagers.
scored.ladder: 1) Custom modules. 2) Qualified power stacks (module, gate driver, cooling, DC-link). 3) Own MV solid-state transformer and DC power products for data centres and EV depots. 4) Owning and operating grid-edge conversion assets (DC microgrids, depot charging, DC power rooms) as energy-as-a-service. Pool $30B+.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: generative layout plus thermal/parasitic surrogates turn a spec into a design in days, and power-cycling, acoustic and X-ray data train yield and lifetime models. Rung 2: stack digital twins from module lifetime data. Rung 3: converter field telemetry with junction-temperature estimation closes the loop to module design. Rung 4: fleet dispatch and predictive replacement of owned assets.
scored.seed_plan: About $2.5-3M for a used sinter press, wire bonder, molding press and power-cycling testers in a 5,000 sq ft cleanroom-lite, with open-market SiC die; win 10-15 design-ins via paid design services; target $2-4M revenue by month 18; avoid automotive initially. Kills: customer concentration on startups, qualification time. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 2, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Unit price: $300-3,000 per module in lots of 50-5,000, as the candidate proposes. One design-in is worth $15k-$15M, but most real lots will be at the small end, about $50k-500k (estimate). Bare SiC die is most of the bill of materials and largely passes through, and contract packaging/assembly usually earns about 20-35% gross margin (estimate). Paid design services (NRE) raise the margin on early revenue. The SiC market is about $3.8B in 2025, rising to $12.0B by 2030 (MarketsandMarkets). SiC modules alone are about $2.5B in 2025, rising to $9.7B by 2031 (LP Information). Capital: no vendor publishes prices; Boschman and PINK sinter presses are quote-only. My estimates for used or refurbished tools: sinter press $0.3-0.8M, heavy-wire/ribbon bonder $0.2-0.4M, transfer molding or gel-fill $0.3-0.6M, power-cycling testers $0.2-0.4M each, X-ray plus C-SAM $0.3M, cleanroom-lite fit-out $0.3-0.5M. Total about $2-3M before payroll, so a $3M seed is tight, and a reliability-qualification campaign (AQG-324-style power cycling runs for months) delays revenue. Reaching $2-4M revenue by month 18 is aggressive (estimate).
scored.buyers: Low-volume OEMs. Funded SST/MV startups: Amperesand ($80M Series A, Nov 2025), DG Matrix ($20M seed plus $60M Series A, >$100M total), Heron Power ($140M Series B, Feb 2026), Hyperscale Power ($5M seed). Also defense primes, eVTOL, mining-truck electrification, solid-state breaker makers, and 800 VDC rack-power vendors. Risk: the best-funded buyers can either use standard 62mm/EconoDual-class modules from Wolfspeed, Infineon or Microchip, or take module design in-house as they scale. That leaves thin, concentrated demand for custom packaging. Defense is the most durable buyer, but it adds ITAR, AS9100 and qualification overhead.
scored.incumbents: Custom module design or prototyping is already offered by: Danfoss Silicon Power (US fab in Utica NY, design-your-module service), Semikron-Danfoss, Prodrive Technologies (custom Si/SiC/GaN modules), Infineon, Wolfspeed, Microchip (SiC modules), CISSOID, Fraunhofer IISB pi-Fab (low-volume prototypes including module assembly), University of Arkansas NCREPT/MuSiC (low-volume module fabrication), NoMIS Power (DOE SBIR, US-made SiC modules), and Chinese contract packagers. No venture-funded startup clearly holds the quick-turn, high-mix US niche. That gap is partly because the niche is small, not because it is overlooked.
scored.end_state: Rungs 3-4 (MV solid-state transformers, DC power rooms, depot and microgrid conversion run as energy-as-a-service) plausibly form a multi-$10B pool (estimate), driven by the 800 VDC AI data-centre transition. For scale, the SiC module market alone is about $2.5B (2025), rising to $9.7B (2031), per LP Information. Rung 3 is already contested by SST startups that raised about $280M combined in roughly a year (Amperesand, DG Matrix, Heron), backed by ABB, MHI, a16z and Breakthrough Energy Ventures. A small packager has no clear edge in reaching rung 3 against them. Rung 4 (owning assets as a service) is a project-finance business that does not depend on module know-how. The chain is large, but the path from packager to operator is not credible.
scored.killer: Thin, lumpy demand: most low-volume OEMs get by with standard modules, and the ones that outgrow those take the work in-house. Customers are concentrated among cash-burning startups. Qualification takes 6-12 months. SiC die prices are falling as Chinese SiC drives commoditisation, which squeezes the value of packaging. The capex jump to rung 3 puts the company up against SST startups with $100M+ each. The software layer (layout generation, thermal surrogates, lifetime models) is useful, but it is a tooling advantage and not a compounding data moat. Incumbents such as Danfoss and Infineon hold far larger reliability datasets.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but small and thinly-margined contract-packaging niche next to incumbents who already offer custom design (Danfoss, Prodrive, Fraunhofer). The higher rungs are already held by well-funded SST startups, and the ML layer is design tooling rather than a compounding moat: about 16/30.

scored.name: Propagation (battery fire-test range to BESS certification and repowering)
scored.industry: Energy storage / safety testing and certification
scored.rung_one: A US large-scale fire-test range (leased remote site, burn pads, gas analysis, instrumentation) for UL 9540A 6th edition and CSA C800 installation-level tests plus cell/module tests, sold to BESS integrators and cell OEMs (Tesla, Fluence, Wartsila, Jinko ESS, CATL/BYD integrators, FEOC-compliant newcomers) at $150-600k per large-scale test and $30-80k per cell/module campaign. Incumbents: UL (Northbrook), Intertek, CSA (often Suzhou), Fire & Risk Alliance/DNV, with long queues.
scored.ladder: 1) Test range. 2) Accredited certification body/NRTL issuing the mark. 3) Site commissioning, NFPA 855 hazard-mitigation analysis and fire-marshal packages. 4) In-service inspection and forensic teardown for owners and insurers. 5) Owner-operator buying underperforming or damaged BESS cheaply, repowering and operating them on its own risk data.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: thermal-runaway propagation surrogates from every burn predict pass/fail and cut customer iterations. Rung 2: model-assisted certification with fewer physical tests. Rung 3: site-specific deflagration models make HMA packages near-free. Rung 4: BMS telemetry plus forensic ground truth yields a risk score sold to insurers. Rung 5: the same score prices distressed acquisitions and runs O&M.
scored.seed_plan: Lease a remote Texas/Nevada site or former range, build one burn pad and instrumentation for about $1.5-2.5M, seek ISO 17025 within 9-12 months, and pre-sell slots to 3-4 queue-frustrated integrators. Kills: open-burn permits, a serious accident, NRTL accreditation taking 2+ years. Est. 21/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: No live web data: the shared web-search budget ran out before any query ran, so every figure here is an ESTIMATE from prior knowledge and needs checking. Price: large-scale BESS fire tests (UL 9540A installation level, CSA C800, the large-scale fire test now asked for under UL 9540 3rd ed / NFPA 855-2026) are plausibly $150-600k per test (EST, matches the candidate's range). Cell/module 9540A campaigns run about $30-100k (EST). Capex: a remote leased site with one or two burn pads, gas analysis (FTIR), calorimetry or HRR hood, cameras, a water supply and a containment and runoff system costs about $2-4M (EST). Accreditation: ISO 17025 takes 9-12 months. OSHA NRTL recognition usually takes 1-3 years. Throughput: one pad can probably do 15-30 large burns a year, because a destructive test needs prep, cooldown and cleanup. That gives about $4-12M a year in revenue from a full pad, with 40-60% gross margin (EST). Costs are consumables, crew, disposal of hazardous residue, insurance, and specimens that customers often supply. Revenue goes to the integrator's certification budget. It is a real but small business, roughly $10-30M a year at maturity on one or two sites.
scored.buyers: BESS integrators and cell/module OEMs: Tesla Energy, Fluence, Wartsila, Powin (now restructured), LG ES Vertech, Samsung SDI, CATL/BYD/Hithium/EVE/Jinko ESS and their US integrators, plus newcomers that want to stay clear of FEOC rules (domestic LFP lines). They are well capitalised and pay per test. Insurers, AHJs and owners (NextEra, Intersect, Plus Power) come in at later rungs.
scored.incumbents: The rung is crowded and well capitalised (all from prior knowledge, no live data). UL Solutions is public, with about $2.8-3B revenue, battery labs in Northbrook and Asia, and growing large-scale fire capacity. Also: Intertek (public); CSA Group (Suzhou and NA labs); TUV SUD and TUV Rheinland; SGS; Element; DNV (Spadeadam large-scale range, formerly a US battery lab); Fire & Risk Alliance (Maryland, does large-scale 9540A burns for many integrators); Southwest Research Institute (San Antonio fire range); Energy Safety Response Group; Exponent and Jensen Hughes (HMA and forensics); and many accredited Chinese labs (CATARC, CQC, TUV China) that are much cheaper for CATL/BYD-supply-chain test articles. The queue shortage is real but likely short-lived as UL, Intertek and others add pads.
scored.end_state: BESS testing, inspection and certification (TIC) worldwide is probably about $1-3B a year (EST). Adding HMA, commissioning and forensics brings it to about $3-5B. Rung 5, owning and repowering BESS, links into a global stationary storage capex pool of roughly $50-100B+ a year (EST, from BNEF-scale deployment), but that rung is an infrastructure-fund game priced by cost of capital. It is not a natural step up from a test lab, and a lab owning assets it might certify is a conflict of interest that would undermine NRTL independence. The chain is large in total, but the link from the lab to the big end-state pool is weak.
scored.killer: 1. Incumbents and Chinese labs add capacity, so the queue premium disappears within 2-3 years and slots become a commodity. 2. NRTL recognition takes 2+ years, during which rung one is only a data provider whose reports UL or Intertek must witness and accept. 3. One serious accident, or a failed open-burn or runoff permit, ends the company. 4. ML cannot cut the number of physical tests, because standards and AHJs require burns. That leaves 'model-assisted certification' with no regulatory acceptance, so software does not compound in a way that earns pricing power. 5. Independence rules block the jump to rung 5 (owning BESS).
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is a real, sellable test-lab business, but it is a crowded TIC niche (UL, Intertek, CSA, FRA, DNV, SwRI, Chinese labs) where regulation requires physical tests that ML cannot replace. Independence rules also block the climb to owning BESS. About 16/30, below the candidate's 21 estimate.
sources: Web search unavailable: the shared per-turn WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any query ran. All numbers are estimates from prior knowledge and need checking.
UL Solutions public filings (FY2024 revenue about $2.8B), prior knowledge
UL 9540A / UL 9540 3rd ed. and CSA C800 large-scale fire test requirements, NFPA 855 (prior knowledge)
OSHA NRTL program recognition timelines (prior knowledge)

scored.name: Rangeline (private counter-UAS test range to certification and site-defence operator)
scored.industry: Security/defense tech: counter-drone test, evaluation, certification and managed protection
scored.rung_one: An owned or long-leased instrumented range of 2,000-10,000 acres near a defense hub or existing restricted airspace (West Texas near Fort Bliss, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota Grand Sky, Oklahoma, Alberta) with FAA COA/restricted-airspace agreements, FCC experimental licences for RF emitters, and a fleet of about 40 Group 1-3 test drones including Shahed-like surrogates, FPV swarms and real adversary airframes. It sells range days and red-team swarm-as-a-service with labelled truth data at $20-120k per day/week and $250k-1M per program evaluation to C-UAS and drone vendors (Anduril, Epirus, DroneShield, Dedrone/Axon, D-Fend, Allen Control Systems, Cambridge Aerospace, about 200 startups), primes, DIU/JCO/Replicator evaluations, allied MoDs and critical-infrastructure owners validating vendor claims under expanded 2026 C-UAS authorities. Government ranges (Yuma, White Sands, Camp Atterbury, Camp Grafton) dominate with queues; private sites (NUAIR, Grand Sky, Mississippi State Raspet) do FAA-UTM flight testing, not adversarial C-UAS rating. The rung is largely open.
scored.ladder: 1) Range days plus ground-truth telemetry. 2) A licensed labelled signature library (RF, radar cross-section, EO/IR, acoustic) of every drone flown ($100k+ a year per vendor). 3) Independent third-party C-UAS scoring and certification (a 'UL for counter-drone') cited by insurers, DHS SAFETY Act, stadiums, utilities and procurement, plus installed-system acceptance testing at substations, prisons, airports and data centres. 4) Owning and operating certified managed C-UAS protection at fixed critical sites as subscription security, using best-scoring sensors. 5) Own sensor-fusion stack and effectors trained on the largest labelled dataset, and a multi-site national airspace-security operator. Pool spans C-UAS (about $10B+ by 2030) and managed physical security.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: an automated truth-capture pipeline (RTK-GPS on every target, time-synced sensor ingest) so each test day yields labelled data at near-zero marginal cost, plus an adversary-behaviour library. Rung 2: the cross-vendor dataset compounds with every test, and the range learns which threat profiles break which sensors to design adversarial scenarios. Rung 3: a scoring engine and digital-twin simulation (terrain, RF clutter, threats) calibrated on real flights makes certification and site design cheap and defensible. Rung 4: fusion and classification models trained on the multi-vendor corpus beat any single vendor's, and each operated site feeds false-alarm data back. Rung 5: national threat intelligence.
scored.seed_plan: About $2.5M: lease a private ranch, airstrip or ag/tribal site next to existing restricted airspace for about $300k a year; buy about 40 commercial and surrogate drones ($400k), RTK and instrumentation ($500k), and a mobile radar and RF truth suite ($600k); get FCC experimental licences and an FAA COA in 6-9 months; pre-sell campaign days to 10-30 funded C-UAS startups queuing for government ranges plus one allied MoD evaluation, targeting $2-4M of range revenue in year one. Kills: spectrum and jamming law (only federal agencies may jam), lumpy DoD budgets, airspace-access dependence. Est. 21/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 4, L4 3, L5 4, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Every figure here is an ESTIMATE. The shared web-search budget ran out before this agent made any query, so none of these numbers was checked against a source this round. Capital: the seed plan's $2.5M is plausible for a sensing-only range (lease at roughly $0.2-0.4M a year, about 40 Group 1-2 drones at $0.3-0.5M, RTK and truth instrumentation at $0.5M, a mobile radar and RF truth suite at $0.5-1M). It does not cover Group 3 or Shahed-class surrogates. Those cost about $50-250k each as expendable targets (for example Griffon MQM-172 Arrowhead class or SpektreWorks FLM-136 class; estimate), so a fleet of real adversary-like targets is a recurring consumable cost, not a one-off. Pricing: $20-120k per range day or week and $250k-1M per program evaluation fits commercial target-services rates (estimate). But the ~200 C-UAS startups are mostly seed or Series A and today test for free, or with the government paying, at JIATF-401 (formerly JCO) demonstrations, Yuma, White Sands and Camp Grafton. Paying demand is likely limited to the top 10-20 vendors plus a few allied ministries of defence. A realistic year-one figure is $1-2.5M (estimate). Margin: about 40-60% gross on range days once the fixed lease, crew and pilots are covered, with the lumpiness of defence services firms. Kill and defeat testing, which is the most valuable kind (jamming, spoofing, HPM, lasers, kinetic), needs NTIA/FCC experimental authority plus range safety and laser/HPM hazard approvals, and federal law largely reserves RF defeat to federal agencies. So rung one at first sells mainly detect/track/identify testing, the less valuable half.
scored.buyers: C-UAS vendors with real budgets: Anduril, Epirus, DroneShield, Dedrone/Axon, D-Fend, Allen Control Systems, plus primes such as RTX, Lockheed, L3Harris, Northrop, SAIC and Leidos. Government programs: JIATF-401, DIU/Replicator, Army RCO, DHS S&T, allied MoDs (UK, Baltics, Gulf, Taiwan). Critical-infrastructure owners, newly able to act under the expanded 2026 C-UAS authorities: utilities, prisons, stadiums, airports, data centres. Buyers are concentrated. Government evaluators prefer government-run, government-witnessed results for procurement, so the private range is mostly a pre-qualification and rehearsal venue unless DoD formally accredits it.
scored.incumbents: Government ranges, free or subsidised to vendors and the most credible venues: Yuma Proving Ground (JIATF-401 demos), White Sands, Camp Grafton / Northern Plains (ND), Camp Atterbury / Muscatatuck (IN), Fort Sill, Dugway, NAWC China Lake, and DHS S&T test events. FAA test sites and semi-private ranges: Northern Plains UAS Test Site, Grand Sky (ND), NUAIR (NY), Pendleton UAS Range (OR, city-owned and commercial), Mississippi State Raspet, New Mexico State UAS FTS (with White Sands access), Texas A&M Corpus Christi LSUASC. Target-drone and red-team suppliers that could move into adversarial C-UAS rating: Kratos (target drones, public company), QinetiQ Target Services, Griffon Aerospace, SpektreWorks, plus vendor-run private test sites (Anduril and Epirus run their own). The pure private adversarial C-UAS rating-and-certification niche looks thinly held, but the free government alternative is the real incumbent. From memory, not verified this round: none of these private niche players has raised more than about $20M specifically for this.
scored.end_state: Global C-UAS market estimated at about $6-15B by 2030 (estimate; analyst reports differ widely). Managed physical and security services are a multi-$10B pool, but they are low-margin and guard-labour-driven. The test, evaluation and certification sub-pool, which the company would actually own, is probably only $0.2-1B a year globally (estimate). The climb to rung 4, operating managed C-UAS at fixed sites, puts it head-on against Dedrone/Axon, DroneShield, D-Fend and Anduril, and the integrators (Securitas, Allied Universal) that already sell this as a subscription. Rung 5, its own sensor-fusion stack and effectors, puts it against Anduril and the primes. It would also undercut the "independent certifier" position, because a scorer that competes with the vendors it scores loses neutrality. So the end state is large on paper, but the path is self-contradictory.
scored.killer: 1) The neutrality paradox: a "UL for counter-drone" (rung 3) cannot later become a competing operator and sensor vendor (rungs 4-5) without losing the vendors' trust and data that fund rungs 1-2. 2) The free government alternative: vendors are evaluated where buyers watch (JIATF-401, Yuma), so private range days are discretionary spend from cash-strapped startups. 3) Spectrum and defeat law: jamming, spoofing and HPM testing need federal authority, so the high-value defeat testing stays on government ranges. 4) Customer concentration and lumpy DoD/allied budgets. 5) Recurring cost of expendable Group 3 surrogates. 6) Certification only matters if DHS SAFETY Act, insurers or DoD adopt it, and nothing so far suggests a private scorer would be named.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is buildable and partly open. But it competes with free government ranges, can't legally offer the high-value defeat testing, and its climb to operator and vendor destroys the neutrality the certification rung depends on. Realistic score is about 16/30, not 21.

scored.name: Bin Keeper (robot-run grain storage that grows into origination)
scored.industry: Agriculture / physical commodity storage (about 25B bushels of US on-farm and elevator storage)
scored.rung_one: Lease or buy one or two under-utilised country elevators (1-5M bushels, often $1-4M) and run them with grain-bin robots (Grain Weevil-type auger and crust-breaking crawlers) plus in-bin temperature and CO2 sensing, selling storage at about $0.03-0.05 per bushel-month plus drying and blending, with basis capture; robots remove bin-entry deaths that make these sites hard to staff. Grain Weevil and Amber Agriculture sell tools, not operations, and ADM, Cargill and CHS are shedding small sites.
scored.ladder: 1) One robot-run elevator. 2) Roll-up of 10-30 stranded rural elevators. 3) Origination and merchandising on real-time network inventory and quality. 4) Identity-preserved and low-carbon grain programmes for food and biofuel buyers. 5) Transload, rail and export logistics.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: spoilage and hot-spot prediction and robot scheduling. Rung 2: network drying, energy and blending optimisation. Rung 3: basis and spread forecasting from proprietary network inventory and quality data. Rung 4: traceability ledger and carbon-intensity scoring.
scored.seed_plan: $2M lease-with-option on 1-2 elevators in Iowa or North Dakota, about $300k on robots and sensors, and an ex-elevator manager hire. Kills: commodity basis risk, thin margins, 'not an ML company' perception, seasonality. Scores 21/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 3, L4 4, L5 4, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: I could not check any live numbers. The workflow's shared web-search budget was already used up, so every figure here is an ESTIMATE from prior knowledge and needs checking. Price: commercial storage usually runs about $0.02-0.04 per bushel-month after a flat fall charge of about $0.10-0.20 per bushel. In practice that comes to about $0.20-0.35 per bushel-year, a bit below the candidate's $0.03-0.05 per month (estimate). A 3M-bushel elevator at about 1.5 turns would make roughly $0.6-1.0M a year from storage and handling, $0.2-0.5M from drying (gas-cost driven) and $0.3-0.9M from merchandising margin at $0.10-0.20 per bushel. Total revenue is about $1.5-2.5M a year (estimate). Gross margin after labour, energy, shrink and insurance is about 20-35%, so EBITDA is roughly $0.3-0.7M a site, before basis losses (estimate). Capital: used country elevators sell for about $0.5-1.50 per bushel of capacity. A 1-5M bushel site is about $1-5M, consistent with the candidate's $1-4M (estimate). Fleet: bin robots plus sensing are about $50-300k a site (Grain Weevil units are about $10-20k each; cable systems are similar, estimate). The hidden capital need is a working-capital line to carry grain inventory: 3M bushels at about $4.50 corn is about $13M of inventory to finance. Licensing also needs bonding and a net-worth floor under a federal (USWA) or state warehouse licence. That makes the real rung-one capital closer to $3-5M of equity plus a $10M+ bank line, not $2M.
scored.buyers: Rung one sells storage, drying and handling to farmers, who are fragmented and loyal to the local co-op. It sells merchandised grain to capitalised buyers: ADM, Cargill, Bunge, CHS, ethanol plants (POET, Valero), feed mills, processors and export terminals. The site itself can be sold to co-ops (CHS, AGP, Heartland Co-op, Landus, Ag Partners) or regional grain companies (The Andersons, Scoular, Bartlett/Savage), so an exit exists. Identity-preserved (IP) and low-carbon grain programmes would sell to food companies and to biofuel/SAF producers going after 45Z credits.
scored.incumbents: Sites are held by farmer co-ops (CHS, about $40-45B revenue; Landus; Heartland Co-op; AGP), the ABCD majors (ADM, Bunge, Cargill, Louis Dreyfus) and regionals (The Andersons, Scoular). They have cheap capital and farmer relationships, and their rationalisation of small sites mostly closes them or moves them to co-ops, not to newcomers (estimate). The robots and sensing are sold as tools by Grain Weevil (Iowa, seed-stage, about single-digit $M raised, estimate), BinSentry (Canada, venture-backed, about $20-30M raised, estimate), Amber Agriculture (sensing), OPI/Intellifarms/AGI BinManager (AGI is a public company) and Sukup/GSI (AGCO) controls. Nobody well funded runs robot-operated elevators, so the operator-plus-robot slot is open. The rung itself, though, is held by deeply entrenched co-ops.
scored.end_state: US commercial (off-farm) storage capacity is about 11B bushels and on-farm about 13B, so about 24-25B in total (USDA NASS Grain Stocks capacity series, from memory). US grain origination and merchandising is a revenue pool in the hundreds of billions; ADM Ag Services and Oilseeds alone is about $60-70B revenue. The margin pool is much smaller: handling and merchandising at about $0.10-0.30 per bushel on about 15-20B bushels moved is roughly $2-5B a year of gross margin (estimate). Add IP and low-carbon premiums (about $0.10-0.50 per bushel on a slice of volume) and rail/export logistics. The full chain is large, but it is a low-margin, scale-and-balance-sheet business. A credible end-to-end path means becoming a regional Scoular or Andersons, which takes decades and billions of balance sheet.
scored.killer: The main killers are balance sheet and basis. Grain merchandising needs large inventory financing, hedging and licence bonding, which pushes real capital well past seed. One bad basis or spread season (for example a 2012-style drought or a 2018-style tariff hit) wipes out a year's EBITDA on a 1-2 site operator. Farmer origination is relationship-driven and co-op patronage dividends are hard to compete with. Seasonality and drying energy cost add pressure. The ML/robot layer improves shrink and safety at the margin, but grain-bin entrapments are only about 40-60 a year across the US (Purdue, estimate), so the robot value is a labour and safety saving of perhaps 1-3 cents a bushel, not a structural cost advantage. Investors will read this as an elevator roll-up with sensors, not a software company. Data advantage at rung 3 needs network scale (roughly 100M+ bushels) before basis forecasting beats public cash-bid data and the majors' own far larger data.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is buyable and sells on its own, but it is a thin-margin elevator business. Inventory and basis risk make the real capital need much larger than a seed round, entrenched co-ops hold the sites and farmers, and robots plus spoilage ML give a cents-per-bushel edge rather than a compounding moat. That puts it at about 16/30, not the candidate's 21.
