scored.name: Spanline (mobile substation bridge fleet)
scored.industry: Grid / power: high-voltage substations for data centers and large loads
scored.rung_one: An owned fleet of 3-5 trailer-mounted mobile substations (69-230 kV to 13.8/34.5 kV, 20-50 MVA), leased as bridge power to data-center developers, AI hosts and industrial loads waiting 2-4 years for a permanent utility substation, plus emergency leases to utilities and co-ops. A new unit costs about $3-5M; leases run about $80-200k per month on 12-36 month terms, so a unit pays back in 2-3 years. Incumbents: Sunbelt Solomon and United Rentals rent temporary substations as a general-rental sideline without owning the developer relationship or interconnection workflow; no venture-backed startup found.
scored.ladder: 1) Bridge-substation leases. 2) Build-own-transfer permanent prefab substations for the same customers, rolling the bridge unit into the permanent design and capturing EPC margin. 3) In-house e-house/skid factory assembling breakers, relays and controls. 4) Owning substation and step-down assets as a substation-as-a-service rate base ($15-40M per site, 20-year contracts). 5) Owning private interconnection/transmission spurs for large loads. End state: an independent owner-operator of HV interconnection infrastructure for large loads, a multi-$10B annual capex pool.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: unit telemetry (DGA, temperature, load profile) builds fleet health and pricing models, and ML forecasts which queued large-load sites will need bridge power from utility large-load tariffs, ISO/utility filings and county permits, driving placement and utilisation. Rung 2: generative substation design reusing validated designs, plus protection-study automation. Rung 3: build-to-stock forecasting from the demand model. Rung 4: asset-health ML on the owned rate base lowers O&M and financing cost. Each lease adds load and equipment data that improves underwriting for the next site.
scored.seed_plan: About $3M equity plus $8-12M equipment ABS/vendor financing secured on contracted leases. Buy 2-3 used or refurbished mobile units from upgrading utilities. Sign the first lease with a neocloud or behind-the-meter campus with an energisation gap, using the demand-forecasting model as the sales engine. Kills: lease-rate cyclicality if transformer lead times normalise, and equipment-debt dependence. Rubric estimate about 22/30: L1 4, L2 5, L3 3, L4 4, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: UNIT COST: In 2016 Riverside Public Utilities paid Delta Star $1.98M for a 30 MVA mobile substation with switchgear (Riverside council record). A small 6.25 MVA, 34.5/13.2 kV unit cost $1.1M (MN Energy). An NC co-op manager put mobile substations at '$1.5M on up' (NRECA). Transformer prices are up about 80% in five years (pv magazine, May 2026), so a 30-50 MVA, 230 kV unit is roughly $3.5-6M today (estimate). The candidate's $3-5M is plausible to slightly low at the top of the range. LEAD TIME: large power transformers now take 80-210 weeks, up to about 4 years (WoodMac, PwC via pv magazine). Mobile units compete for the same transformer slots, so you cannot quickly build a fleet of new units. Used units are scarce because utilities keep them as storm and contingency spares, and co-ops share theirs through the NRECA pool, which shrinks the 'buy used from upgrading utilities' plan. LEASE RATES: I found no published rates. The candidate's $80-200k per month is an UNVERIFIED estimate; one source's $1.5-4k per month is clearly junk. If $100k per month on a $4.5M unit holds, gross yield is about 27% a year with a payback of about 3.5-4 years after transport, commissioning, field crews (Sunbelt Solomon bundles delivery, setup and its field-services team), insurance and idle time. CAPITAL: $3M of equity buys well under one new unit. Each 20-50 MVA unit covers only a fraction of a 100-300 MW campus, so a single customer may need 3-6 units ($15-30M). Rung one therefore depends on equipment debt from day one, and lenders will want signed leases first.
scored.buyers: Data-center developers and neoclouds with line capacity available but a late permanent substation; industrial loads such as fabs, battery plants and crypto/AI hosts; utilities and co-ops needing emergency or maintenance cover (the most frequent current use per Sunbelt Solomon case studies); EPCs (Black & Veatch, Burns & McDonnell) needing temporary energisation during commissioning. Buyers are well capitalised. But the true large-load bottleneck is usually transmission and generation capacity, not substation hardware, and a mobile substation adds no MW. The group that has deliverable capacity but a late substation is a narrow niche. Utilities also gate the point of interconnection and protection coordination, so a third-party unit needs utility sign-off.
scored.incumbents: Sunbelt Solomon (part of Ashtead/Sunbelt Rentals, about $11B a year in revenue) runs mobile substations as a core product line, not a sideline: a nationwide fleet of units up to 230 kV and 50 MVA, with delivery, commissioning and field services, plus an asset-recovery and reconditioning division. It is buying transformer refurbishers (Valley Transformer 2024, Holland Industrial Services), and it publishes data-center bridge case studies such as a 20 MVA unit for a delayed utility feed. United Rentals (about $15B in revenue) markets data-center bridge power. Aggreko and Caterpillar dealers cover bridge generation. Utility and co-op pools (NRECA mobile substation pool) also compete. OEMs that build and sometimes lease units: Delta Star, ABB/Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, Virginia Transformer, WEG. Rung-2 EPC and prefab: Black & Veatch, Burns & McDonnell, Quanta, Caverion, NV5 (design). Bridge-generation startups take the 'energisation gap' budget instead of substations: VoltaGrid, Crusoe, Bloom Energy deals. My search found no venture-backed mobile-substation lessor, but the rung is held by a scaled, well-financed rental incumbent.
scored.end_state: US T&D capex is well over $100B a year (utility capex estimate), and data centers plus new manufacturing could add up to 100 GW by 2030 (DOE via CIGRE B3 2026). The chain from transformers to substations to interconnection spurs is clearly a multi-$10B pool. The mobile substation market itself is small: about $1.18B globally in 2024 at about 4.8% CAGR (MarketsandMarkets). The end-to-end path is shaky. Large-load substations and spurs are mostly utility-owned rate base, with the customer paying CIAC; Intel/SVP Santa Clara is an example where the utility keeps ownership. Customer-owned transmission-voltage substations exist, but the hyperscaler owns them, not a third party. Independent 'substation-as-a-service' rate base and private spurs run into utility franchise rules, FERC/state regulation, and EPC giants and OEMs with factories. Rung 3 (an e-house factory) competes with ABB, Siemens and Eaton. So the pool is large, but a startup's credible share of the chain is small.
scored.killer: 1) Incumbent: Sunbelt Solomon already offers this exact product nationwide, up to 230 kV and 50 MVA, with field crews, and can outbid on price and availability. 2) Capex and supply: units cost $3.5-6M (estimate), need transformers with 2-4 year lead times, and used units are hoarded by utilities, so a seed company cannot get fleet scale fast. Everything rides on equipment debt that needs signed leases first. 3) Demand mismatch: the large-load wait is mostly for transmission and generation capacity, which a mobile substation does not fix, and 20-50 MVA units are small against 100-300 MW campuses. 4) Cyclicality: lease rates collapse when transformer lead times normalise (OEM capacity expansions are under way). 5) Utility gatekeeping of the point of interconnection, plus regulation, blocks rungs 4-5. 6) ML moat is thin: telemetry from 3-5 units is no data flywheel, and demand forecasting from filings is a sales tool anyone can copy.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but niche rental business that Sunbelt Solomon already runs nationwide. It needs heavy capex beyond seed, depends on a transformer-shortage cycle, and the upper rungs are utility-owned regulated assets, so software does not compound into a defensible ladder (16/30, below the candidate's own 22).

scored.name: CoreLine (grain-oriented steel transformer core cutting and stacking)
scored.industry: Energy machines: electrical steel processing, transformer cores and transformers
scored.rung_one: An owned GOES/amorphous slitting and step-lap core cutting line with robotic stacking, selling finished stacked or wound cores to US distribution and medium-power transformer makers (ERMCO, Howard, Hammond, Prolec GE, Virginia Transformer, new entrants) that are capacity-starved by 2-4 year lead times. About $4-8/kg of finished core, $5-60k per mid-size core; one automated line yields $15-30M a year. US GOES comes only from Cleveland-Cliffs Butler, and core cutting is fragmented among in-house OEM lines and a few service centers (Central Moloney, Tempel). Startups (Ampace, Heron Power) are in solid-state, not cores.
scored.ladder: 1) Core cutting and stacking service. 2) Own-brand pole and pad-mount distribution transformers for co-ops and munis. 3) Medium-power and data-center substation transformers, plus solid-state hybrids. 4) Domestic amorphous ribbon casting and GOES finishing (laser scribing, coating). 5) Transformer-as-a-service fleet with monitoring, refurbishment and core recycling. End state: a vertically integrated US transformer maker in a $15B+ US and $60B+ global market.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML core design optimising lamination geometry and step-lap patterns for no-load loss against DOE 2027 rules per spec, plus vision QC and robotic stack planning. Rung 2: generative transformer design reusing every core's measured loss data. Rung 3: thermal and dielectric surrogates for fast bespoke quoting. Rung 4: scribe and coat process control tied to measured core loss. Rung 5: fleet DGA and thermal telemetry feeding failure models back into design. The measured-loss-per-design dataset compounds across rungs.
scored.seed_plan: $3M, partly equipment-financed: buy a refurbished Georg or Soenen cut-to-length and step-lap line ($1-1.5M), build robotic stacking, lease a Southeast building, secure prepayments or offtake from 2-3 OEMs, and source GOES from Cliffs plus Japanese/Korean coil via a service center. First cores by month 9, about $8M run-rate by month 18. Kills: GOES allocation and tariffs (mitigate with amorphous and multi-source) and a utility capex slowdown. Rubric estimate about 22/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 4, L4 5, L5 4, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Rung one is mostly a commodity spread. The pitch's own figure is $4-8/kg of finished core. The input steel alone is roughly $3-6/kg: the EU GOES safeguard thresholds are EUR 2,800-5,000/t ($3.2-5.7k/t), and US prices behind Section 232 are likely at or above that (estimate; the last public US figure I found is about $2.6k/t from 2018). So the steel is roughly 55-75% of the selling price, and the cutting and stacking add only about $1-2/kg (estimate). Gross margin is probably 10-20% (estimate), not software-like. Capital: a refurbished Georg or Soenen cut-to-length/step-lap line at $1-1.5M is plausible (founder estimate, not verified). The bigger cash need is steel inventory and working capital. An $8M run-rate means about 1,300-2,000 t/yr of GOES, so $1.5-3M of coil sits in stock at any time (estimate), plus ISO qualification and a 6-12 month OEM approval cycle. On $3M of seed money that is very tight. Demand side: US imports of transformer cores grew from $126M (2018) to $524M (2025), per Breakthrough, an advocacy source. GOES is about 20% of a transformer's cost. Since August 2025, transformers containing non-US steel pay a 50% tariff on that component value.
scored.buyers: US makers of distribution and medium-power transformers: ERMCO, Howard, Hammond, Prolec GE, Virginia Transformer, WEG, Eaton, plus new entrants. These are capitalised buyers, so the rung can be sold on its own. Two caveats. First, many large OEMs cut cores in-house and treat it as core IP. Second, the big new plants (Hitachi Energy's $528M Mississippi plant and $1.5B US program, Siemens Energy's $1B US plan) bring their own core lines. Distribution transformer lead times have also eased to about 30 weeks in Q2 2025, down from a 100+ week peak in 2023 (Wood Mackenzie). The 2-4 year shortage now applies mainly to power transformers and GSUs, whose large cores the OEMs build themselves.
scored.incumbents: Worthington Steel / Tempel: a public company with more than $3B in revenue. It is expanding transformer laminations in Apodaca, Mexico (185k sq ft; about $17M spent by March 2024) and building a core line for large transformers in Burlington, Ontario (due end of 2025). Cleveland-Cliffs is the only US GOES maker (Butler Works, $200M expansion with a $75M DOE grant, finishing 2028-29) and is integrating forward with a $150M Weirton distribution transformer plant ($50M state loan, due 1H 2026). That makes the only domestic steel supplier a direct competitor. Flux Steel Works: a new GOES mill in Ohio, 260kt/yr, 2029. Also Central Moloney, Mexican and Canadian core converters (the subject of a Section 232 circumvention fight), and in-house lines at Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, Prolec GE, Eaton and Hyundai. Metglas (Proterial, formerly Hitachi Metals) dominates amorphous ribbon. The rung is held by well-capitalised players, not empty.
scored.end_state: Transformers are a large pool: about $15-20B a year in the US and $60-70B+ globally (estimate, consistent with the pitch). Demand growth since 2019 is +116% for power and +41% for distribution transformers (WoodMac), and about $2B of US transformer factory capex is in progress (Industrial Info). Doing it end to end is credible only in theory. Rungs 2-4 put the company head to head with Hitachi, Siemens, Cliffs and Eaton. Each spends $0.15-1.5B per plant. Rung 4 (amorphous casting or GOES finishing) is a steel-mill-scale capex wall.
scored.killer: The killer is GOES supply. The only US mill (Cliffs) is integrating into transformers itself, and imported coil or cores face 50% Section 232 component tariffs plus policy whiplash. A converter with no steel allocation has no product. Second, the business is a thin spread over commodity steel, about $1-2/kg added, so margins don't look like a venture company's. Third, it sells to a handful of OEMs that can bring cutting in-house. Fourth, distribution lead times have already normalised to about 30 weeks, so the urgency in the pitch is fading. Finally, ML's edge is small: step-lap core design and loss are mature physics already well handled by FEM and decades of OEM know-how, so the measured-loss dataset is unlikely to be a moat.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is real and sellable, but it is a thin-margin steel-conversion spread. Worthington/Tempel and in-house OEM lines already hold it, its only domestic steel supplier (Cliffs) is integrating forward against it, and ML adds little to mature core physics: about 15/30, not the 22 the pitch estimates.

scored.name: Steamline (thermal-storage steam utility for food and beverage plants)
scored.industry: Energy: industrial heat / thermal storage
scored.rung_one: Own and operate one 3-10 MWth electric heater with thermal store (resistive heating plus molten salt, rock or concrete, or bought Rondo/Kraftblock modules) at a dairy, brewery, ethanol or food plant in SPP or ERCOT West where curtailment drives negative prices, selling steam under a 10-year heat purchase agreement at about $8-14/MMBtu (roughly $1-3M a year per site) to Cargill, Leprino, Anheuser-Busch or POET-style owners. Hardware vendors (Rondo, Antora, Electrified Thermal, Kraftblock) mostly sell; heat-as-a-service operators are few (Rondo financing arm, Exowatt, Caldera early).
scored.ladder: 1) Single-site HPA. 2) Fleet of 10-50 sites in negative-price nodes. 3) REP or QSE licence to buy wholesale directly and earn ancillary revenue (ERCOT CLRs). 4) In-house standardised heater and store module. 5) Co-located behind-the-meter wind or solar, an integrated industrial energy utility. 6) Process-heat decarbonisation across the roughly $50B+ US industrial-heat fuel pool.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: nodal price plus plant steam-demand forecasting sets charge timing and margin. Rung 2: siting model over EIA plant data, EPA GHGRP boiler records and LMP histories. Rung 3: trading and ancillary bidding treating the fleet as one flexible load. Rung 4: operating data cut store sizing and cost.
scored.seed_plan: About $1M on development and engineering, financing the first 3 MWth project ($3-5M capex) with project equity, 48E/48C-style or state grants and tax-equity bridge loans; sign a dairy or ethanol plant on a negative-priced Kansas, Oklahoma or Texas Panhandle bus inside 9 months. Kills: gas price collapse, host interconnection upgrades, site-by-site grind. Self-score about 22/30: L1 3, L2 5, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Unit: 3-10 MWth electric heater plus store at a food or ethanol plant, selling steam under a 10-year heat purchase agreement (HPA). Capex is about $3-5M for 3 MWth (founder's figure, estimate). EPRI-style US models use storage at about $62/kWh installed, 90% round trip, 7% WACC (SwRI/EPRI 2024 deck), so a 3 MWth x 12 h (36 MWh) store comes to about $2.2M for storage alone, plus heater, steam generator, interconnection and an electrical service upgrade (estimate $3-6M all in). Revenue: about 3 MWth x 8,760 h x 0.9 load factor is roughly 80,000 MMBtu a year. At $8-14/MMBtu that is about $0.65-1.1M a year for a 3 MWth site, not $1-3M; only about 10 MWth reaches $2-3M (estimate). Cost to beat: Henry Hub about $3-4/MMBtu (2026, estimate), delivered industrial gas in KS/OK/TX about $4-6, so gas-boiler steam runs about $5-7.5/MMBtu at 80% efficiency. The $8-14 HPA price is therefore ABOVE gas parity unless the host pays a green premium or ITC/48E-type credits and grants close the gap. IEA says a standalone electric boiler costs about 4x a gas boiler to run in the US. A 2025 HAW Hamburg thesis found an electrode boiler plus heat battery was still 20-32% more expensive on levelized cost of heat than gas. Fraunhofer notes that grid fees and demand charges erode the advantage of charging at negative spot prices. SPP Kansas and western Oklahoma saw negative prices in more than 25% of hours (LBNL, 2021 data), which is the real tailwind, but a behind-the-meter host still pays transmission and distribution plus demand or 4CP charges unless the site is structured as a wholesale load or CLR. Equity need: seed $1M plus project equity of about $1-1.5M, with the rest as tax equity or debt. Lenders will not finance a first-of-a-kind project from an unknown sponsor without a bankable vendor warranty and host credit, so in practice it means buying Rondo or Antora modules and accepting their margin.
scored.buyers: Hosts paying for steam: dairy and cheese plants (Leprino, Hilmar, Dairy Farmers of America), ethanol plants (POET, Valero, Green Plains in KS/NE/TX Panhandle), brewers (AB InBev, Molson Coors), and meat and food processors (Cargill, Tyson, JBS). Buyers of the project or fleet: infrastructure funds and yieldcos (Generate Capital, Brookfield, EDP, Engie), which already buy heat-as-a-service portfolios. Ethanol is the best fit (24/7 steam, thin margins, carbon-intensity incentive under 45Z/LCFS), but plant credit is weak.
scored.incumbents: Heat-as-a-service rung is already contested. Zero Industrial (US/Canada) raised a $10M Series A (Apr 2025) for exactly this model: it fully finances each project and sells heat and steam under long-term HaaS contracts. Rondo Energy (raised over $100M, estimate; Breakthrough Energy backed; Calgren ethanol HaaS deal since 2023; Heineken Vialonga with EDP as owner-operator under HPAs, go-live 2027). Antora Energy (Series C of $550M in Jul 2026, about $1B total corporate plus project financing, a signed industrial pipeline, and its own project finance). Exowatt ($70M Series A plus a $50M extension, data-center focused). Electrified Thermal Solutions ($19M, Dec 2024). Kraftblock (EUR 20M Series B, Shell Ventures). Graphite Energy (AU$40M Apr 2026, installing at two multinational food and beverage firms). MGA Thermal ($17M, Mar 2026). Utilities and IPPs such as EDP, Engie and Constellation can offer the same HPA with a far lower cost of capital.
scored.end_state: US industrial process heat fuel spend is roughly $50-80B a year (estimate: about 7-8 quads of industrial fuel use for heat, at $4-10/MMBtu across gas, coal and oil). Low-temperature steam (<200C) for food, beverage, ethanol, pulp and chemicals is about a third of that (estimate, IEA framing). The end-to-end path (own modules, a REP/QSE licence, co-located renewables, becoming an industrial energy utility) is credible on paper, but every rung is a capital-intensive project-finance business competing with billion-dollar balance sheets, so a seed-stage team reaches the end state only by becoming a developer or IPP.
scored.killer: Gas-parity economics plus cost of capital. With US delivered gas at $4-6/MMBtu, the proposed $8-14/MMBtu steam is a green premium that only clears with ITC/48E-type credits and grants, while delivered power (transmission, distribution and demand charges) erases much of the negative-LMP advantage. The winner is whoever has the cheapest capital and module cost (Antora at about $1B, Rondo, EDP-style utilities), not whoever has the best dispatch model. Secondary kills: 10-year HPA concentration on a single thin-margin host (ethanol or dairy plant closures), interconnection and service upgrades at rural co-op hosts, and a commoditised software layer (charge scheduling is a solved optimisation problem that vendors bundle for free).
scored.one_line_reason: The HPA itself is a real, sellable asset, but heat-as-a-service is already a crowded developer game (Zero Industrial, Rondo, Antora with about $1B, EDP). The steam price sits above gas parity without subsidy, and the ML (dispatch and siting) does not compound into a moat, so this is a capital-cost contest rather than a software-compounding ladder. Scores 15/30, against a self-score of 22.

scored.name: Flexgrid Capacity (owned BESS that buys data centres interconnection)
scored.industry: Energy storage / grid interconnection
scored.rung_one: An owned 5-20 MWh battery behind the meter at an existing colo or new DC site, letting the site accept a flexible (curtailable) interconnection and energise years earlier. Revenue: a capacity-enablement fee ($/kW-month, roughly $8-15M contract value over 10 years per site), plus wholesale and ancillary revenue in unneeded hours and UPS/genset displacement. Players: Emerald AI (software only), Fluence and Tesla (hardware), GridStor and Jupiter (front-of-meter IPPs), Enchanted Rock (gen-based); nobody clearly owns BTM flexibility BESS as an interconnection-unlock product, but the space is warming.
scored.ladder: 1) Single-site flexibility BESS under a tolling-style contract. 2) Fleet aggregated as a VPP in ISO capacity and ancillary markets. 3) On-site generation (gas recips, solar) for full bring-your-own-capacity. 4) Owned powered campuses with flexibility-secured queue positions leased to hyperscalers. 5) Load-serving and retail supply to DC tenants.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: co-optimisation of DC load (including GPU workload shifting via operator APIs), battery state and utility curtailment signals with guaranteed SLA. Rung 2: multi-site price forecasting and bidding. Rung 3: gen-plus-storage dispatch. Rung 4: an interconnection study engine trained on utility queue data and the fleet's actual curtailment history, which persuades utilities to grant flexible terms. Rung 5: retail hedging and load forecasting.
scored.seed_plan: About $2M equity for engineering, interconnection filings and the controls stack, with the first BESS ($4-6M) financed by ITC/tax-equity lenders against a signed 10-year DC contract; target a mid-size colo stuck in the ERCOT or PJM queue. Kills: utility tariff rules for flexible interconnection and battery financing at seed scale. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Capex: Modo Energy's 2026 survey of 100+ participants puts all-in BESS capex at about $201/kWh for 4-hour systems and $325/kWh for 2-hour. Commercial-scale installs run higher, about $180-300/kWh for containerised systems over 100 kWh (vendor figure, low reliability). At those prices a 5-20 MWh unit costs roughly $1.5-6M (estimate), so the candidate's $4-6M figure holds. The size is the problem. A data centre that needs curtailable headroom typically needs tens of MW over 2+ hours, not 5-20 MWh. The reference deal, Calibrant's system at Aligned's Pacific Northwest campus, is 31 MW / 62 MWh, which is roughly $15-25M of capex at the prices above (estimate). Revenue: a capacity-enablement fee of about $8-15M over 10 years per site (the candidate's estimate, unverified), plus merchant and ancillary revenue in hours the site does not need. Margins look like an infrastructure IPP's: low-teens unlevered IRR at best. Capital: $2M of seed equity cannot fund rung one. ITC transferability helps, but tax-equity and debt lenders want a sponsor with a balance sheet and an investment-grade offtaker. A seed startup with one colo contract usually needs a development partner (as Calibrant has Macquarie), which hands away most of the economics.
scored.buyers: Colocation and data-centre developers stuck in interconnection queues (Aligned, mid-size colos in ERCOT and PJM), hyperscalers, and utilities offering flexible or non-firm service. In PJM, large-load bring-your-own-capacity pathways and Voltus-style BYOC programs also count as buyers. Buyers are capitalised, but they prefer counterparties with balance sheets (Macquarie/Calibrant) or established integrators.
scored.incumbents: Rung one is already contested by well-funded players. Calibrant Energy (backed by Macquarie Asset Management) is delivering a 31 MW / 62 MWh behind-the-meter BESS at Aligned's campus, energising in 2026, to speed its grid connection. Verse raised a $54M Series B (Bessemer lead, with NVIDIA and GV) in June 2026 for Dispatch Intelligence, which orchestrates on-site batteries and solar at AI data centres so they draw less from the grid in constrained hours. It targets 100 DC deployments by 2027 with Calibrant as hardware partner. Branch Energy raised a $33M Series B (Piva, Clean Energy Ventures) to sell behind-the-meter battery capacity to data centres in PJM through bring-your-own-capacity. Electric Era's CoPower owns and operates behind-the-meter batteries plus MV transformers as capacity-as-a-service. Voltus runs a BYOC program and is acquiring Brightfield AI for DC storage, with Sunrun capacity behind it. FlexGen markets BESS for fast, flexible DC interconnection. Others: Emerald AI (software), Fluence and Tesla (hardware), Enchanted Rock (generation-based), and Form Energy and Eos at larger scale. The idea that nobody owns this rung is false as of 2026.
scored.end_state: Large. US data-centre power demand is heading to tens of GW, so the pool spanning storage, on-site generation, powered campuses and retail supply to DC load runs to multi-$10B per year (estimate, not sourced in this pass). A Google-funded Camus whitepaper (Dec 2025) estimated that bring-your-own-capacity plus flexible-connection arrangements could cut data centres' wait for a grid connection by 3-5 years, which supports the value of the unlock. Rungs 3-5 (gas plus solar, powered campuses, load-serving entity) are each well-trodden IPP or developer businesses, so the chain is credible in principle but is a capital-heavy developer roll-up.
scored.killer: Three things. First, the capital wall: realistic sites need $15-25M+ of storage each, and seed equity cannot win project finance against Macquarie-backed Calibrant. Second, crowding: Verse ($54M, NVIDIA), Branch ($33M), Electric Era, Voltus and FlexGen arrived in 2025-26. Third, utility tariff rules for flexible interconnection are bespoke and set utility by utility; as one commentary on Verse put it, there is no shared rulebook yet for how on-site batteries earn quicker connections. Concentration risk is extreme, since the first site is the company. The flexibility software (the GPU workload shifting and dispatch in rung one) is the piece being commoditised by Verse and Emerald AI. The ML is not a moat; capital and developer execution are, and the round already judged that model to be a developer, not an ML company.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is real and valuable, but it was taken in 2025-26 by capitalised players (Calibrant/Macquarie at Aligned, Verse $54M, Branch $33M, Electric Era, Voltus), the realistic unit is a $15-25M project rather than a seed-financeable 5-20 MWh box, and the moat is project finance and utility execution, not compounding ML. That gives about 15/30, not 20.

scored.name: Penstock (robot-run roll-up of small, surrendered and orphaned hydro, US and Canada)
scored.industry: Energy: small and run-of-river hydropower (0.3-10 MW, FERC-licensed or exempt; BC/Ontario independent producers)
scored.rung_one: Buy one or two small hydro plants (0.3-5 MW) from retiring family owners, mills, munis or utilities facing surrender, relicensing, refurbishment they cannot fund, or expiring BC Hydro EPA / Ontario HESP contracts. Surrender-docket plants (e.g., the 900 kW Au Train in Michigan, McGee Creek in Oklahoma, Sugar River II in New Hampshire, from the 2026 FERC surrender docket and ORNL HydroSource) can be had for near $0-2M because decommissioning costs more; operating distressed plants run about $0.5-3M. Output sells as energy, RECs and capacity under 10-20 year PPAs to utilities, co-ops or corporates at about $60-120/MWh (or $150-400/MWh to off-grid First Nations replacing diesel in Canada), about $0.15-2M a year per plant at 60%+ EBITDA once automated. The edge is replacing on-site operators with automatic trash-rack rakers, a tethered ROV for intakes and penstocks, remote SCADA and price-aware ML dispatch, lifting capacity factor from about 40% to 55% and roughly halving O&M. Incumbents Eagle Creek (Ontario Teachers'/OPG), Brookfield, Enel, Rye Development, Cube Hydro, Innergex, Boralex and Capstone buy larger plants; Voith/Sintaksa sell automation without owning plants. The sub-5 MW tail is open and no venture-backed automation-led roll-up was found.
scored.ladder: 1) One owned plant, run remotely. 2) A 20-100 plant roll-up across New England, New York, the Midwest, the Pacific Northwest and BC/Ontario/Quebec with one remote ops centre and roving robot crew, sold as aggregated 24/7 firm clean PPAs to data centers and utilities. 3) In-house relicensing and dam-safety unit taking over plants others cannot afford to relicense (about 40% of US non-federal hydro licences expire by 2035; roughly 2,000 small plants), plus third-party remote O&M. 4) Turbine, generator, governor and gate refurbishment shop fed by fleet fault data. 5) Powering non-powered dams (about 80,000 in the US) with a standardised modular turbine, small pumped storage and hybrid hydro plus battery, including off-grid hybrid microgrids co-owned with First Nations. 6) A mid-size firm-power hydro and storage IPP with its own equipment line.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: an ML underwriter over FERC eLibrary dockets, USGS streamgauges, ORNL HydroSource, EIA-923 output and BC Hydro/IESO contract registries that ranks every surrender, relicensing, contract-expiry or idle plant by restart cost against flow value (public but unreadable at scale), plus inflow forecasting from gauges, snowpack and weather, price-aware dispatch and vision-triggered debris raking. Rung 2: a fleet model of turbine wear, cavitation, vibration and bearing signatures; every plant added makes the next acquisition cheaper to underwrite and run. Rung 3: an LLM drafting relicensing documents from the fleet's own past filings, cutting relicensing from about $1-5M to a fraction; the remote-O&M stack sold to third parties adds training data. Rung 4: failure prediction sizes the refurbishment parts inventory. Rung 5: site screening for non-powered dams and pumped storage plus a standardised turbine design generator trained on real fleet costs and measured flows.
scored.seed_plan: Raise $2.5-3M: about $1.5M as equity in one or two plants (near-zero surrender-docket plants plus about $0.5M each to recommission controls, or a $2-4M distressed operating plant with seller notes or a small infrastructure-debt tranche), the rest on a remote-ops kit (PLC/SCADA retrofit, automatic raker, ML dispatch). Use USDA REAP grants, the Section 242 hydro incentive and state REC buyers; hire a retired hydro operator advisor and outsource FERC compliance. Target New England/NY and the Pacific NW where merchant prices and RECs are high; a Canadian variant via an Indigenous development corporation equity partner fits Terranox's base but has weaker L1 ($5-30M per plant). Within 12-18 months show capacity-factor uplift and O&M cut on 1-2 plants plus a ranked pipeline of 200+ targets, then raise a $20-50M asset fund for plants 2-20. Kills: FERC relicensing cost and timing, uneconomic fish-passage conditions, dam-safety liability, drought; mitigate by screening licence status and environmental conditions in the model first. Scores about 24/30: L1 4, L2 5, L3 4, L4 3, L5 5, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: A typical rung-one plant is 2 MW. At a 40-45% capacity factor it makes about 7,000-7,900 MWh a year, which at $60-90/MWh energy plus RECs is about $0.45-0.7M of revenue a year (estimate). Small hydro installed cost is $1,300-8,000/kW and O&M runs 1-6% of capex a year (IRENA cost analysis). That puts O&M at roughly $13-480/kW-yr; I'd put a sub-5 MW plant at about $100-250/kW-yr, or $0.2-0.5M a year (estimate). Halving O&M saves only about $100-250k a year per plant, and the remote-ops kit costs $0.3-0.5M a plant (estimate), so payback takes years, not months. The claimed capacity-factor lift from 40% to 55% is not credible. Capacity factor is limited by water; automation recovers availability (debris, trips, unattended outages), which is worth a few points, not 15 (estimate). Surrender-docket plants are cheap because they lose money once relicensing, fish passage and dam-safety work are counted. A law-firm review says FERC relicensing has become 'prohibitive, particularly for small projects', and ORNL finds small plants spend a larger share of cost on environmental mitigation. Every acquisition also needs FERC approval to transfer the licence. Capital: $1.5-3M of equity buys one or two plants, which fits the seed. But a fleet of 20 plants needs $40-80M of asset capital at about $1,500-3,000/kW for operating small hydro (estimate), so the company becomes an infrastructure fund. Once automated, EBITDA of about $0.2-0.4M per plant (estimate) is real but small.
scored.buyers: Output: utilities, co-ops, munis, and New England and New York REC buyers (Class I/II), plus corporate PPAs; data centers want hundreds of MW, not aggregated 1-2 MW plants. Rung exit: the plant itself sells easily to existing consolidators such as Eagle Creek, Gravity Renewables and Ampersand, or to infrastructure funds, so L2 holds up. Canada: BC Hydro and IESO contract renewals, and off-grid First Nations replacing diesel. The diesel-offset price is higher, but there are few sites and each needs a $5-30M build.
scored.incumbents: The rung is not open. Gravity Renewables (Colorado) is already a sub-5 MW small-hydro roll-up. It holds 10+ Northeast plants, including Wyre Wynd 2.78 MW, Stillwater 3.5 MW, Glendale 1.14 MW, Texon 1.5 MW, Moomaws 3.7 MW and Seneca Falls/Waterloo, and reports 50+ MW; SEC filings show about $3.2M raised in early rounds. Eagle Creek Renewable Energy (owned by Ontario Teachers') closed up to $100M of equity to fund acquisitions and bought 10 small plants from Algonquin, reaching 39 plants then and more since. Others buying small hydro (from memory, not checked this run): Ampersand Hydro, KEI (USA) Power, Patriot Hydro, Littleville Power, Brookfield, Enel (which has been selling small plants), Cube Hydro (I Squared) and Rye Development. In Canada, Innergex, Boralex, Capstone, Kruger and Sigma Energy. Voith, Andritz and Sintaksa sell automation. No venture-backed automation-first roll-up was found, but the rung itself is contested by patient infrastructure capital with a lower cost of capital.
scored.end_state: The end-state is small. Grand View Research puts the US small-hydro equipment and construction market at about $366.5M by 2030, growing 2.6% a year. Sub-10 MW US generation is roughly 1,500-2,000 plants and about 4-5 GW. At a 45% capacity factor and $60-90/MWh that is about $1-1.5B a year of revenue (estimate). All US conventional hydro is about 250 TWh, or $12-15B a year, but most of it is federal (TVA, USACE, BPA) or utility-owned and not for sale. ORNL puts non-powered-dam potential at about 12 GW, mostly in tiny, uneconomic sites (from memory). Adding pumped storage and turbine refurbishment makes it a mid-size IPP of a few hundred MW to perhaps 1-2 GW, worth $0.2-1B of revenue. That is a good infrastructure business, but not a multi-$10B chain an independent can own end to end.
scored.killer: The biggest problem is that unit economics are too small for venture scale. A 2 MW plant earns about $0.5M a year, and the software edge (O&M cut plus a few points of availability) is worth about $0.1-0.3M a year per plant. Below that, the cheap plants carry negative option value. Surrender and orphan plants are cheap because FERC relicensing, fish-passage conditions and dam-safety liability (including uncapped dam-failure liability) exceed what the plant is worth. The ML underwriter only re-ranks a universe of about 2,000 assets that brokers and Gravity and Eagle Creek already know. Growth is a capex wall of $1,500-3,000/kW funded by asset debt, against infrastructure funds with a lower cost of capital. Hydrology (drought) and FERC licence-transfer timing add risk.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is buyable and sellable. But Gravity Renewables and Eagle Creek already roll up sub-5 MW hydro, the automation edge is worth about $0.1-0.3M a year per plant, cheap surrender plants are cheap for real liability reasons, and the whole sub-10 MW US pool is only about $1-1.5B a year. It is a decent infrastructure fund, not a venture ladder: 15/30.

scored.name: Gearline (wind-drivetrain remanufacturer climbing to owning aging wind farms)
scored.industry: Energy / wind generation equipment and assets
scored.rung_one: An owned reman plant plus exchange pool of rebuilt gearboxes, main bearings and generators for out-of-warranty 1.5-2.5 MW turbines (GE 1.5, Vestas V82/V90, Siemens 2.3), about 40-50 GW in the US now 10-20 years old. Buyers: NextEra, Invenergy, Clearway, Pattern, utilities and PE funds. Gearbox reman $150-350k, generator $60-150k; the pool cuts downtime from months to days; rung one is a $20-60M revenue unit. Incumbents: Gearbox Express (PE), ZF, Stork/Fluor, Moventas, Winergy, OEM service arms; contested, but none combines a data-led exchange with farm ownership.
scored.ladder: 1) Reman drivetrain components and exchange pool. 2) Spares-as-a-service and per-turbine-year uptime contracts. 3) Full independent O&M for fleets leaving OEM full-service agreements. 4) Buying aging farms or their PTC-expired tail at distressed valuations, life-extending and partly repowering them. 5) Integrated owner-operator with component supply, O&M and power sales.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: teardown failure database linked to each component's SCADA history predicts rebuildability and parts, pricing exchanges by fleet risk. Rung 2: fleet failure prediction from customer SCADA/CMS prices uptime contracts below OEM and pre-positions inventory. Rung 3: O&M dispatch and crane-logistics optimisation. Rung 4: acquisition underwriting with a true remaining-life information edge per turbine model.
scored.seed_plan: $3M: lease a shop with a gearbox test stand (about $0.7M or partner), buy 10-15 failed cores cheaply from IPP boneyards, hire ex-OEM drivetrain engineers, sign a first exchange-pool contract with a mid-size IPP or PE fund exiting a GE/Vestas FSA. Kills: rung-4 capex wall, wind policy/PTC changes, concentration on a few platforms. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 2, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: I found no public price list for a rebuilt gearbox exchange. The best public figure (FAPESP summary of the literature) says a 1.5 MW gearbox replacement costs more than $250k once you add cranes, labour and lost revenue. Anecdotal all-in repairs reach about $800k (forum post, unverified). NREL's cost example puts a new 5 MW gearbox at $628k. So the candidate's $150-350k exchange price for a 1.5-2.5 MW machine is plausible (estimate). A reman shop's gross margin is likely 25-40% (estimate). Most of the cost is the core, bearings and gear sets, test-stand time and the warranty reserve; GBX gives a 5-year warranty that includes crane costs, which shows how big the warranty liability is. Capital: a regenerative test stand plus shop is about $0.7-1.5M (estimate). For scale, GBX's founding capital was a $3.4M state loan plus private equity (NASEO). The real capital need is the exchange pool. 10-15 cores at $50-100k each, plus $100-200k of parts to rebuild each one, ties up $2-4M of working capital before the first swap (estimate). That uses up most of a $3M seed. Rung-one revenue at maturity is about 100-200 units a year at roughly $250k, so $25-50M, which fits the $20-60M claim.
scored.buyers: Large IPPs and utilities (NextEra, Invenergy, Xcel, MidAmerican, Clearway, Pattern, AES) and PE/infrastructure owners whose OEM full-service agreements are rolling off. Xcel already buys rebuilt gearboxes from GBX under a master supply agreement (2014), so the buyer behaviour is proven. The biggest fleet owners (NextEra, Berkshire/MidAmerican) have their own drivetrain repair capability, so the addressable buyers are mid-size owners and PE funds. That concentrates revenue in a few dozen accounts.
scored.incumbents:
The rung is already held:
- Gearbox Express (Mukwonago WI) has run a US gearbox exchange-inventory model since about 2012 and has the Xcel supply deal. Its seed funding was a $3.4M state loan plus private capital, and RNWBL LLC (Houston) bought it in Feb 2022, terms undisclosed.
- Gearbox makers with US service shops: ZF Wind Power, Winergy/Flender (Flender is Carlyle-owned) and Moventas (offers up-tower GE 1.5 planetary repair "at a fraction" of a swap).
- Stork (Fluor) and Brad Foote.
- OEM service arms: GE Vernova runs repair centres for its own 1.5 MW fleet; Vestas bought the ISP UpWind Solutions in 2016; Siemens Gamesa.
- Data-led drivetrain analytics already exist: ONYX Insight (Shell-owned), Sentient Science (DigitalClone, which partnered on exchange programs), and SKF/Schaeffler condition monitoring.
So the "data-led exchange" angle is not new either.
scored.end_state: Global wind O&M is $25-46B in 2025 depending on the source (Straits $24.9B, GMI $36.2B, Fortune $46.2B). US onshore O&M is perhaps $6-10B a year (estimate: about 150 GW at $40-60/kW-yr). The full chain adds power sales from owned aging farms, which makes US wind generation revenue tens of $B a year. Doing it end to end means buying farms at about $0.3-0.8M/MW (estimate) for aging assets, so $30-80M per 100 MW farm. That is a project-finance / infra-fund business, not a venture compounding one. The US fleet is roughly 75,600 turbines at about 1,500 farms (CNBC 2025), with about 7,500 turbines already 20+ years old (LBL/PNNL 2026).
scored.killer:
1) Rung one is crowded by GBX, ZF, Winergy, Moventas and OEM arms. The biggest buyers do it in-house, and up-tower repair is cutting into whole-gearbox swaps.
2) The exchange pool takes heavy working capital, and the warranty/crane liability is serious. A few early failures of rebuilt units could sink a seed-stage company's credibility.
3) Moving to rung 4 hits an infrastructure-capital wall where cheap-capital funds win, not ML.
4) The software edge is thin. ONYX, Sentient and SKF already sell drivetrain prognostics, and teardown data is gated by the OEMs.
5) Policy (OBBBA wind credit phase-out, permitting hostility) cuts both ways. It may lengthen life extension of old turbines, but it shrinks the long-run fleet and the appetite for repowering.
6) Commodity power prices limit what the end-state owner-operator can earn.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is a real, sellable business (about $250k exchange units, proven buyers like Xcel), but GBX and the gearbox OEMs have held it since about 2012. Drivetrain prognostics software already exists (ONYX, Sentient). Climbing to farm ownership is an infra-capital game, so this scores a skeptical 15/30, not 21.

scored.name: Bladeworks (blade-robot O&M that becomes a buyer of ageing US wind farms)
scored.industry: Energy / wind O&M and repowering (about 70 GW of US wind past its 10-year PTC window)
scored.rung_one: An owned crawling blade-repair robot fleet (leading-edge erosion, lightning-receptor and crack repair) with 2 technicians per truck instead of rope-access teams, sold to independent wind owners at about $8-20k per blade or $40k per turbine campaign; erosion costs 2-5% of annual energy. Funded competitors: Aerones (about $60M+ raised), Rope Robotics, BladeBUG.
scored.ladder: 1) Blade repair crews. 2) Full-scope third-party O&M for out-of-warranty fleets. 3) Acquiring post-PTC, under-maintained 20-150 MW farms at distressed prices. 4) Partial repowering (blades, rotors, controls) on owned farms. 5) Blade remanufacture and recycling plant. 6) Wind-plus-storage IPP.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: vision damage classification from drone and robot imagery plus robot tool control. Rung 2: fleet SCADA and vibration ML predicting gearbox and bearing failures, prioritised by lost-MWh value. Rung 3: acquisition underwriter using EIA-860/923, FAA turbine data and O&M ground truth to find cheaply fixable underperformers. Rung 4: repower-design ML.
scored.seed_plan: $2.5M: license, buy (Aerones-class) or build robots, field 3 trucks, sign 5 independent owners, and get to rung 3 quickly as the differentiated move. Kills: US wind policy hostility, seasonality, blade OEM warranty fights, rung-3 capex. Scores 20/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 2, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Price: a manual rope-access leading-edge repair costs about EUR 32k and a robotic standard repair with inspection about EUR 7k (CORDIS project page; these are vendor-side figures, likely pre-2022). Rope Robotics claims half the cost of manual work and less than one day per blade. The candidate's $8-20k per blade is therefore at or above the robotic price point. Estimate: robotic campaigns run about $10-25k per turbine. Market: IntelStor puts 2025 US turbine repair spend at about $2.92B, with blades at 37% (more than $1B per year), lightning damage at $256M and blade root failures at $222M. Cost (estimate): about $0.5-1M per truck-crew per year. In-house robot hardware is about $0.3-0.8M per unit and takes 2-3 years to field-prove; Aerones raised more than $100M to get there. Licensing Aerones robots is unlikely, because Aerones sells the service, not the hardware. Northern US seasonality allows about 6-8 working months, so revenue per truck is about $1-2M per year at perhaps 30-45% gross margin. $2.5M covers 2-3 crews at most and none of rung 3. Rung 3 capital: the German benchmark is EUR 100k-1M/MW (repowering assets trade at EUR 400-700k/MW), so a 20-150 MW farm costs about $10-100M+. That needs project equity or debt, not seed money.
scored.buyers: Out-of-warranty US wind owners: independent IPPs, tax-equity SPVs, and mid-size owners such as Enel, Invenergy, Pattern, Clearway, EDPR and Avangrid. ISPs and OEM service arms (Vestas, GE Vernova, Siemens Gamesa) buy subcontract work. Large owners such as NextEra and MidAmerican mostly use in-house crews or OEM full-service agreements. Blade work is bid campaign by campaign, which makes it a procurement-driven commodity.
scored.incumbents: Rung one is held by funded players. Aerones (Riga, US operations in Texas) raised $62M in June 2025 (Activate, S2G), on top of a $30M round in 2023, a $9M seed and a EUR 4.4M EU grant. It also has $15-20M of venture debt planned, about $100M+ in total, and already services major US owners. Rope Robotics (Denmark) has the BR-8 robot. BladeBUG (UK) is grant-funded. Drone inspection and analytics are held by SkySpecs (about $80M+ raised, estimate) and others. Hundreds of rope-access ISPs compete on price, among them Rope Partner, Sky Climber, GEV and Global Wind Service. Rung 2 (third-party O&M) is held by OEMs and large ISPs. Rung 3 (asset buying) is contested by repowering-focused buyers such as Enova (targeting 1.5 GW) and infrastructure funds.
scored.end_state: The US fleet is about 1,500 onshore farms and 75,600 turbines (CNBC). US repair spend is about $2.9B per year (IntelStor 2025). NREL estimates US repowering investment could reach $25B per year by 2030, though current policy makes that optimistic. US wind generation revenue is roughly $15-20B per year (estimate: about 450 TWh at $35-45/MWh). The full pool clears multi-$10B. But end-to-end means becoming an IPP, and in that business the moat is cost of capital, not ML. The climb from crew to farm owner is a jump from a services balance sheet to project finance, not a gradual climb.
scored.killer: The decisive gap is the capex and cost-of-capital wall between rung 2 and rung 3. A seed-stage robot crew cannot buy $10-100M farms, and infrastructure funds and repowering specialists outbid it for the cheap underperformers. Rung one also faces Aerones' roughly $100M head start, with a fielded robot fleet and US customers, plus price competition from rope-access crews. Further risks: US federal wind hostility (OBBBA phase-out of wind credits, permitting freezes) depresses owner capex budgets and repowering economics; the work is seasonal; OEM warranty disputes; and owner concentration.
scored.one_line_reason: Blade repair is a real, sellable $1B per year US niche, but Aerones already holds it with about $100M raised. The differentiating jump to buying farms runs into a project-finance wall that ML underwriting does not solve, so this scores 15/30.

scored.name: Respindle (machine-tool remanufacturer that operates its own precision machining cells)
scored.industry: Machines / advanced manufacturing (CNC machine tools, contract machining)
scored.rung_one: Buy used 5-axis and horizontal machining centers (DMG Mori, Makino, Okuma, Haas; $50-250k at auction, 10-20 years old), remanufacture them (new spindle, ballscrews, retrofit controls, probing and sensor kit) and resell with warranty for $150-450k to job shops and defense primes' supplier base facing 9-18 month new-machine lead times, keeping about 30% to run in an owned machining cell. Players: Hadrian and Re:Build (owned factories on new machines), rebuilders Machine Tool Builders Inc and Gosiger (service); the reman-plus-own-cell combination is open.
scored.ladder: 1) Remanufactured, sensorised machines with warranties. 2) Owned lights-out machining cells selling parts per-part to defense, aero and semicap. 3) Machine-as-a-service paid per spindle-hour. 4) Respindle-branded new machines on proven reman castings with in-house spindles and controls. 5) A network of owned factories and the parts-to-assembly chain for defense hardware.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: used-machine valuation and condition models (auction listings, arrival vibration and backlash tests) plus standard retrofit kits with spindle-health and thermal-drift models. Rung 2: CAM/toolpath automation and process models (chatter, tool wear, thermal compensation) trained on fleet sensor data. Rung 3: fleet telemetry from placed machines feeding reman specs and predictive service. Rung 4: new-machine design from the largest labelled dataset of real-world wear.
scored.seed_plan: $3M: buy 6-8 machines at bankruptcy and auction sales (about $1M), lease a 25k sq ft building with crane capacity, hire 2 ex-OEM rebuild techs, sell the first 4 machines for cash flow, and run the rest as a cell quoting via Xometry, Paperless Parts and primes' small-business programs, pursuing AS9100 from day one. Kills: per-part price competition, 12+ month quality certification. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Rebuilders put a full rebuild at about 50-75% of a new machine's price, and treat roughly 60-75% of replacement value as the point where a rebuild stops making sense (CTE mag, MMS). A full remanufacture (rebuild plus control retrofit) usually only makes sense on machines that cost more than $400k new. My estimates, not sourced: a 10-15 year old DMU-class 5-axis costs $80-150k at auction. Bringing it back takes a spindle rebuild ($15-40k), ballscrews and ways ($10-25k), a 5-axis control retrofit ($60-150k) and 400-800 technician hours. That puts all-in cost at about $180-300k against a resale of $250-400k, so gross margin is roughly 15-30% (about $40-80k per machine). Each job takes 2-6 months. Two techs can turn about 6-10 machines a year, which is about $2-3M revenue and $0.4-0.6M gross profit. That covers its costs but does not grow on its own, because output is set by labour, not software. Capital: $1-1.5M of working capital tied up in machines, plus building, crane and probing kit, so the $3M seed is realistic. The pitch rests on lead-time arbitrage, and that is cyclical. One 2026 report gives more than 9-month lead times for high-end 5-axis machines in China (aziendeaccordi.ice.it, citing CMTBA). AMT and Japanese orders are up about 30-50% year on year with shipments lagging (twbs.com). When backlogs clear, the premium for a rebuilt machine over a new one shrinks.
scored.buyers: Rung 1 (rebuilt machines): independent job shops and tier-2/3 aero and defense suppliers. Most are small, credit-limited buyers wary of rebuilt 5-axis machines and their warranty risk. They can also just buy used machines as-is from dealers such as Hurco and Machinery Network, or from auctions. Rung 2 (parts): defense primes, aero OEMs and semicap firms (Applied Materials, Lam) through supplier programmes. These buyers have money, but they qualify suppliers slowly, usually needing AS9100, ITAR registration and first-article inspection, often taking 12+ months.
scored.incumbents: Owned AI-native machining factories: Hadrian raised a $260M Series C (Jul 2025), a $360M credit line (Aug 2026), then $1.37B at a $7.87B valuation (2026, Reuters/BNN), so it is very well funded and growing fast. Re:Build Manufacturing (about $100M+ raised, unverified in this search), and Daedalus (DE) and Isembard (UK) (venture-funded, figures not verified). Machining software: CloudNC has raised $128M in total, including a $20M round with Lockheed Ventures (Sep 2026), and its CAM Assist runs in more than 1,000 shops. Rebuild and retrofit: Machine Tool Builders Inc, Gosiger, Advanced Machine & Engineering, plus many regional rebuilders, and the OEMs' own certified pre-owned and remanufacturing programmes (Okuma, Mazak, Makino, DMG Mori). Combining a rebuild business with an owned machining cell is technically an open niche, but I think it is open because it is weak, not because others missed it.
scored.end_state: The chain is large. Global machine-tool consumption is about $70-90B a year (estimate, Gardner/VDW range), and US contract machining is about $50-60B (estimate, IBISWorld 'machine shop services' range). A defense hardware assembly layer sits on top of that. The path end to end is not credible. Rung 4 (branded new machines with in-house spindles and controls) means competing with DMG Mori, Mazak, Okuma and Fanuc, which have decades of R&D and large service networks. Rung 5 (a network of owned factories) is the race Hadrian is already winning with billions of dollars.
scored.killer: 1) Rung 1 throughput is set by technician labour, at 15-30% margins, and the 'skip the new-machine lead time' premium goes away whenever the machine-tool cycle turns down. 2) Rung 2 runs straight into Hadrian ($7.87B valuation, funded with billions) and into per-part price competition on Xometry and Paperless Parts, after a 12+ month AS9100/ITAR qualification. 3) Software does not compound much: a fleet of tens of rebuilt machines is too small a dataset to beat CloudNC or the OEMs' own condition-monitoring tools. 4) Warranty liability on 15-year-old castings and rotary axes. 5) Neither founder has machining-domain or OEM-rebuild credibility, and the plan depends on 2 hired ex-OEM techs.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung 1 is a real but labour-bound, cyclical rebuild business at 15-30% margins with only a thin ML layer. Rungs 2-5 run straight into Hadrian ($7.87B valuation, funded with billions) and the big OEMs, so the ladder does not compound: about 15/30, well below the self-estimate of 21.

scored.name: Coldfleet (cryocooler remanufacturing and rental fleet climbing to cryogenic subsystems)
scored.industry: Cryogenics / deeptech infrastructure
scored.rung_one: A rebuild line plus rental fleet of GM and pulse-tube cold heads and helium compressors (Sumitomo, Cryomech/Bluefors, Edwards CTI cryopumps): rebuilds $6-25k, rentals $1.5-4k per month per cold head with hot-spare swap guarantee. Buyers: MRI service organisations, quantum labs and startups, fabs (cryopumps), HTS magnet and fusion developers, space test chambers, all facing 6-12 month OEM lead times. Players: Sumitomo SHI, Bluefors/Cryomech, Edwards (CTI), Ulvac, small rebuilders with no fleet or telemetry.
scored.ladder: 1) Rebuild and rental fleet. 2) Remanufactured then new-design compressors and cold heads as drop-in second source. 3) Turnkey cryogenic subsystems (conduction-cooled HTS cryostats, quantum precooling, cryogen-free test chambers). 4) Large cryoplant and helium recovery/reliquefaction run as a utility at quantum and fusion campuses. Pool $25B+.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: telemetry sidecar on every unit; a fleet model predicts displacer and seal wear and adsorber saturation for pre-failure swaps. Rung 2: failure data drives seal and regenerator design changes. Rung 3: cooldown and thermal-load optimisation trained on the fleet. Rung 4: plant-level helium recovery and power optimisation.
scored.seed_plan: About $1.2M for a rebuild bench, helium leak detection, purification manifold and 60-100 used cold heads and compressors from MRI decommissioning brokers and lab surplus; sell swap-guaranteed rentals to quantum startups and university cores first, then MRI ISOs; target $2-3M revenue by month 15. Kills: OEM parts restrictions, low MRI ticket size; move to rung-2 parts within 24 months. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 5, L2 4, L3 3, L4 3, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Unit prices: rebuilt Sumitomo RDK-408A2 cold heads are listed on DOTmed at $6,750 and $10,500. RDK-408 exchange units are $22,000, with loaners available and an exchange core required. An RDK-408A3 is listed at $27,900. Rebuilt F-50 compressors are sold as quote-only exchanges or repairs. So the candidate's $6-25k rebuild range checks out. Rental at $1.5-4k per month per head is unverified. No public rental price list was found, and loaners already come bundled free with rebuilders' exchanges (estimate). Cost: used cores cost about $2-8k each from MRI decommissioning brokers (estimate). Seals, displacers, regenerators and adsorbers cost $1-4k per rebuild (estimate). The bench plus helium leak detector plus purification manifold costs about $250-400k (estimate). Gross margin on a rebuild is plausibly 40-55%. Rental fleet payback is about 12-18 months at 60-70% utilisation (estimate). Capital: about $1.2M as proposed is plausible for 60-100 units. Revenue per head is low, though. To reach $2-3M ARR by month 15 you need roughly 80-150 heads on rent, or 150-300 rebuilds a year. That is aggressive for a fleet of 60-100 units (estimate).
scored.buyers: MRI independent service organisations and hospitals, the largest and most price-sensitive volume, already served by many rebuilders. Fab cryopump users, served mainly by the OEM service programmes of Edwards/CTI and Ulvac. Quantum startups and university cores, who mostly buy new Bluefors dilution systems with the pulse tube and service bundled. HTS magnet and fusion developers (CFS, Tokamak Energy). Space test chambers. Most of these are capitalised, but tickets are small, and the quantum and fusion buyers are concentrated among a few dozen firms.
scored.incumbents: OEMs: Sumitomo SHI Cryogenics, the dominant GM/pulse-tube maker, which runs its own exchange and repair. Bluefors, about EUR 200M revenue in 2024, which acquired Cryomech in 2023 for about 600 combined staff and bundles pulse-tube service. Edwards (Atlas Copco) / CTI-Cryogenics, which runs fab cryopump service programmes. Ulvac Cryogenics. Independent rebuilders selling on DOTmed with exchange, 1-year warranty and loaners: CryoSRV and Image Technology, among many others. Large MRI ISOs (GE/Siemens/Philips multivendor service arms) also rebuild in-house. None of these is a venture startup, but the rebuild rung is already a fragmented, served market, and loaners are already offered. The only open sliver is telemetry plus hot-spare rental to quantum and fusion labs, and that niche is small.
scored.end_state: The global cryocooler market is about $3.2-3.9B in 2025 (IMARC about $3.5B, rising to $5.5B by 2034; MarketsandMarkets $3.48B, rising to $4.9B by 2030 at 7.1% CAGR). The candidate's $25B+ pool only works if it adds industrial cryoplants, helium recovery and LNG-scale cryogenic equipment. That segment belongs to Linde, Air Liquide, Chart Industries and Air Products. A small rebuilder has no credible path there. The realistic addressable chain (cryocoolers plus cryogen-free subsystems plus service) is about $5-8B (estimate). That is a solid niche, not a multi-$10B end-to-end chain.
scored.killer: Sumitomo and Bluefors control seals, displacers, regenerator materials and firmware, and can restrict parts or void service. Rung one is a low-ticket, fragmented MRI repair business already served by many rebuilders offering loaners, so it is a service shop rather than a venture-scale wedge. Fleet telemetry on about 100 units is too thin a dataset for ML to be the moat; GM wear prediction is mostly hours-run plus pressure/temperature thresholds. Quantum and fusion demand is concentrated, and those buyers bundle the cooler with a new Bluefors system. The rung-2 jump to designing new cold heads and compressors is a multi-year, $10M+ hardware programme against Sumitomo's scale and cost. That is the capex and competence wall.
scored.one_line_reason: The rebuild line is winnable and makes money, but rung one is an already-served, fragmented MRI repair market, the ML layer is thin predictive maintenance, and the $25B end state only adds up by including industrial-gas cryoplants owned by Linde and Air Liquide, so it scores about 15/30.

scored.name: Vacuumworks (independent fab dry-pump and cryopump remanufacturing climbing to subfab-as-a-service)
scored.industry: Semiconductor equipment / machines
scored.rung_one: A remanufacturing plant for semiconductor dry, turbomolecular and cryopumps (Edwards, Ebara, Pfeiffer, Kashiyama, CTI) with exchange rebuilds at $8-40k, sold to trailing-edge and specialty fabs (200mm analog, MEMS, SiC, GaN, compound semi) and university fabs that pay OEM exchange prices and wait months. Players: Edwards (Atlas Copco), Ebara, Pfeiffer/Busch, Kashiyama, independent rebuilders without fleet telemetry.
scored.ladder: 1) Pump exchange and rebuild. 2) Pump fleet under per-hour uptime contracts. 3) Subfab-as-a-service (pumps, abatement, chillers, gas-line maintenance). 4) Second-source components and own harsh-process pump design. 5) Refurbished 200mm tools and subfab packages for new specialty fabs. Pool $15B+.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: teardown data (deposition chemistry, bearing wear, rotor fouling) labelled against fab process telemetry trains a rebuild-interval model. Rung 2: predictive swap scheduling across a multi-OEM fleet. Rung 3: subfab energy and abatement optimisation with shared savings. Rung 4: design from a process-specific failure library. Rung 5: tool-condition data for refurbished-tool pricing.
scored.seed_plan: About $2M for a rebuild shop near a 200mm cluster (Texas, Oregon or New York), an exchange pool from fab closures and surplus, and an ex-Edwards service lead; start with university and compound-semi fabs; target $3M revenue by month 18. Kills: OEM service lock-in via warranty and fab contracts, cyclicality. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 3, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Unit price: the candidate's $8-40k exchange price is optimistic for dry pumps. The only public price list I found (a 2009-era Ideal Vacuum flyer) puts rebuilt Edwards iQDP-40/80 units at about $4.9-10.9k, says a rebuilt unit costs under 20% of a new pump, and gives a 90-day warranty. Turbo and cryo rebuilds are probably in the same $5-15k range (my estimate, not found in search). Cost: Edwards major repair kits list at about $1.7k (iQDP-40) to about $4k (iH600/1000), and an Ebara A70W kit at about $1.7k. Add roughly 10-20 hours of skilled labour and cleaning of hazardous deposits (my estimate). Gross margin is probably 35-50%, the normal range for a job shop (estimate). Capital: about $1-2M covers a shop with cleanroom bench, leak and run-in test stands, fume and hazmat handling, and an exchange pool of about 100-200 cores. Seed money is enough. Volume: the $3M revenue target at month 18 means about 300-500 rebuilds a year at $6-10k each. That is possible, but it is a services-scale business with margins capped by OEM kit pricing.
scored.buyers: Trailing-edge 200mm fabs (TI, Microchip, onsemi, SkyWater, X-Fab Lubbock, Bosch, Wolfspeed and other SiC/GaN fabs), compound-semi and MEMS fabs, university and government nanofabs, and solar, coating and R&D vacuum users. All are capitalised, but many large fabs sign fleet service contracts with Edwards or Ebara. Universities are small, slow-paying accounts. Buyers come from a short regional list, so customer concentration is high.
scored.incumbents: OEMs: Edwards (Atlas Copco Vacuum Technique, which reports growing semi service and an aftermarket strategy) runs a remanufacturing and exchange programme and uses only genuine parts. Ebara (by one unverified estimate about 40-50% share of semi dry pumps) has five dry-pump overhaul factories in Japan, plus Dresden (opened 2021) and Hefei (2021), with a second Korean plant due in 2027. Pfeiffer is now under Busch, and Kashiyama and Ulvac are also present. Independents already serve rung one: Ideal Vacuum (sells rebuild kits and rebuilt pumps), PTB Sales (Azusa CA, founded 1996, about 35 staff, about $9M revenue by a third-party estimate), PolVac (PA), Grauling Research, Trillium (dry pumps, cryo cold heads, He compressors, chillers, abatement), and Korean shops such as Vacuum World and Hyesung. The incumbents are a crowded long tail of small, bootstrapped shops plus OEMs pushing into overhaul. No venture-funded independent appeared in search, but the rung is not open.
scored.end_state: The semiconductor vacuum pump market is about $4.9-5.2B in 2025, growing about 6.5-7% a year to about $9B+ by 2034-35 (DataM Intelligence, Dataintelo). The top six vendors (Edwards, Atlas Copco, Pfeiffer, Ulvac, Busch, Ebara) hold about 62%. Adding abatement, chillers, gas systems and refurbished 200mm tools could plausibly reach about $10-15B (estimate). That only reaches the $15B+ figure if subfab and refurbished tools are counted generously. The end state is to become an Atlas Copco/Ebara-scale subfab supplier, competing head-on with OEMs that own the pump designs, the parts supply and the fab master service agreements. The refurbished-tool rung is already contested by surplus-tool dealers. A credible end-to-end path is weak.
scored.killer: The OEMs control the parts (genuine kits, rotor and stator supply) and hold fab-wide service MSAs and warranty terms. Ebara and Edwards are building overhaul capacity specifically to cut lead times, which removes the "wait months" wedge. Rung one is a commoditised job shop already served by many independents, so its margins are low. The ML layer is thin: an independent sees teardown deposits but not the fab's process telemetry, and fabs rarely share it, so there is no defensible data flywheel. Semi capex and utilisation cycles (Vacuum Technique fell 6% organically in Q3 2025) add cyclical risk. Concentration in a few regional fabs adds more.
scored.one_line_reason: Seed money can win rung one, but it is a crowded, low-margin rebuild-shop business already held by OEM overhaul factories and many independents (PTB, PolVac, Ideal Vac, Trillium). The fab telemetry the ML needs is out of reach, and climbing means fighting Atlas Copco and Ebara on their home turf. Score: 15/30.

scored.name: Assured Time (owned terrestrial timing and GNSS-jamming detection network)
scored.industry: Critical-infrastructure protection / resilient PNT
scored.rung_one: An owned network of GNSS interference-detection sensors bundled with a holdover timing appliance (chip-scale atomic clock plus RF-locked backup), installed at customer sites as a $1.5-4k per site per month subscription for grid substations (microsecond PMU and relay timing under NERC pressure), telecom, data centres, ports and airports, starting in documented jamming regions (Baltic, Eastern Mediterranean, US Southwest, Texas/Mexico border). Incumbents: NextNav, Satelles/Iridium STL, UrsaNav, Hidden Level, HawkEye 360, Septentrio/Spirent; none owns a utility-site timing-plus-detection subscription network.
scored.ladder: 1) Per-site jam detection plus holdover. 2) Regional interference map and jammer geolocation sold to FAA, ports, coast guards and insurers. 3) Owned terrestrial timing transmitters (eLoran-class or licensed-band) on leased towers selling wholesale time and position. 4) A sovereign national backup-PNT network under government concession (US and UK eLoran mandates stalled). 5) PNT receivers and modules for autonomy, drones and vehicles.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: anomaly detection distinguishing jamming, spoofing and benign interference, improving with every site. Rung 2: cross-site TDOA jammer geolocation that improves with density. Rung 3: transmitter siting and ASF propagation-correction maps from the sensor base. Rung 4: integrity monitoring and authentication. Rung 5: receiver fusion firmware tuned on the largest field interference corpus.
scored.seed_plan: Build the box from SDRs, CSACs and multi-constellation receivers ($6-10k BOM), land 2 co-op/municipal utilities and 1 port in a jamming-affected region (Finland, Estonia, Poland via EU resilience funds, or a US border utility) for 100-200 sites ($3-6M ARR potential in 18 months), plus an AFWERX/DIU SBIR for geolocation; about $2M spend. Kills: slow utility procurement and the capex and spectrum needs of rung 3. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 3, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: No web searches ran (the shared search budget was used up), so all numbers are from prior knowledge and are estimates. Box BOM: a Microchip SA65 chip-scale atomic clock is about $3-5k (est). A multi-constellation timing receiver plus SDR is about $1-3k (est). The candidate's $6-10k BOM is plausible. Price check: utilities today buy substation GPS clocks once, e.g. SEL-2488 at about $3-6k (est), which already has anti-spoofing and holdover options. Safran (Orolia) SecureSync with BroadShield jam/spoof detection and Meinberg units sell as one-time hardware at about $5-20k (est). The proposed $1.5-4k per site per month is $18-48k a year, roughly 5-10x the 10-year cost of what utilities already own. A realistic subscription is about $100-400 per site per month (est). At that price, 100-200 sites give about $0.2-1M ARR, not $3-6M. Gross margin on a $250/month subscription with an $8k box: payback is about 30+ months, hardware-financed. Seed capital of about $2M is enough to build the box and pilots. It is not enough to finance the fleet: about $1-2M of deployed hardware for 200 sites (est). Rung 3 eLoran-class transmitters are about $5-20M+ per station including site, antenna and spectrum (est, from US/UK eLoran programme estimates).
scored.buyers: Utilities: NERC CIP and PMU/relay timing, but co-ops and munis procure slowly, and today's GPS clocks are capex line items with no recurring budget. Telecom operators: they already run PTP/SyncE grandmasters from Microchip, Oscilloquartz/Adtran and Ericsson. Data centres. Ports, airports and ANSPs. Baltic and Nordic governments, which are actively buying jamming monitoring after GNSS interference since 2023. Militaries via DIU/AFWERX and NATO. Rung 2 data buyers: FAA, EASA, coast guards, insurers. The most capitalised and motivated buyers are governments and defence, not utilities. Even then, the ministry usually wants to own the sensor network, not subscribe to a startup's.
scored.incumbents: Funding and price figures are estimates from prior knowledge; no searches ran. Timing hardware with built-in jam/spoof detection: Safran (bought Orolia in 2022, about EUR 0.5B est; SecureSync/VersaSync with BroadShield), Microchip (CSAC maker, TimeProvider grandmasters, BlueSky GNSS firewall), SEL (SEL-2488, dominant in substations), Meinberg, Oscilloquartz/Adtran. Interference detection: GPSPatron (Latvia, GP-Probe networks sold in the Baltics), Chronos Technology (UK, CTL3520), Spirent GSS200D, Septentrio, Focal Point, infiniDome, Zephr (VC-backed), Hidden Level (passive RF network, VC-backed), HawkEye 360 (more than $400M raised, est), Spire/ADS-B-derived maps (gpsjam.org, Flightradar24 free). Alternative PNT: Iridium STL (bought Satelles for about $115M, 2024, approx), NextNav (public, about $1-2B market cap est; pursuing 900 MHz terrestrial PNT at the FCC), Xona Space (LEO PNT, about $90M+ raised est), TrustPoint, UrsaNav (eLoran), Hellen Systems. The utility-site subscription bundle is technically unowned. But it is unowned because SEL, Safran and Microchip already sell the same capability as hardware into the same substations.
scored.end_state: Sizes are estimates from prior knowledge. The timing/synchronisation equipment market is about $3-5B a year (est). GNSS interference detection and monitoring is in the low hundreds of millions to about $1B (est). Sovereign backup PNT (eLoran or terrestrial) is a few billion dollars of government programme spend, spread over decades, with US and UK eLoran repeatedly stalled or underfunded (approx). The broader GNSS downstream market is about $200B+ (est), but it is overwhelmingly chipsets and devices owned by Qualcomm, Broadcom and u-blox. Rung 5 (receivers for autonomy) means competing with u-blox, Septentrio, Trimble and Hexagon/NovAtel. The credible end-to-end pool is roughly $5-10B, not multi-$10B. Rung 4 depends on winning a government concession, which a startup cannot climb to through the sensor network.
scored.killer: Three things could kill it. First, the price: utilities already own one-time-purchase GPS clocks with spoof detection from SEL, Safran and Microchip, so a $1.5-4k/month subscription collapses to about $100-400. That makes rung one hardware-financed and tiny. Second, buyer and data concentration: the real buyers are governments and defence, which prefer to own the networks. Jamming maps are partly free already (ADS-B-derived gpsjam.org) and are sold by HawkEye 360 and Hidden Level. Third, the ladder's later rungs: rung 3 to 4 needs spectrum, transmitter capex and a sovereign concession that historically stalls, and NextNav, Iridium STL and Xona are already pursuing that position. Commodity hardware plus slow utility procurement completes the picture.
scored.one_line_reason: The physical rung is buildable and the jamming threat is real. But rung one asks utilities to rent, for about 10x the price, what SEL, Safran and Microchip already sell them as a one-time box with spoof detection, and the ladder tops out in government concessions and receiver markets held by NextNav, Iridium and u-blox. About 15/30, below the candidate's own 20.
