scored.name: Cleared Capacity (classified facility and compute as rentable capacity)
scored.industry: Security tech / sovereign infrastructure (SCIFs, IL6/TS GPU compute)
scored.rung_one: Owned, ICD-705-accredited SCIF suites near defense hubs (El Segundo, Austin, Huntsville, Colorado Springs, NoVA) sold as cleared seats at about $3-6k per seat per month or $40-120k per month per private suite, with facility-clearance sponsorship support, to venture-backed defense startups winning classified programs that cannot spend 18-24 months and $2-5M building a SCIF, plus primes' overflow and allied entrants. Competition: local SCIF builders (construction, not operators), a few shared-SCIF coworking operators, and hyperscale Secret regions (AWS, Microsoft, Oracle); moderately open.
scored.ladder: 1) Shared SCIF space. 2) Classified network drops and an IL6/Secret enclave with on-prem GPU racks rented per GPU-hour. 3) Multi-city TS/SCI compute pods as a classified neocloud. 4) Hardened accredited AI data centres sold to agencies and allies. 5) Sovereign classified cloud development for allied governments.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: accreditation automation turning ICD-705 build packages, TEMPEST/RF test data and inspection history into templated, faster accreditations. Rung 2: a compliance-as-code ATO pipeline with continuous monitoring and auto-generated RMF artifacts. Rung 3: utilisation optimisation across classified GPU pools. Rung 4: cross-tenant insider-threat and anomaly ML. Each accreditation and ATO shortens the next.
scored.seed_plan: Lease one 8-12k sq ft shell near a defense cluster, build a 40-seat modular SCIF ($1.5-2M with prefab RF panels), pre-sell to 5-8 defense startups via LOIs, accredit through a sponsoring government customer in 9-12 months, run at 80% utilisation (about $2M ARR), and expand on debt. Weakness: thin ML at rung one and a real-estate-like business. Rubric estimate about 19/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 2, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: ALL FIGURES ARE ESTIMATES. The search budget for this turn was used up before any query ran, so nothing here is web-verified. Build cost: a SCIF built to ICD-705 typically runs about $300-1,000 per sq ft on top of the shell, depending on TEMPEST/RF shielding, acoustic treatment, IDS/access control and the need for a 24/7 or response-force alarm posture. So a 40-seat SCIF of about 8-12k sq ft costs about $2.5-5M fully fitted, not $1.5-2M; prefab RF panel modules lower the cost but do not halve it. Add shell lease (about $35-60/sq ft per year in NoVA or El Segundo), a cleared FSO/ISSM staff of 2-4 at $150-200k each, guard or IDS monitoring and a classified network drop (SIPR/JWICS connections need a sponsor and 6-18 months). Opex is about $1-1.5M per year. Revenue: 40 seats at $3-6k per month and 80% occupancy gives about $1.2-2.3M ARR. Gross margin on that looks real-estate-like (about 30-50%), with payback of 2-4 years. Capital needed: about $3-5M per site, which is right at or above the seed ceiling, before any GPU enclave. Timing: accreditation depends on a government Accrediting Official, and it only happens once a sponsoring contract (a DD-254) exists. 9-12 months is optimistic; 12-24 months is typical. The founders do not control that critical path.
scored.buyers: Venture-backed defense startups with new classified contracts (SBIR Phase III, OTAs, DIU awards) who need cleared space before they can perform; primes' program overflow; allied or foreign-owned entrants operating under FOCI mitigation; cleared consultancies. Buyers have capital but are fragmented and churny. A startup that wins a big program usually builds its own SCIF within 2-3 years (examples of firms that did: Anduril, Palantir, Shield AI). Rung-two GPU buyers would be the same startups plus intelligence community and DoD program offices, who mostly buy through hyperscaler classified regions under JWCC.
scored.incumbents: Not verified this session because the search budget was exhausted; this list is from prior knowledge. Rung one (shared SCIF): local and regional shared-SCIF and cleared coworking operators already run near Huntsville, NoVA, Colorado Springs and San Diego. Defense accelerators and campuses (for example Catalyst Campus in Colorado Springs, plus university-affiliated and FFRDC spaces) offer sponsored SCIF access. SCIF builders and integrators (Leidos, Iron Bow, many 8(a) construction firms) build turnkey SCIFs, and modular SCIF vendors sell prefab units. Government programs aimed at shared classified space for non-traditional vendors also compete at near-zero price. Rung two and up (classified compute): AWS Secret and Top Secret regions; Microsoft Azure Government Secret and Top Secret; Oracle Cloud for US Government Secret and Top Secret; Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped (authorised at Secret/TS); CoreWeave and other neoclouds pursuing federal accreditation; Second Front Systems (IL5/IL6 PaaS, raised over $100M, estimate); Defense Unicorns; Palantir FedStart. The JWCC contract vehicle ($9B ceiling) is held by AWS, Microsoft, Google and Oracle. Rung one is fragmented but not empty. Rungs 3-5 are held by the best-capitalised companies in the world.
scored.end_state: Estimates. US classified and defense cloud plus IC IT spending is tens of $B per year: DoD IT/cyber budget is about $60B+ per year, JWCC's ceiling is $9B, and the IC's C2E contract is reported at "tens of billions" over its life. The sovereign and allied classified cloud market is likely $10B+ globally. The pool is large, but end-to-end capture means displacing AWS, Microsoft, Oracle and Google inside accredited regions, which requires multi-$B capex and agency AO trust. The credible end state for a startup is a regional classified colocation and neocloud player at about $0.5-2B revenue, not the whole chain.
scored.killer: Five killers. (1) Sponsor and accreditation dependence: the government AO, the DD-254 sponsor and DCSA/agency inspection set the timeline, and no software shortens their human review in a way that compounds. (2) Capex wall and real-estate economics: each site costs about $3-5M with 30-50% margins, so growth is debt-financed real estate. (3) Churn and concentration: successful tenants graduate to their own SCIFs, and tenant demand tracks a few program awards and continuing resolutions. (4) Free or cheap government alternatives for shared classified space for non-traditional vendors. (5) Rung three onward runs head-on into hyperscaler classified regions under JWCC, where a startup cannot win on price, trust or capex. Security-incident liability is a further risk: one spill can lose the accreditation for every tenant.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real, sellable but low-margin cleared real-estate business: the government sets the accreditation timeline, so the software and ML layer barely compounds. Rung one costs more than seed money, and every rung above two belongs to the hyperscalers' classified regions. That puts it at about 15/30, below the proposer's 19.

scored.name: Perimeter (autonomous security operations for substations and remote energy sites)
scored.industry: Security tech / energy infrastructure
scored.rung_one: An owned and operated sensor-plus-robot security service at unmanned substations, BESS sites and solar farms (thermal/radar towers, a docked drone, acoustic gunshot and intrusion sensors) with a 24/7 SOC, sold to utilities and IPPs at $3-10k per site per month, satisfying NERC CIP-014 and insurer requirements. Incumbents: Percepto, Skydio Dock, Asylon, Ambient/Evolv-type software, Allied Universal guards; none is an energy-focused owned-fleet operator with bundled inspection revenue.
scored.ladder: 1) Per-site monitored security. 2) Fleet-wide utility contracts with copper-theft and vandalism recovery guarantees. 3) The same fleet doing remote inspection (thermal hot-spots, vegetation, equipment condition) for O&M revenue. 4) Counter-UAS and physical-hardening installation. 5) Insurance and risk transfer underwritten on incident data. 6) Operator of record for physical security and remote ops across distributed energy assets.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: multi-sensor fusion ML cutting false alarms so one operator covers hundreds of sites. Rung 2: cross-site threat prediction (theft patterns, attack precursors). Rung 3: inspection-defect models from repeated imagery of the same assets. Rung 4: drone detection and classification from deployed radar/RF. Rung 5: actuarial models from incident data.
scored.seed_plan: About $2M: integrate COTS sensors and a docked drone into a $60-120k site kit financed through monthly contracts, and pilot with 2-3 co-ops/munis and BESS IPPs under fire-department and insurer scrutiny. Kills: utility procurement cycles, FAA BVLOS rules (eased by Part 108), hardware commoditisation; the moat must be operational data and contracts. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 3, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: I could not verify any numbers live. The shared web-search budget for this turn was already used up, so every figure below is an estimate from prior knowledge, not a fetched source. Unit price: $3-10k per site per month, as the candidate states. For comparison, LiveView Technologies-style mobile AI camera towers lease for about $1-3k per month (estimate), so the premium has to come from adding a drone and inspection. Kit cost: about $60-120k per site (candidate's figure; a docked drone at $50-150k plus thermal/radar towers at $20-60k makes this plausible, estimate). The SOC operator costs about $70-90k per year fully loaded (estimate). If ML lets one operator cover 100+ sites, gross margin on a $5k/month site would be about 50-65% once hardware is depreciated over 4-5 years (estimate). Capital: each site needs $60-120k up front for a contract that pays back in 15-30 months. About $2M of seed money funds roughly 10-20 sites before debt or lease financing is needed. That proves the product but leaves the company capex-bound: every new site has to be financed before it earns.
scored.buyers: Investor-owned utilities with sites covered by NERC CIP-014. CIP-014 applies only to a few hundred to roughly 1,000 critical transmission substations (estimate), and the big IOUs already secure those through integrators. Co-ops and municipal utilities run about 2,800 of the ~3,000 US utilities, but they have thin budgets and slow board-driven procurement. BESS and solar IPPs face insurer and fire-department pressure and are probably the fastest buyers. They are capitalised, but they push for low opex. The roughly 55-70k US transmission and distribution substations (estimate) are mostly not mandated to have this kind of security, so buyers pay for it discretionarily. Copper-theft losses and attacks like Moore County 2022 create demand, but the budget is episodic.
scored.incumbents: Figures are estimates from prior knowledge, not verified this turn. Percepto: drone-in-a-box focused on energy and utility sites, which overlaps directly with rungs 1 and 3; raised about $100M+ total. Skydio: Dock, sold to utilities; raised about $740M+ total, including a ~$230M Series E in 2023. Asylon: robotic perimeter security as a service with an owned fleet and SOC, which is exactly this model; raised about $40M+, including a Series B around 2024. LiveView Technologies (LVT): owned, monitored AI camera towers at remote sites; raised about $100M+ in growth equity. Knightscope: public, but weak. Ambient.ai and Evolv: software and venue screening, not energy. Allied Universal and Securitas: guard services worth tens of $B, already contracted to utilities. CIP-014 integrators such as Black & Veatch, Burns & McDonnell and Hitachi Energy design and install the hardening. Rung one is crowded: Asylon plus LVT already deliver an owned, monitored fleet, and Percepto already sells drone inspection to utilities.
scored.end_state: All figures are estimates. US physical security for utilities and energy assets is probably a $3-8B a year spend, guards included. Drone inspection for utilities is about $1-3B. Counter-UAS for critical infrastructure is still small and federally restricted, since only DOD, DOE, DHS and DOJ hold mitigation authority today. Insuring physical-security risk for energy assets is a small niche of property insurance. Combined, the rungs reach a pool in the high single-digit $B. That is a security-services roll-up. It does not lead to owning an energy chain: being 'operator of record for remote ops' is O&M contracting, and asset owners will not give up control of their assets.
scored.killer: The owned hardware fleet means a capex wall per site, and the hardware commoditises (Skydio, DJI-alternative docks, LVT towers). Procurement is slow and concentrated: co-ops and municipal utilities take 12-24 months, and IOUs buy through incumbent integrators. Asylon, LVT and Percepto already hold the operated-fleet position. Counter-UAS mitigation is legally closed to private operators. The ML false-alarm edge is an efficiency gain competitors can match, so the moat falls back on contracts and field operations. That makes this an execution business in the same way the powered-brownfield ideas were.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but crowded security-as-a-service niche (Asylon, LVT, Percepto, Skydio) that tops out as a single-digit-$B security and inspection services roll-up, not a vertical energy chain, with weak data compounding across the rungs. Total 15/30.

scored.name: Steelback (robotic selective dismantling of steel-frame buildings into certified reusable structural steel)
scored.industry: Construction / materials (US structural steel, about $100B+ a year; embodied-carbon rules)
scored.rung_one: Robotic deconstruction contracts on mid-size steel-frame commercial and industrial buildings at about $10-30/sq ft against conventional demolition, plus ownership of recovered beams, which are scanned, tested and recertified and sold at about $900-1,400/ton to fabricators and GCs needing near-zero embodied carbon under Buy Clean (California, New York, GSA), LEED and EU taxonomy rules: owners pay to demolish, GCs pay for low-carbon steel. Competitors: conventional demolition firms (scrap to EAF), UK reuse firms CleanSteel and EMR, Material Cycles; largely open in the US.
scored.ladder: 1) Deconstruction crews with robotic cutters plus a beam yard. 2) Certified reclaimed-steel stockyard and marketplace with per-beam digital twins. 3) Design-for-reuse fabrication shop building from reclaimed members. 4) Buy-old/build-new developer partnerships offering carbon-negative frames. 5) Other materials (glass, facade, MEP) through the same flow.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: pre-demolition lidar plus OCR of old drawings for member inventory, robot cut planning and lifting-load ML. Rung 2: beam grading from scan, ultrasonic and hardness data, predicting section and grade from geometry and era, making certification cheap. Rung 3: combinatorial inventory-to-design structural matching. Rung 4: carbon accounting and EPD generation.
scored.seed_plan: $2.5M: start as a licensed demolition subcontractor in the Bay Area or NYC, buy 2 used Brokk-class remote demolition machines plus the cutting and scanning stack, lease a yard, engage a structural engineer to certify reclaimed steel under AISC/SCI reuse guidance, and pre-sell steel to 2-3 low-carbon GCs. Kills: liability and certification friction, niche reuse demand, project timing mismatch. Scores 22/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 3, L5 5, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: All estimates. The web search budget ran out before any query ran and the one fetch failed, so nothing here is checked against a source. Conventional US commercial demolition runs about $4-10/sq ft. Selective deconstruction costs about 1.5-3x that, because it is crane-and-torch ironworker labour. Owners pay a premium for it only when a mandate or LEED points force them, so the pitched $10-30/sq ft is high. Recovered beams have a floor at scrap value (heavy melt about $300-400/t). New US wide-flange sells at about $1,000-1,400/t at the mill or service centre. UK reclaimed-steel practice prices reused sections near new, or 10-30% below it, once testing and recertification are paid for. Testing, coupon, blasting and storage costs are probably $100-300/t. Gross spread over scrap is about $400-800/t on paper, but yield is low: about 10-25 kg of frame steel per sq ft, and only part of it is reusable without damage (bolted, unencased, unmodified sections). A 100k sq ft building gives roughly 1,000-2,000 t of steel and maybe 40-60% reusable, so about $0.3-0.8M of steel margin a project, earned only if a matching buyer exists at the right time. Capital: Brokk-class machines cost about $250-600k new, and US demolition also needs bonding, about $5-10M general liability plus umbrella insurance, a yard and crane rental. $2.5M is enough for a few jobs, not a business. Brokks also do not fit steel-frame disassembly well: they are concrete and interior demolition tools, while frames come down by crane-held member cutting.
scored.buyers: Rung-one demolition is bought by property owners, REITs and developers clearing sites. They are capitalised but price-driven, and they buy deconstruction only under mandates such as Portland's or San Antonio's residential deconstruction ordinances, or when a LEED or embodied-carbon target applies. Reclaimed steel would be bought by GCs and fabricators on Buy Clean or LEED projects and by tech or corporate campuses with Scope 3 targets. That demand is thin and needs a matched spec. In the US, Buy Clean steel limits are already met by EAF mill steel, so reuse is not required to comply.
scored.incumbents: US demolition is held by regional, often family-owned contractors: NorthStar/Brandenburg-scale nationals, Lindamar, Dem-Con, Manafort and many locals. They send steel to scrap processors (Radius/Schnitzer, CMC, Nucor's David J. Joseph). Reclaimed-steel stockholding is a UK and EU niche: Cleveland Steel & Tubes (long-running UK reclaimed stockist), EMR's CleanSteel reuse operation, Material Cycles and Arup-backed reuse pilots. Robotic demolition equipment comes from Brokk, Husqvarna and Conjet; construction-robot startups such as Built Robotics work on other tasks. As far as I know, no venture-funded US company does certified reuse of reclaimed structural steel at scale, so rung one is open, but likely because the economics are weak rather than because nobody has seen it. No funding figures could be checked.
scored.end_state: The US structural steel market (mill shapes plus fabrication and erection) is roughly $40-80B a year (estimate; the candidate's $100B+ likely includes rebar, plate and sheet). The reachable pool is the reused share. Even optimistic EU circular-economy studies put structural reuse at single-digit percent of supply, because reusable demolition supply is tiny compared with new-build demand and member sizes rarely match. That is a pool of maybe $1-4B in the US (estimate). The later rungs (design-for-reuse fabrication, developer partnerships, other materials) are each lower-margin businesses run by entrenched local trades, so an end-to-end chain looks less like a multi-$10B ML compounder and more like a regional rollup of demolition, stockyard and fabrication businesses.
scored.killer: US steel is already low-carbon. About 70% of US crude steel and nearly all wide-flange sections come from EAF mills (Nucor, Steel Dynamics, CMC, Gerdau) at roughly 1.0-1.2 tCO2e/t fabricated (AISC industry EPD figure, from memory). Buy Clean CA, NY and GSA limits are met by new EAF steel, so the reuse carbon premium that makes UK and EU reuse viable (against blast-furnace steel at about 2+ t) mostly disappears in the US. On top of that: supply and demand timing rarely line up (a building comes down when it comes down, while designs need sections specified 12-24 months ahead); yield of reusable members is low; liability and engineer-of-record reluctance to sign off on reclaimed members of unknown grade; bonding and insurance walls on demolition; low-margin, labour-heavy, local demolition economics; and robots add little to crane-and-torch frame dismantling. The software layer is mostly a cost-reducer for grading and matching, not a compounding moat. ML does not unlock mispriced value here.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is open, but mostly because US EAF steel already meets Buy Clean, which leaves the reuse premium thin. The value is in demolition and stockyard work that wins on execution, with software as a modest cost-reducer rather than a compounding ML moat (about 15/30, not the 22 claimed; scored from prior knowledge because the search budget ran out before any query ran).

scored.name: AlloySort Yard (alloy-specific aluminium scrap to billet)
scored.industry: Materials recycling and casting: secondary aluminium, extrusion billet and sheet ingot
scored.rung_one: An owned sortation plant buying shredded aluminium (Twitch/Zorba) from auto shredders and sorting it via LIBS, X-ray and vision ML into alloy-specific streams (6061/6063, 5xxx, cast A356, high-Cu 2xxx) for extruders and billet casthouses (Hydro, Novelis, Constellium, Kaiser) at about 15-30c/lb over Zorba; a 50 kt/yr plant is about $100-150M revenue at thin spreads. Incumbents: Sortera Technologies (funded), Tomra/Steinert (sorter vendors), shredders SDI/OmniSource and Schnitzer/Radius selling mixed Zorba to export.
scored.ladder: 1) Sorted alloy-specific scrap. 2) Owned remelt and DC casthouse making low-carbon 6xxx billet from 90%+ scrap ($400-700/t premium). 3) Extrusion presses for EV, solar-frame and data-center rack profiles. 4) Fabricated parts and OEM closed-loop buy-backs. 5) Sheet ingot and upcycled auto sheet; a $40B+ US aluminium product market favoured by CBAM and Section 232.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: alloy classifier, per-bale melt-chemistry forecasting and shredder-feed provenance. Rung 2: charge optimisation minimising primary sweetening, the main margin lever. Rung 3: extrusion die and process ML using known billet chemistry. Rung 4: part-level traceability and carbon accounting.
scored.seed_plan: $3M: two used LIBS and XRT sorters plus conveyors and an in-house classifier, sited in a shredder's yard under a tolling split (no land or permit wall), with offtake to one or two extruders by month 9. Kills: thin commodity spreads, rung-2+ capex, funded competitor Sortera. Rubric estimate about 18/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 4, L4 4, L5 2, L6 1.
scored.rung_one_economics: Not verified: web search budget was exhausted, so all figures are from prior knowledge and are estimates. Feed: shredded Zorba (mixed nonferrous) has historically traded around 55-75% of LME aluminium. That is roughly $0.70-1.10/lb in 2024-26 (est., Fastmarkets/AMM-style quotes). Sorted 6063 extrusion-grade or alloy-specific scrap gets roughly a 15-35c/lb uplift (est.). A 50 kt/yr plant (110M lb) handles about $100-150M of material throughput. Gross spread at 15-25c/lb is about $15-25M/yr before recovery losses (5-15% of feed comes out as off-grade or residue, est.), energy, labour and the shredder's tolling share. With a 50/50 tolling split, the startup keeps about $5-10M gross margin at full scale (est.). Capital: one LIBS or XRT sorter line runs about $1.5-4M installed (est.), and a 50 kt plant needs 3-6 lines plus a heavy-media/eddy-current front end, about $15-30M (est.). The $3M seed buys about 1-2 lines, which is roughly 10-20 kt/yr, about $1.5-4M gross spread, about $1-2M to the startup. Working capital is the hidden wall: about 2-4 weeks of inventory at $1/lb on 20 kt is $2-4M of metal on the balance sheet, or else a tolling arrangement where the shredder owns the metal and keeps most of the upside. Rung 2 (remelt plus DC billet casthouse, about 100-200 kt) costs roughly $150-400M (est.; for comparison, Hydro Cassopolis cost about $150M for 120 kt).
scored.buyers: Billet and extrusion makers, and sheet rollers, that need low-carbon, high-recycled-content feed: Hydro (North America extrusion and recyclers), Novelis, Constellium, Kaiser, Arconic, Matalco, Vista Metals, Gränges, Bonnell/Tredegar, plus secondary smelters (Real Alloy, Smelter Service) for cast streams. These buyers are well capitalised and want the material. Section 232 tariffs on primary metal (raised to 50% in 2025) and EU CBAM raise the value of verified scrap-based metal. The catch is that the largest buyers are building their own sorting.
scored.incumbents: Unverified, from memory. Sortera Technologies (Fort Wayne/Markle, Indiana) runs its own LIBS/ML alloy-sorting plant(s), which is this exact rung one. It has raised several tens of millions of dollars (Series A about $9.5M in 2022; later rounds reportedly $30M+, est.) and is expanding with a second site. Integrated majors already sort in-house or are building it: Hydro (Cassopolis MI recycler with sorting, about $150M), Novelis (Guthrie KY recycling centre, about $365M), Constellium/Muscle Shoals, and Steel Dynamics/OmniSource. SDI built aluminium scrap-processing and sorting capacity to feed its Columbus MS flat-rolled mill (about $2.5B program), which captures its own Zorba. Radius/Schnitzer (taken private by Toyota Tsusho in 2025, est.) and other large shredders add their own sorting. Sorter OEMs (TOMRA with AUTOSORT PULSE LIBS, Steinert, Redwave, MSS, Sesotec) sell turnkey alloy-sorting lines to any shredder, which commoditises the startup's classifier. AMP Robotics (about $90M+ raised) and Greyparrot work adjacent ML sorting.
scored.end_state: Very large but mostly owned by incumbents. US aluminium shipments are about 12 Mt/yr, a US aluminium product market of about $40-60B (est., Aluminum Association figures as recalled). Billet and extrusion alone are about $15-20B in North America (est.). There is a credible path from sorting to remelt/billet to extrusion; Matalco and Hydro have done remelt plus billet. Each step from rung 2 up is a $150M-$1B+ capex project competing against Hydro, Novelis and SDI, and it would be a project-finance company rather than a venture-style one.
scored.killer: Three overlapping kills. (1) The rung is taken: Sortera already runs this exact model (an owned LIBS/ML alloy-sorting plant) with tens of millions raised and a head start. Shredders can buy TOMRA LIBS lines off the shelf. The biggest feed sources (SDI/OmniSource, Radius) and buyers (Hydro, Novelis) are integrating sorting themselves. (2) Feed dependency and concentration: a startup sited in a shredder's yard under tolling is captive. The shredder can take the process in-house once it is proven, and only a few extruders are buyers. (3) Commodity spread risk plus a capex wall: the Zorba-to-sorted spread is a thin 15-30c/lb, Zorba-to-LME ratios swing with China/India export demand, and rung 2 needs $150M+, so the ML layer never becomes the moat. Classifiers are vendor-supplied and copyable; the data flywheel is real but small next to who controls the feed.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real, growing ladder (scrap to low-carbon billet, helped by Section 232 and CBAM), but rung one is already held by a funded startup doing exactly this (Sortera), turnkey LIBS sorters from TOMRA and Steinert, and integrating majors (SDI, Hydro, Novelis). On top of that the spreads are thin and the business depends on feed it does not control, so it scores about 15/30, below the proposal's own estimate.

scored.name: ReMag Rotor (rare-earth magnet reuse via motor take-back)
scored.industry: Magnets and machines: NdFeB recovery, reconditioning and remanufactured motors
scored.rung_one: An owned motor teardown and magnet-harvest cell buying end-of-life servo motors, HDD voice-coil assemblies, wind PM generator segments and EV traction cores from recyclers, repair shops and wind O&M; robotic disassembly plus ML grade ID (alloy, Dy/Tb, coating) pulls magnets intact for recoating, remagnetising and resale as graded reuse magnets to rewinders and small motor/actuator makers at about $40-80/kg against $5-15/kg scrap. Distinct from the crowded HPMS powder rung (HyProMag, Noveon, Cyclic Materials, REEcycle).
scored.ladder: 1) Harvest and graded reuse magnets. 2) Remanufactured rotors and motors with reuse magnets for MRO channels. 3) Grain-boundary diffusion and resintering of mixed lots (partner with or acquire HPMS). 4) Own-brand PM motors for robotics, drones and defense actuators with guaranteed non-Chinese magnet content (FY2027 NDAA). 5) OEM fleet take-back contracts; $20B+ magnet and $100B+ PM motor pools.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: vision and teardown planning per motor SKU (library grows with every unit) and non-destructive flux-mapping grading. Rung 2: inventory-aware generative rotor redesign. Rung 3: process ML mapping lot chemistry to diffusion and resinter settings. Rung 4: motor design co-optimised with recycled supply.
scored.seed_plan: $2M: lease a teardown unit, build a semi-automated disassembly cell and flux-mapping grader, source feed from e-waste processors and wind O&M (repowering releases PM generators), first graded-magnet revenue to rewinders and defense prototyping by month 6, reman servo line by month 15. Kills: heterogeneous feed limiting yield and HPMS incumbents moving into harvest. Rubric estimate about 19/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 4, L4 4, L5 2, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: The web search budget ran out (a 200-call cap shared across agents), so only one source was checked. Everything else here is an ESTIMATE from prior knowledge. Checked figure: global NdFeB output was about 220-240 kt in 2024, with at least 85% made in China (Wikipedia). Estimated prices: new Chinese sintered N42-N52 magnets cost about $30-60/kg; non-Chinese or Dy-bearing grades cost $60-120/kg; mixed magnet scrap sells for about $5-20/kg and moves with the NdPr oxide price. The pitched $40-80/kg for reused magnets assumes buyers accept whatever geometry comes out. In practice reused magnets must be re-machined (losing 20-40% of the material) or matched to an existing design, so a realistic price is about $15-35/kg (est.). Estimated cell costs: a semi-automated teardown cell with a flux-mapping grader costs $0.5-1.5M. Labour is about 0.3-1 hr per motor. Magnet yield is roughly 0.1-3 kg per servo or EV motor, about 10-20 g per HDD voice-coil, and hundreds of kg per direct-drive wind generator. Gross margin is about $5-20 per kg sold. A $1-3M/yr run rate needs about 50-100 t/yr of clean feed. Most of the cheap feed is shredded for data security (HDDs) or bonded into EV rotors and breaks on extraction. Wind repowering volumes are early and lumpy. A $2M seed buys the cell but not enough feed or working capital to prove yield.
scored.buyers: Motor rewinders and repair shops: fragmented, buy small volumes, price-sensitive. Small robotics, drone and actuator makers: they want new magnets to spec, not mixed reused geometries. Defense prototypers: the NDAA rules on non-Chinese magnets create real pull, but volumes are tiny and qualification is slow. HPMS recyclers (HyProMag, Noveon, Cyclic) as a fallback buyer at a little above scrap price. Wind OEMs and owners mostly run their own end-of-life programmes.
scored.incumbents: These are from memory except the first; amounts are unverified estimates. Vulcan Elements: $620M conditional Pentagon loan, which is verified (Wikipedia). Noveon Magnetics (US): sintered magnets made from recycled feed, already takes back and harvests motors, raised more than $100M (est.). HyProMag (Mkango/CoTec): UK plant, plus a planned Texas plant of about 750 t/yr from about 2027 (verified, Wikipedia). Cyclic Materials (Canada): Series B of about $50M+, backed by BMW, Hitachi and Microsoft (est.); works the feed take-back and harvest step itself. REEcycle, Ionic Technologies, Heraeus Remloy, MagREEsource: HPMS or chemical recycling. Hitachi built automated HDD and compressor magnet extraction years ago. The EU SUSMAGPRO project ran direct-reuse pilots. Siemens Gamesa runs its own PM generator end-of-life work. The harvesting step is not open: the HPMS players need the same feed and already pay for it.
scored.end_state: Estimates: the NdFeB magnet market is about $20-25B/yr (220-240 kt at about $60-100/kg blended); PM motors for EVs, industry, robotics and drones are $100B+. Doing it end to end means competing with Nidec, Bosch, Kollmorgen, Yaskawa, plus magnet makers like Noveon, Vulcan, Neo/Niron and MP Materials (which is also moving downstream). The market is big, but the path from harvested magnets to motors doesn't lean on reused magnets, since reuse feed will never supply more than a few percent of magnet demand this decade.
scored.killer: Mixed geometry and grade in the feed means intact magnets mostly can't be dropped into other products, so the reuse business falls back to selling scrap to the HPMS recyclers that already own the next step. Feed is contested by well-funded recyclers and shredded upstream for data security. Magnet value tracks NdPr pricing, which China controls. Rewinder demand is small and fragmented.
scored.one_line_reason: The defense and supply pull is real, but intact-magnet reuse has a geometry-mismatch problem and thin feed. Well-funded HPMS players (Noveon, Cyclic, HyProMag) already compete for the same feed, and ML grading is a modest edge rather than one that compounds. About 15/30, below the candidate's own estimate of 19.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neodymium_magnet (2024 NdFeB output 220-240 kt, >=85% China; Vulcan Elements $620M Pentagon conditional loan; HyProMag USA ~750 t/yr from ~2027)
Every other figure is an estimate from prior knowledge; the search budget was used up before more could be checked

scored.name: Rewind Power (remanufactured large power transformers for data centres)
scored.industry: Grid / power: 20-100 MVA substation transformers
scored.rung_one: A single remanufacturing bay (30-50k sq ft brownfield with a 50-ton crane and vapour-phase or oven dry-out) that buys retired or failed 20-100 MVA substation transformers from utilities, IPPs, closed plants and insurance write-offs, rewinds or rebuilds and recertifies them, and sells or leases them to data-centre developers and IPPs facing 3-4 year lead times on new units. Units sell for about $1.5-4M against $0.3-0.8M of core-plus-labour cost; 8-12 units a year makes a profitable shop. Incumbents: Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, Virginia Transformer, and small regional repair shops (SPX Waukesha service, independents); none runs reman as a scaled, data-driven product line.
scored.ladder: 1) Reman bay and resale of rebuilt large units. 2) Rental fleet of mobile and bridge transformers so campuses energise before permanent units arrive. 3) New 30-150 MVA units built on the same floor, starting with standard data-centre campus designs. 4) Prefabricated skid substations (transformer, switchgear, protection) delivered turnkey. 5) Owning and operating customer-side substations under capacity-as-a-service contracts.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: remaining-life ML from DGA, oil chemistry, FRA and loading history prices used cores before purchase and improves with every teardown. Rung 2: rental fleet telemetry and a dispatch/utilisation optimiser. Rung 3: generative and parametric winding/core design trained on cross-brand teardown failure physics, cutting design time and copper. Rung 4: configure-to-order engine for skids. Rung 5: predictive maintenance and dynamic thermal rating across the owned substation fleet, earning more MW from the same iron.
scored.seed_plan: About $1.2M fit-out of a leased bay, 2-3 veteran winders from a closed regional repair shop, first 3 cores bought from utility surplus or insurance write-offs at about $0.3M each, and a deposit-backed pre-sale of the first rebuilt unit to a data-centre developer or solar IPP. Founders build the DGA/teardown pricing model and the sourcing pipeline from utility surplus lists. Kills: large-core supply, warranty and liability on rebuilt units, and per-unit working capital. Rubric estimate about 22/30: L1 3, L2 5, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: The demand side is real. Average US lead times for new units are about 128 weeks, and the largest units are quoted at 3-5 years (The Next Web). Prices are up about 79% (FT, via aiweekly). Wood Mackenzie puts the 2025 power-transformer supply deficit at about 30% (Power Magazine). One unverified source (Datacentres.com) says secondary or refurbished units sell at a 35-50% premium with 12-18 month lead times. New-unit cost benchmarks: about $7-13k per MVA in an older Missouri PSC filing, far below today's prices. My estimate of the current US price for a new 20-100 MVA unit is about $1.5-6M. So the pitch's resale price of $1.5-4M is plausible. The pitch's core-plus-labour cost of $0.3-0.8M is optimistic (estimate). Copper rewind is priced per kg of winding (BHEL tender structure). A full rewind of a 50-100 MVA unit plausibly costs $0.5-1.5M in copper, insulation, labour and testing, plus core acquisition, freight and heavy haul (estimate). The capital plan is undercooked. A 100 MVA unit weighs 80-150 t, beyond a 50 t crane. Recertification needs factory acceptance testing (applied, induced and impulse tests, plus heat run), and an in-house test bay is a multi-$M item; outsourcing the tests to an OEM is a dependency. Working capital per unit is $0.5-1.5M for 6-12 months. Realistic rung-one capital is $5-10M, not $1.2M (estimate). The rung only works at the low end (20-40 MVA).
scored.buyers: Data-centre developers and hyperscaler campus builders facing 3-4 year interconnection-side lead times. Also solar, storage and IPP developers, industrials, and utilities replacing failed units (insurance-driven emergency replacements). All are well capitalised and pay a premium for speed. The 35-50% premium (one source) suggests buyers will pay more for lead-time relief.
scored.incumbents:
Rung one is already a scaled, PE-backed business.
- Sunbelt Solomon: remanufactured substation units up to an 85 MVA base, plus a temporary-power rental fleet (rung 2). Owned by Trilantic North America; a sale to TJC was pending in July 2026, financed by private credit (Cahill).
- RESA Power / PARC (North Canton, OH): sells used and rebuilt substation transformers from 5 to over 100 MVA and redesigns or rewinds units up to 200 MVA. PE-backed (sponsor not verified here).
- OEM service arms (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, which offers onsite rewind services) and many regional independents.
- New-build startups attacking rung 3: Ayr Energy ($25M raised, order book above $500M), Heron Power ($140M Series B, a16z and BEV, solid-state), DG Matrix ($60M Series A).
Used-unit sourcing and data-centre resale is exactly the arbitrage these dealers already run.
scored.end_state: Rough sizes (estimates from public industry figures, not verified here): global power and distribution transformers about $60-70B a year; substation and switchgear EPC adds several $10B; owned customer-side substations under capacity-as-a-service are an infrastructure-finance pool. That is large, but doing it end to end means competing with Hitachi, Siemens and GE Vernova (including Prolec), all expanding US capacity by about 2027-2029. The final rung, capacity-as-a-service, is a balance-sheet business rather than an ML business.
scored.killer:
Four things can kill it.
1. The rung is already held: PE-backed reman and rental roll-ups (Sunbelt Solomon, RESA/PARC) do this today, with sourcing networks and test bays in place.
2. Supply of large cores: retired 50-100 MVA cores are scarce and their owners know the shortage, so arbitrage pricing erodes the spread.
3. The premium is cyclical: OEM capacity expansions through 2027-2029 compress lead times and the reman premium just as the company would scale.
4. Capital and risk: the test, crane and working-capital wall is far above $1.2M, and warranty and failure liability on rebuilt 100 MVA units is a single-event company killer.
The ML layer is also weak. Remaining-life models from DGA and FRA already exist (Doble, Dynamic Ratings, OEM APM tools). The binding constraint is skilled winders and floor time, not prediction.
scored.one_line_reason: The demand is real, but rung one is a PE-consolidated reman and rental niche (Sunbelt Solomon, RESA/PARC). It is limited by labour and core supply, and the pitch's $1.2M seed plan misprices the cost of testing and heavy handling. ML would be a marginal pricing aid, not a compounding moat. Total about 14/30.

scored.name: Gridspare (co-op and muni spare-transformer and mobile-substation resilience pool)
scored.industry: Grid / power: T&D capital equipment and critical-infrastructure resilience
scored.rung_one: An owned, regionally stored pool of long-lead critical spares: substation transformers (12-60 MVA, 69-138 kV), HV breakers, GSU spares, voltage regulators and mobile substations, with ballistic shielding kits. Co-ops, munis and mid-size IOUs pay resilience subscriptions of about $50-500k per year per utility for guaranteed deployment within 72 hours, plus $50-200k per deployment event or a purchase/lease fee on draw-down. Demand is driven by 2-4 year lead times and physical attacks (Moore County). Incumbents: Grid Assurance (IOU-owned) and the EEI STEP program serve large transmission IOUs; OEM rentals (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Hitachi mobile subs) and Sunbelt Solomon are closest. The roughly 2,800 munis and co-ops are mostly unserved apart from informal G&T sharing and NRECA programs.
scored.ladder: 1) Spares and mobile-substation subscription pool. 2) Lease-to-own and replacement-as-a-service, plus substation hardening as a service (ballistic walls, sensors, AI video analytics, counting toward NERC CIP-014). 3) Refurbishment and rewinding of returned and failed units into fleet inventory. 4) Standardised build-to-stock designs that co-ops adopt as default spec, leading to own-label transformer manufacturing. 5) Owning and operating distribution substations for small utilities under asset-management concessions, and modular pre-built substations for data centres and renewables. End state: an independent T&D equipment owner/lessor plus OEM in a multi-$10B co-op/muni T&D capex pool.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: an actuarial failure model across member fleets (nameplate inventories, age, loading, DGA, weather/geomagnetic and threat exposure) sets pool sizing, premiums and pre-positioning; FERC Form 1, EIA-861 and RUS borrower filings are mined to target and price members. Rung 2: perimeter-intrusion detection trained on every hardened site, and fleet replacement-planning ML. Rung 3: refurbishment-yield model linking teardown findings to failure modes, feeding back into risk pricing. Rung 4: spec standardisation and design/QA from a cross-utility equipment database. Rung 5: operating data feeds the failure model. More members means better risk models and lower premiums, an insurance-like flywheel.
scored.seed_plan: $3M equity plus $10-20M asset-backed equipment debt or inventory financing (transformers hold resale value), possibly with a specialty insurer or RUS-friendly lender. Sign 5-20 co-ops/munis through one G&T or statewide association as anchors before buying the first 5-10 units and 2 mobile substations in one region (Southeast or Texas), using DOE 40101 grid-resilience grants as matching funds. Kills: slow co-op sales cycles, inventory capital intensity, and fewer events lowering perceived need. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 4, L4 3, L5 4, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Unit cost: about $15-35k/MVA for new power transformers (USITC/NLR benchmark $15-21k/MVA; Rystad reports $30-35k/MVA for 50-100 MVA European awards). That puts a 12-60 MVA, 69-138 kV spare at roughly $0.5-2.5M (estimate). A real Michigan muni bid for a substation transformer came in at about $1.3M. Lead times average 128 weeks (Wood Mackenzie Q2 2025) and DOE found 120-210 weeks; one muni bid had a 70-75 week vendor and a 194-246 week vendor. Mobile substations are about $2-5M each (estimate, no source found). The proposed starting pool of 5-10 transformers plus 2 mobile subs therefore needs about $10-30M of inventory (estimate). Equity of $3M plus $10-20M of asset-backed debt might just cover it, but new units ordered at seed would not arrive for 2-4 years. The pool would have to be stocked with used or refurbished units, the market Sunbelt Solomon already works through asset recovery. Revenue: for 15 members at about $150k/yr, plus a few $50-200k deployment events, about $2.5-4M/yr (estimate). That is roughly a 10-15% yield on $20-30M of inventory before storage, testing, rigging and insurance costs: a lessor/infrastructure return, not venture margin. Grid Assurance's model is cost-share subscription plus purchase at original cost on a qualifying event (JCP&L NJ BPU order), which implies thin, regulated-utility-style margins.
scored.buyers: The buyers are distribution co-ops (about 800), munis/public power (about 2,000), G&Ts, joint action agencies and mid-size IOUs, all capitalised and mostly creditworthy (RUS/CFC lending). But the decision often sits with the G&T. The G&Ts already run their own pools: NCEMC has 8 mobile subs serving 15+ co-ops with capacity-share dues, and Great River Energy has 3 mobile subs and 12 shared transformers for 27 members. So the sale is often to a G&T that already does this, against an informal option that costs it little.
scored.incumbents: Sunbelt Solomon is the main one: PE-owned (Trilantic, with a reported 2026 sale to TJC) and doing over $350M/yr in revenue per Baird. It rents mobile substations (up to 230 kV / 50 MVA), sells new and refurbished transformers, and has made roll-up acquisitions (Maxima Power and Valley Transformer in 2024; Titan, Trinity, Delta Testing earlier). Grid Assurance is owned by AEP, FirstEnergy, Eversource, National Grid, BHE, NV Energy and Evergy, and serves transmission owners in 23 states. EEI STEP is open to co-ops and munis but only triggers on terrorism. NERC SpareConnect is another sharing channel. The OEMs (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Hitachi Energy) rent mobile substations. G&T pools (NCEMC, GRE, and others) cover many co-ops. Refurbishment and rewind shops (e.g. Virginia Transformer, SPX/Waukesha service) hold rung 3. The unserved co-op/muni gap is narrower than the pitch claims.
scored.end_state: US T&D capex runs at tens of billions a year, with IOUs above $100B (EEI) and co-op/muni distribution a multi-$10B slice (estimate). The US transformer market is roughly $10-20B (estimate). So the end state of independent lessor plus own-label OEM plus substation concessionaire is a large pool. But the path from a spares pool to manufacturing power transformers is not credible on a startup's balance sheet. Climbing it means competing with Hitachi, Siemens, GE, Virginia Transformer and Hyundai, all expanding capacity now. Sunbelt Solomon at about $350M of revenue after decades of roll-ups shows the realistic ceiling for rungs 1-3.
scored.killer: The edge is cyclical scarcity. Rystad reports that lead-time and price growth has largely stalled, and OEM capacity expansions are landing in 2026-28, so the 2-4 year lead-time premium that justifies the subscription shrinks just as the inventory is bought. Other threats: (1) capex wall, since $10-30M of inventory is needed before meaningful revenue and new units cannot be bought in time for seed; (2) entrenched substitutes, with G&T pools, Sunbelt Solomon rentals, OEM mobile subs and STEP/SpareConnect all cheap or free; (3) co-op sales cycles of 12-24 months through boards; (4) the ML layer is weak, because transformer failures are rare, heterogeneous and poorly logged, so an actuarial model across a few dozen members has little data and the flywheel is really insurance pooling, not ML compounding. It is a good equipment-finance/rental business with execution moats, not a software-compounding ladder.
scored.one_line_reason: Real pain, but rung one is an inventory-heavy rental business that PE-backed Sunbelt Solomon (over $350M revenue) and G&T pools largely cover. It depends on a lead-time shortage that is plateauing and has thin failure data for ML, so it scores about 14/30 versus the 20 self-estimate.
sources: https://nj.gov/bpu/pdf/boardorders/2024/20241218/2I ORDER JCP&L and Grid Assurance Agreement.pdf

scored.name: Islandgrid (acquire-and-operate microgrids at C&I and critical sites)
scored.industry: Grid / power: behind-the-meter distribution assets and microgrids
scored.rung_one: Buying existing, underperforming behind-the-meter assets (CHP plants, standby genset fleets, small solar plus storage) at hospitals, cold storage, water utilities and manufacturing for $1-8M per site and running them as islanded microgrids, earning energy-as-a-service fees, demand-charge reduction and ISO demand response/capacity payments (ERCOT ERS, PJM capacity, CAISO DSGS). Incumbents Enchanted Rock, Scale Microgrids, Bloom, Ameresco and Edison Energy build new; the acquire-and-retrofit rung for stranded assets is thinner.
scored.ladder: 1) Acquire and optimise existing BTM sites. 2) Aggregate into a VPP bidding as a single resource. 3) Build new microgrids for AI inference and edge data centers. 4) Own distribution-level assets (feeders, small substations) as a microutility where law allows (e.g., Texas private-use networks). 5) Wholesale-scale firming. End state: an independent distributed power company in a multi-$10B C&I energy services plus capacity pool.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML dispatch optimiser across tariffs, DR and fuel, predictive maintenance on old gensets and CHP, and an acquisition model scoring sites from public interval data, air-permit generator registrations and tariffs. Rung 2: portfolio bidding ML improving with every asset. Rung 3-4: siting and design models trained on the operated fleet. Rung 5: fleet-wide forecasting.
scored.seed_plan: $3M equity plus project debt: mine state air-permit registries for sites with registered gensets plus CHP in ERCOT/PJM, buy or lease 2-3 assets or take over O&M on revenue share, and enrol them in DR within 6 months. Kills: capacity-price swings and gas emissions permitting. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 2, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Revenue side (sourced): PJM 2026/27 BRA cleared at the cap, $329.17/MW-day (about $120k/MW-yr), and 2027/28 at $333.44/MW-day. Both sit inside a FERC-approved $175-$325 collar that only covers those two auctions, so the price after 2028 is unknown. Constraint (sourced): emergency-certified RICE gensets may run only 50 hr/yr in non-emergency DR, and only when the balancing authority dispatches them. The 2015 DC Circuit vacatur removed the 100-hr emergency-DR allowance. So the "stranded standby genset fleet" can earn capacity/DR payments but cannot do energy arbitrage or tariff optimisation without being repermitted as non-emergency, which means aftertreatment and Tier 4 retrofit capex. Estimates: a 2 MW genset site in PJM earns roughly $150-240k/yr in capacity/DR at current capped prices, less the 20-40% aggregator take that incumbents keep. Buying CHP/solar+storage sites at $1-8M targets about 8-12% unlevered yield, which is infrastructure-fund economics, not venture. With $3M equity and 60-70% project debt you could fund 2-3 small sites. First-time sponsors without an O&M track record will struggle to get non-recourse debt on aging brownfield CHP (estimate). Realistic year-2 revenue is about $0.5-2M across a handful of sites (estimate). The O&M revenue-share variant needs less capital but is a CSP/aggregator business, which Voltus, CPower and Enel X already run.
scored.buyers: Hosts (hospitals, cold storage, water utilities, manufacturers) pay energy-as-a-service and resilience fees. ISOs (PJM, ERCOT, CAISO) pay capacity/DR. As exits for operated portfolios, infrastructure funds buy at scale: EQT bought Scale Microgrids in Jan 2025, and Balfour Beatty Infrastructure Partners funded Texas Microgrid/Enchanted Rock. Rung one is sellable, but only once it reaches tens of MW. 2-3 sites are not a portfolio any infra fund would price.
scored.incumbents: Crowded at every layer. Enchanted Rock/ERock: 350+ dual-purpose gas microgrids in Texas, EIP $10M and BBIP equity for Texas Microgrid 50 MW, IPO filing reported. Scale Microgrids: about $225M raised (CB Insights), acquired by EQT Transition Infrastructure in Jan 2025, about 250 MW operating plus 2.5 GW pipeline including CHP and gas gensets, MUFG debt in Mar 2025. Budderfly: acquire-and-operate EaaS model, over $1B raised, $550M debt facility in Mar 2026 led by GIP, 7,500+ sites. Redaptive: $650M credit facility from CDPQ/Nuveen in May 2025. PowerSecure (Southern Co) owns and operates distributed gensets for utilities and C&I. Voltus, CPower and Enel X already enrol customer-owned standby gensets in PJM/ERCOT DR on revenue share, which is the proposed seed plan. Ameresco, Veolia, Engie and Edison Energy run CHP O&M and ESCO acquisitions. The "thin" acquire-and-retrofit rung is in fact Budderfly's and Redaptive's model plus aggregator CSPs.
scored.end_state: US C&I distributed energy services plus capacity is multi-$10B. PJM's 2026/27 capacity procurement alone is about 134 GW x $329/MW-day, roughly $16B/yr gross (calculated from PJM results). The C&I EaaS/ESCO market is commonly cited at $10B+ (estimate). The path end to end is weak. Rung 4 (owning feeders or a microutility) runs into state utility franchise law almost everywhere: Texas private-use networks are narrow exceptions, and ERCOT behind-the-meter rules apply. Rung 3 (AI and edge datacenter power) is where Enchanted Rock, Bloom, Scale, Prometheus/VoltaGrid-type bridge-power players and the hyperscalers' own developers are already racing with billions.
scored.killer: 1) Regulation: under EPA RICE NESHAP, emergency gensets get only 50 non-emergency hr/yr, dispatched by the balancing authority, so the core "optimise old standby gensets" thesis mostly reduces to capacity/DR enrolment, which aggregators already do. Turning gensets into dispatchable assets requires air-permit changes and emissions retrofit capex. 2) Capacity-price risk: PJM's capped prices are a temporary collar through 2027/28, and DR accreditation (ELCC) keeps tightening. 3) Capital and credit wall: brownfield asset acquisition is project-finance driven, and seed founders lack the track record lenders require. 4) Incumbents with $200M-$1B+ of capital already run this exact acquire-and-operate playbook. 5) Customer site control: hosts own the land and interconnection, and contracts are bespoke and slow to sign (hospital procurement cycles of 12+ months). 6) The ML moat is thin: dispatch optimisation is commoditised (Voltus, Enel, Generac Concerto, GridBeyond), and the air-permit acquisition model is a one-time lead-generation trick, not a compounding data asset.
scored.one_line_reason: Scores 14/30. The acquire-and-operate C&I microgrid/DR rung is already held by heavily capitalised players (Budderfly, Redaptive, Scale/EQT, Enchanted Rock, Voltus/CPower). The EPA 50-hour rule caps what old gensets can earn, and the economics are infrastructure-fund yields rather than an ML-driven value jump, so this is another execution-moat developer.

scored.name: Second Wind Storage (distressed early-vintage BESS rollup)
scored.industry: Energy storage: grid batteries (ERCOT/CAISO/PJM)
scored.rung_one: Buy one degraded 2016-2021 vintage grid battery (5-20 MW, often first-gen LG/Samsung NMC at 50-70% state of health, with expiring capacity contracts or a collapsed frequency-regulation model) from a tired IPP, utility or fund at about $50-150k/MW (10-25% of new-build). Recondition it (rebalance strings, swap worst modules for salvaged packs, retune inverters) and sell output as an ERCOT ancillary/arbitrage stack, a CAISO RA contract or PJM capacity. An interconnected 10 MW site earns $0.8-2M a year; the interconnection position is the hidden value given 4-6 year queues. Incumbents (Jupiter, Plus Power, Key Capture) develop new; nobody owns buy-and-revive.
scored.ladder: 1) One distressed site. 2) Portfolio of 10-30 model-identified sites. 3) Capacity augmentation: bolt new LFP onto existing interconnection rights and re-contract. 4) In-house module reman and recycling from pulled cells. 5) Storage added to gas peaker and solar brownfield interconnections. 6) A full IPP selling firm capacity to utilities and hyperscalers.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: per-cell degradation and fire-risk models from BMS and SCADA history set bid price and module pulls. Rung 2: fleet-trained screening of EIA-860/860M, ERCOT and ISO records finds and prices underperforming batteries. Rung 3: degradation-aware dispatch and augmentation sizing. Rung 4: cell grading decides reman vs recycle. Degradation data compounds into pricing, warranties and insurance.
scored.seed_plan: About $1.5M of seed as equity in one 5-10 MW ERCOT or CAISO site from a closing fund or first-gen owner, rest via seller notes or asset-backed debt; field-recondition in 6 months, ancillary revenue from month 9. Kills: old-NMC fire liability, thin seller pipeline, squeezed ERCOT ancillary prices. Self-score about 23/30: L1 4, L2 5, L3 4, L4 4, L5 4, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: The pitch's revenue number is too high, by about 3-6x in ERCOT. Modo Energy's nowcast puts 2025 ERCOT battery revenue at $29.4/kW-yr, down from $56 in 2024 and $193 in 2023. Ancillary revenue fell from $1.52 to $0.50/kW-month (Oct 2024 to Oct 2025), and arbitrage is now 76% of the stack. On those figures a new 10 MW / 2-hour ERCOT battery earns about $0.3M/yr. A degraded 1-hour first-gen NMC unit earns less, because it captures less of the spread (estimate $0.15-0.25M/yr), not the $0.8-2M claimed. CAISO pays better. Modo says resource adequacy is over 50% of battery revenue, contract prices are up about 66% since 2020 and battery strikes reach about $35/kW-month at the top. But RA needs 4-hour duration at rated power, so a battery at 60% state of health has to be derated. CAISO merchant revenue also hit record lows: $1.89/kW-month in Feb 2026 and $2.55 in Jun 2026. PJM frequency regulation revenue rose after the October 2025 redesign: about $20 before vs $62/kW-month after, per Modo (unit unverified). That gives PJM owners of early regulation batteries a reason to keep them, not dump them. Capital (estimates): buying at $50-150k/MW is $0.5-1.5M for 10 MW. Reconditioning plus swapping modules costs about $0.3-0.8M. Repowering with new LFP at about $150-250/kWh installed would cost $3-5M for 10 MW / 2 h. That is beyond seed and gets financed at an IPP's cost of capital. Gross margin on the operating asset is perhaps 40-60% after O&M, insurance and augmentation reserve, but in ERCOT the absolute dollars cannot pay for a team. One site cannot carry the company.
scored.buyers: Revenue comes from ISO markets: ERCOT energy and ancillary services (merchant), CAISO resource adequacy offtakers (load-serving entities, CCAs) and the PJM capacity and regulation markets. Exit and refinancing buyers for a revived site or portfolio are infrastructure funds and IPPs: Brookfield (agreed to buy Aypa at about $7B EV, July 2026), NextEnergy Capital and Hunt Energy Network. Hunt bought the 100 MW merchant Fort Duncan site in Feb 2026. Mercom counts 65 storage project M&A deals in 2025, up from 38 in 2024. The buyers are well capitalised but price on contracted cash flow and state of health, which is exactly what these assets lack.
scored.incumbents: No company I found is branded as buy-and-revive for early-vintage batteries. The rung is still not open, because three groups already cover it. (1) Original owners repower in house: Cordelio Power is replacing the BYD batteries at its 2015 McHenry site in PJM (20 MW / 44 MWh) with Kore Power systems, and Amarenco repowered its Claudia site in France. Owners keep the interconnection value themselves. (2) Rollups and funds buy operating sites: Hunt Energy Network (33 ERCOT sites, 420 MW), ENGIE/Broad Reach, Key Capture (SK E&S), Plus Power, Jupiter, Brookfield/Aypa, and UK precedents such as NextEnergy and Pulse Clean Energy. (3) Battery analytics, the ML layer: TWAICE (about $100M+ raised), ACCURE, and Fluence/Wärtsilä/Tesla running their own fleet analytics under service contracts with owners. They already hold per-cell degradation data at fleet scale. The supply pool is also small. Energy-Storage.news counted only about 1.5 GW / 3 GWh of US grid batteries 4+ years old, and much of it is still under OEM service agreements or tolls.
scored.end_state: The end state is a full storage-and-firm-capacity IPP. The pool is large: US grid storage installs are tens of GW a year, CAISO alone had 15.7 GW / 59.6 GWh at end 2025, and storage capex plus revenue runs to multi-$10B a year (estimate). But that end state is a capital-markets IPP competing with Brookfield, NextEra, ENGIE and Plus Power on cost of capital. The degraded-asset niche that is supposed to be the wedge is small: about 1.5 GW of 4+ year-old US batteries, a pool worth maybe $0.1-0.5B a year in revenue (estimate). Climbing from it to the full IPP is a change of business model, not a step up the same ladder.
scored.killer: Revenue is collapsing because new batteries cannibalise each other. ERCOT revenue fell 85% from 2023 to 2025, and CAISO merchant revenue hit record lows in 2025-26 as the fleet grew 42%. Distressed assets are cheap because the cash flows are disappearing, and degraded short-duration units are the first to be priced out. The other killers: (1) fire and insurance liability on first-gen LG/Samsung NMC, with LG having recalled modules after fires. (2) A thin seller pipeline: about 1.5 GW of old US batteries in total, owners repower themselves or sell to funds at full price, and PJM regulation revenue just recovered. (3) The interconnection value goes to whoever can fund augmentation at the cheapest capital, an IPP or fund, not a seed startup. (4) Software is not a moat here: TWAICE, ACCURE and the OEMs already run degradation analytics on far larger fleets.
scored.one_line_reason: The economics in the pitch rest on revenue figures 3-6x too high. 2025 ERCOT batteries earned about $29/kW-yr, so 10 MW makes about $0.3M/yr. The supply of distressed assets is about 1.5 GW, owners repower in house or sell to funds, and the climb ends as a cost-of-capital IPP race where ML is not the moat. My total is about 14/30, against the pitch's own score of 23.

scored.name: Northlight Power (remote off-grid hybrid microgrid IPP, Canada and Alaska)
scored.industry: Energy: firming and storage for diesel-dependent remote grids
scored.rung_one: Own and operate solar or wind plus battery plus controls bolted onto one remote community's or mine camp's diesel plant (northern Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nunavut, NWT, Alaska), selling displaced-diesel kWh under a 15-20 year PPA to Qulliq, NTPC, SaskPower remote or a mine operator at $0.30-0.60/kWh against $0.60-1.20/kWh diesel. A 1-2 MW site earns $0.5-2M a year, with CERRC and Indigenous loan guarantees lowering capex. No exploration: mines are customers. Incumbents: ATCO, BBA, local Indigenous energy corporations, Hatch (engineering); few dedicated owner-operators.
scored.ladder: 1) One community or camp hybrid. 2) Portfolio of 10-30 remote grids under one O&M and controls stack. 3) Full diesel-plant takeovers as the community generation utility. 4) Long-duration and seasonal storage (thermal district heat, hydrogen, iron-air) to push displacement from 30% to 80%+. 5) Owned standard containerised power-module line. 6) Remote-grid utility across northern Canada (about 300 diesel communities), Alaska (200+) and remote Australia.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML dispatch holding diesel at minimum runtime under icing, snow-cover and cold-derate conditions. Rung 2: fleet remote predictive maintenance cutting fly-in O&M, the largest cost. Rung 3: load forecasting sizes diesel replacement. Rung 4: seasonal storage sizing from years of fleet weather and load data.
scored.seed_plan: Use Dhruv's Saskatchewan and northern relationships: with about $1M seed, partner with one First Nation as co-owner (unlocking CERRC and the Indigenous loan guarantee), sign a PPA with a remote utility or fly-in camp for a $2-4M hybrid about 60% grant-funded, and commission in 12-18 months. Kills: slow utility procurement, small tickets, logistics. Self-score about 20/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 3, L4 3, L5 4, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Price: the pitch assumes $0.30-0.60/kWh, but real offtake prices are lower. Qulliq Energy's IPP program pays avoided diesel fuel cost, about C$0.2476/kWh (QEC/trade.gov). Pembina's commissioned study proposed C$0.402/kWh plus a C$0.04-0.08 Inuit-ownership adder, but I found no confirmation that it was adopted. The utilities value only the fuel saved, not the full $0.60-1.20/kWh cost of diesel generation. Full diesel cost is real: Hartley Bay ~$0.67/kWh, Nunavik 65-132 c/kWh. Revenue: a 1 MW solar array at roughly 1,000-1,100 kWh/kWp in the north yields about 1 GWh/yr, so about $250-400k/yr at QEC rates (estimate). That is below the $0.5-2M claimed. Only a mine PPA or a wind site reaches the top of that range. Capex: northern solar or wind costs about $7,000-8,000/kW installed against about $1,500/kW for diesel (Narwhal). A 1-2 MW hybrid with a battery is therefore $8-20M, not $2-4M. Sayisi Dene (Tadoule Lake, a small community) drew C$8.6M from CERRC plus C$4.2M from the Energy Innovation Program, $21.6M federal in total. It was funded in 2024 and is due to commission in fall 2026, which shows how long grant-led projects take. Margin: an infrastructure-style unlevered IRR of 6-10% (estimate), and only with 50-70% grant funding. On roughly $1M of seed, the founders hold a minority sponsor stake in a $10M+ project they cannot finance themselves. The sealift and winter-road calendar adds a year of delay on top.
scored.buyers: The buyers are monopsony territorial or provincial utilities: Qulliq Energy (Nunavut), NTPC (NWT), ATCO Electric Yukon, Hydro-Quebec (Nunavik), SaskPower and Manitoba Hydro for their few remote sites, plus Alaska co-ops (AVEC, AP&T). Mine operators are the better buyers: Glencore Raglan signed a 20-year PPA with Tugliq. However, mine life of 10-20 years caps PPA tenor and concentrates credit risk in one mine. Built assets can be sold to infrastructure funds or Indigenous partners, but the tickets are small.
scored.incumbents: Tugliq Energy (Quebec) is the clear owner-operator precedent. It owns and runs Raglan I and II (2 x 3 MW wind plus storage) under a 20-year PPA with Glencore. ATCO owns utilities and remote generation in Yukon and NWT. Hydro-Quebec and QEC are self-developing. Indigenous energy corporations already lead community projects with grants, such as Three Nations Energy (Fort Chipewyan) and Sayisi Dene. Engineering firms include Hatch (Raglan EPC), BBA, ABB and SMA (controls), and Bridge Gap Renewables (financing for First Nations microgrids). Diavik built a 9.2 MW wind-diesel plant in-house. In Australia, the mine-hybrid IPP rung is held by EDL, Zenith Energy, Pacific Energy and Aggreko, all large, capitalised players with decades of track record. Rung one is not taken by a VC-backed startup, but it is far from empty.
scored.end_state: The total pool is small. Canada has about 257-292 remote off-grid communities, about 86% on diesel (MaRS 2015). Reference points: 25 NW Ontario communities cost about $68M/yr for diesel generation (IESO 2012), and Nunavut pays about $60M/yr in diesel subsidies. Total remote diesel generation spend is roughly $1-1.5B/yr in Canada and $0.4-0.7B/yr in rural Alaska (my estimates). Remote Australian mine power adds a few $B. The total is about $3-6B/yr, not multi-$10B. The Conference Board says displacing 25% of diesel in 106 communities needs only 84-116 MW of renewables. The Ontario pool is also shrinking as the Wataynikaneyap transmission line connects communities to the grid. The owned containerised power-module line (rung 5) would compete with SMA, Schneider and ABB.
scored.killer: The killer is grant dependence plus avoided-fuel-cost pricing set by a monopsony utility. Projects pencil only with 50-70% federal grants (CERRC, Indigenous loan guarantees). Those grants go to community proponents, so a VC-backed sponsor holds a small, low-IRR share of each project. Procurement and the sealift calendar stretch each project to 2-3 years, and Sayisi Dene took from 2024 funding to a 2026 commissioning. Tickets are small: $0.3-2M/yr per site. Software does not compound much. Diesel-minimum-runtime dispatch is commodity, sold by ABB, SMA, Hatch and Schneider, and fly-in O&M savings are real but incremental. The result is an infrastructure-fund or Indigenous-utility business, not a venture-scale ML company.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real, mission-aligned infrastructure niche, but utilities pay only avoided fuel cost (about C$0.25/kWh at QEC), projects need $8-20M and 2-3 years of grants, Tugliq, ATCO and Indigenous utilities already hold the rung, and the whole pool is about $3-6B/yr: 14/30.

scored.name: Carbonheat (repurposed CVD diamond reactors for thermal-grade diamond on AI and RF chips)
scored.industry: Deeptech materials / semiconductor thermal management
scored.rung_one: A farm of 20-40 microwave-plasma CVD reactors bought used or distressed from lab-grown gem producers as jewelry prices collapse, retuned to grow polycrystalline thermal-grade diamond wafers and heat spreaders (1,500-2,000 W/mK) at about $15-80/cm2 for spreaders and $1-5k per 100mm wafer, sold to GaN RF and radar module makers, laser-diode packagers and AI accelerator thermal teams. Incumbents: Element Six (De Beers), Coherent/II-VI, Akash Systems, Diamond Foundry, Ningbo Crysdiam.
scored.ladder: 1) Thermal-diamond wafers and spreaders. 2) Metallised, lapped spreaders bonded to customer die (assembly). 3) Diamond-integrated packages (lids, interposers for HBM/GPU hotspots, GaN-on-diamond transfer). 4) Electronic and quantum-grade single-crystal diamond. 5) Diamond-integrated devices. Pool $10B+.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: per-reactor closed-loop plasma control (OES, pyrometry, in-situ imaging) trained on every run lifts growth rate and conductivity; every reactor-hour is training data. Rung 2: bond-void and thermal-resistance prediction from metrology. Rung 3: surrogate thermal/warpage co-design with customer floorplans. Rung 4: plasma model retargeted to single-crystal growth. Rung 5: device yield feeds growth recipes.
scored.seed_plan: Buy 15-20 used MPCVD reactors cheaply from overbuilt Indian and Chinese gem producers, lease a unit with 3-4 MW of power, hire one plasma physicist; about $2.5M seed; first revenue from laser and RF packagers buying spreaders in quarterly lots, $2-4M by month 18. Kills: Chinese price pressure and long AI-chip qualification. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Reactors: new CVD gem reactors cost about INR 1.2 crore (~$140k) each including ancillaries (artofjewellery), and the industry-average equipment unit price is about $250k in 2025 (Intel Market Research). India had ~6,000 LGD reactors by May 2024 and ~10,000 producing units by 2025. Gem prices fell from ~Rs60k to ~Rs20k/carat and producers are struggling with machine loans (GTRI via BusinessWorld; Indian Jeweller), so used units at an estimated $30-80k each are plausible. That puts 20 reactors at an estimated $0.6-1.6M, which fits a $2.5M seed. Technical catch: gem reactors are small-area 2.45 GHz, ~6-10 kW machines tuned for single-crystal growth on mm-to-cm seeds. Thermal-grade 100mm polycrystalline wafers normally come from large-area 915 MHz, 30-100 kW reactors (Element Six, Diamond Materials). So the gem farm can realistically make small laser-diode and RF submounts and few-cm plates, not 100mm wafers at scale (estimate). The stated 3-4 MW is also oversized: 20 reactors x ~8 kW is ~0.2 MW. Pricing: no public $/cm2 found. The pitch's $15-80/cm2 for spreaders is an unverified estimate. Pool: the global diamond heat-spreader market is only ~$0.18-0.4B in 2025, rising to ~$0.3-0.8B by 2032-35 (Roots Analysis $0.35B, Marketintelo $0.4B, ReportPrime $185M, GII $216M). Getting to $2-4M revenue by month 18 means ~1% of the global market inside long qualification cycles (estimate: aggressive). Gross margin could be 40-60% on cheap used tools (estimate), but buyers are price-anchored by Chinese supply.
scored.buyers: Laser-diode packagers (submounts), GaN RF and radar module makers (defence primes, Qorvo/MACOM-tier and their packagers), and photonics and power-electronics houses. These are capitalised buyers, but there are few of them, qualification is slow (6-18 months for laser/RF, multi-year for AI accelerators), and they already source from Element Six, Coherent/II-VI and Chinese suppliers. AI accelerator thermal teams are the big prize, but they are years from volume diamond adoption and buy through OSATs and hyperscaler-qualified vendors.
scored.incumbents: Element Six (De Beers/Anglo; decades of thermal-grade polycrystalline CVD, the market leader). Coherent/II-VI (thermal diamond line). Diamond Materials GmbH, Sumitomo Electric, Orbray (Japan). Diamond Foundry (single-crystal wafers for chip cooling; ~$1.8B 2021 valuation, $315-515M raised, plus EU/Spanish state support reported). Akash Systems (GaN-on-diamond and diamond-cooled GPUs; Founders Fund/Khosla backed; ~$68M CHIPS Act preliminary award; $27M NxtGen contract; reported $300M MI350X order). Chinese producers: Ningbo Crysdiam, Huanghe Whirlwind, Compound Semiconductor (Xiamen) (sells thermal-grade polycrystalline heat sinks and GaN-on-diamond), plus many Henan/Hebei shops. Others include Diamond Quanta, AKHAN and Applied Diamond. Rung one is not open: it is crowded at both the premium and the low-cost end.
scored.end_state: Today's diamond heat-spreader pool is only ~$0.2-0.4B (2025), rising to ~$0.3-0.8B by 2032-35 (Roots Analysis, Marketintelo, ReportPrime). Single-crystal diamond heat sinks add ~$0.2B (pmarketresearch). A multi-$10B pool exists only if diamond becomes standard in advanced packaging (HBM/GPU lids, interposers) or electronic-grade diamond devices commercialise. Both are speculative, 5-10+ year bets, and Diamond Foundry and Akash already target them with $100M+ war chests. The broad thermal-management and advanced-packaging pool is $10B+, but diamond's share is unproven (estimate). A credible end-to-end path through devices needs fab-scale capex well beyond seed.
scored.killer: The main killer is commodity pricing from Chinese thermal-diamond capacity and the same distressed gem-reactor glut. Anyone, including Indian and Chinese gem shops themselves, can repurpose these tools, so cheap reactors are a non-moat. A small rung-one market (~$0.3B) compounds this, with slow qualification and concentrated buyers. A technical mismatch adds to it: gem reactors are small-area single-crystal tools, while 100mm polycrystalline wafers need large-area 915 MHz systems. Ladder risk: rungs 3-5 face Diamond Foundry and Akash, which are far better funded, plus CHIPS-backed and defence-ITAR dynamics. Plasma-control ML is real but incremental; Element Six has decades of recipe know-how.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap distressed reactors make rung one winnable, but the market is only ~$0.3B, already contested by Element Six, Coherent, Chinese producers, Akash and Diamond Foundry. The arbitrage is open to every gem shop, gem tools fit wafer-scale polycrystalline growth poorly, and the multi-$10B end state depends on speculative diamond-in-packaging adoption that better-funded players are already chasing. The pitch's own 21/30 is too high; this scores 14/30.

scored.name: Halflife (theranostic radiometals from owned cyclotrons)
scored.industry: Medical isotopes / radiopharmaceutical supply chain
scored.rung_one: One owned or refurbished medium-energy cyclotron vault with solid-target stations in a leased hospital or university bunker (a used 16-24 MeV machine plus targetry and hot cells for about $2-3M, or a capacity lease) producing GMP Cu-64, Zr-89, Sc-44/47 and Ga-68 for radiopharma trials and imaging CROs (Novartis/AAA, Lilly/POINT, AstraZeneca/Fusion, BMS/RayzeBio, 100+ biotech programmes) at $2-15k per GBq batch or $0.5-2M a year contracts. Competitors on radiometals: Nusano, NorthStar, BWXT Medical, Eckert & Ziegler, Zevacor, ITM, SpectronRx; F-18 incumbents (Cardinal, PETNET/Siemens, SOFIE, Jubilant) don't focus on solid-target radiometals.
scored.ladder: 1) Single-site radiometal supplier. 2) Network of 3-6 cyclotron sites for 24-hour coverage and redundancy. 3) Radiolabeling and fill-finish CDMO for finished patient doses. 4) Therapeutic isotopes (Ac-225 from Ra-226, Pb-212 generators, Tb-161) by accelerator routes. 5) Owned radioligand assets. Radiopharma projected at $15-30B+ by the 2030s.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML on irradiation logs raises yield and specific activity, and an LLM drafts batch records and DMF/CMC sections. Rung 2: decay-aware cross-site scheduling and routing. Rung 3: radio-TLC/HPLC QC models cut failed doses. Rung 4: Geant4/FLUKA plus surrogate target design brings up new routes faster. Rung 5: real-world dosimetry data feeds drug development.
scored.seed_plan: Partner with a hospital or university with an idle cyclotron after the morning F-18 run, add solid-target capability for about $1M, get a state radioactive-materials licence and a DMF for Cu-64 and Zr-89, and sign 5-10 clinical-trial supply contracts. Kills: big pharma vertically integrating supply (Novartis already has). Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Prices: UC Davis CMGI (rates from 7/1/2025) charges private industry $7,926 for a 150-200 mCi (5.5-7.4 GBq) cyclotron Cu-64 batch, or about $1.1-1.4k per GBq. That is 2-10x below the pitch's $2-15k per GBq. UNMC charges $40 per uCi for Cu-64 and $100 per uCi for Zr-89, but those are small research aliquots. BV Cyclotron VU sells GMP Zr-89 weekly through Revvity, with no public price; my estimate is low-thousands of dollars per GBq. Capital: the pitch's $2-3M for a used 16-24 MeV cyclotron, solid-target station, hot cells and a GMP suite is plausible as a refurbish-and-lease estimate. A new medium-energy cyclotron plus vault is typically $5-15M (estimate). Revenue: one site making 2-4 batches a week at about $8-15k realistically earns about $1-3M a year (estimate), against $1-1.5M a year for staff, QA/QP, targets (enriched Ni-64 / Y-89), licence and DMF upkeep. So rung one runs near breakeven, not a cash engine. Real volume comes only from a commercial diagnostic, and those deals go to scaled CDMOs.
scored.buyers: Radiopharma sponsors running trials: Clarity (Cu-64 SAR-bisPSMA), Curium (Detectnet Cu-64), immuno-PET Zr-89 programmes, and the big-pharma radioligand units (Novartis/AAA, Lilly/POINT, AZ/Fusion, BMS/RayzeBio). Imaging CROs and academic PET centres also buy. Demand is spiky, programme-specific and concentrated. Sponsors prefer suppliers that hold a DMF and can scale commercially, and they lock in one or two of them early (Clarity signed SpectronRx for supply in 2024, clinical manufacturing in 2024 and a 5-year commercial deal in 2025).
scored.incumbents: Cu-64: SpectronRx (Indiana) holds Clarity's commercial Cu-64 isotope and finished-product deal, with capacity for up to 400k doses a year, 5 years from June 2025. NorthStar, Nusano (Series C of $115M+ in Oct 2024; Cu and Sc planned from 2025), Zevacor, ITM and Eckert & Ziegler are also present. Zr-89: BV Cyclotron VU, a GMP supplier since 2003 with Revvity as exclusive distributor, plus 3D Imaging and many academic cyclotrons.
