Ga-68: mostly Ge-68/Ga-68 generators (Eckert & Ziegler, ITM) and Novartis kits; cyclotron Ga-68 is niche. Sc-44/47: PSI and university programmes; Nusano is entering. Behind them all sit 100+ university and hospital cyclotrons selling isotopes at near-cost rate-card prices (UC Davis, UW, WashU, UAB, MSKCC). The pharma majors are vertically integrating supply (Novartis, and RayzeBio's Indianapolis plant).
scored.end_state: The radioligand/radiopharma revenue pool is large but estimates vary: BCC puts radioligand cancer therapeutics at $2.1B (2024) rising to $4.8B (2030), MarketsandMarkets at $3.15B (2025) to $10.9B (2035), and Novartis-cited figures at about $30B by 2034. The isotope-supply slice is likely 5-15% of drug revenue (estimate). That puts the isotope plus CDMO pool at a low single-digit billions. Multi-$10B scale needs rung 5 (owned radioligand drugs), which is a biotech pipeline bet rather than climbing a supply chain. Ac-225/Pb-212 by accelerator (rung 4) needs high-energy or electron accelerators and Ra-226 handling, a capex wall in the tens to hundreds of millions that Nusano, NorthStar, BWXT and TerraPower Isotopes are already climbing with far more capital.
scored.killer: Rung one is a commoditised, half-life-limited regional service. University cyclotrons undercut it on price (about $1.1-1.4k per GBq for Cu-64), and scaled CDMOs (SpectronRx, BV Cyclotron VU/Revvity, NorthStar, Nusano) win the commercial contracts. Sponsors integrate vertically once a drug works. Customer concentration is severe: losing one Phase III programme halves revenue. ML yield tuning on a cyclotron gives a few percent at most, since yields are set by physics and target chemistry. The climb to therapeutic isotopes hits a capex wall that incumbents with $100M+ already hold.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a crowded, low-margin isotope service with weak ML compounding. Rung one runs near breakeven against near-cost university cyclotrons and scaled CDMOs (SpectronRx already holds commercial Cu-64), and multi-$10B scale exists only by becoming a drug company. Total 14/30, below the pitch's 21.

scored.name: Rad-Qual (radiation test lab that climbs to space-grade components)
scored.industry: Deeptech / space and defense electronics qualification
scored.rung_one: An owned radiation-effects test facility: a Co-60 or X-ray TID bench plus a pulsed-laser SEE bench (about $1-2M) and contracted block beam time at proton and heavy-ion sites (TRIUMF, MGH, TAMU, LBNL, NSRL, backlogged for months), selling test campaigns at $20-250k to constellations (SpaceX, Kuiper, Planet, Apex, K2, York), defense primes and New Space startups qualifying COTS parts. Incumbents: Radiation Test Solutions, VPT/HEICO, Frontgrade, Renesas/Microchip/TI rad-hard lines, Zero-Error Systems, Vorago, university labs; fragmented and capacity-starved.
scored.ladder: 1) Test-as-a-service lab. 2) Lot upscreening and RLAT: buying COTS lots and selling qualified rad-tolerant parts from own inventory at 5-20x. 3) Own rad-tolerant component line (power converters, FPGA boards, POL modules, memories). 4) Qualified subsystems (avionics, power) and nuclear/fusion instrumentation. 5) Trusted rad-hard supply chain with a defense foundry partnership.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML predicting radiation response from die/process features and past tests plus adaptive test plans cut beam hours 30-60%. Rung 2: a proprietary lot-level radiation database decides which lots to buy and upscreen, with error falling as data grows. Rung 3: design-for-radiation tools for owned modules. Rung 4: on-orbit SEE telemetry feeds back into predictors.
scored.seed_plan: Lease a light-industrial bay (X-ray TID first to avoid a Co-60 licence), build the laser SEE bench, pre-buy beam blocks and resell as packaged fast-turn campaigns to 10-20 New Space customers, and start upscreened-parts inventory in month 9-12. Kills: beam-time access, government lab competition, space funding cycles. Rubric estimate about 22/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 5, L4 3, L5 4, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Owned X-ray TID bench plus pulsed-laser SEE bench costs about $1-2M (candidate's estimate; plausible). Proton and heavy-ion beam would be rented, not owned. 2018 rates (National Academies; dated): TAMU about $800-1,200 per beam hour with about 3,500 hours available a year; LBNL 88-inch cyclotron about $2,300/hr; NASA NSRL (Brookhaven) about $6,000/hr. A typical SEE campaign of 8-24 beam hours is $10-30k in beam alone. Packaged with engineering, boards and a report, campaigns sell for about $30-150k (estimate). Gross margin on the owned TID and laser benches could be 50-60% (estimate). On resold beam it is thin. Facilities allocate beam time to requesters and do not sell blocks wholesale, so the plan to pre-buy and resell is doubtful. Realistic rung-one revenue is $2-6M/yr per site (estimate). A ~$3M seed builds the lab but not an accelerator; TAU Systems needed $35M for its own beam source.
scored.buyers: Funded New Space hardware startups qualifying COTS parts (Apex, K2, York, Astranis, Muon). Defense primes and MDA/SDA tranche suppliers. Large constellations are weaker buyers: SpaceX and Kuiper mostly test in-house or book beam time directly. Nuclear and fusion instrumentation buyers are secondary. These buyers have capital but pay per campaign, and their spend follows space funding cycles.
scored.incumbents: Radiation Test Solutions (Colorado Springs) acquired Cobham RAD, gaining heavy-ion SEE services and a 35,000 sq ft facility. TAU Systems has raised $35M total ($20M extended seed led by Quantonation, 2025) to build a private laser-plasma accelerator in Carlsbad selling Beamtime-as-a-Service for space radiation testing, with a major satellite manufacturer as first customer. That is exactly this rung, with better beam access. Auburn AUARI installed a 200 MeV superconducting proton accelerator (announced Aug 2026; 2,000 hrs/yr; testing starts Jan 2027; Missile Defense Agency anchor customer), which directly eases the roughly 3,000 hr/yr US proton shortage behind the "capacity-starved" thesis. Also: Alter Technology (TUV Nord), VPT/HEICO, Frontgrade, Renesas/Microchip/TI rad-hard lines, Vorago, Zero-Error Systems ($7.5M seed, Mar 2026, rad-hard ICs), Space Micro, in-house radiation teams at Astranis and SpaceX, university labs, and Europe's RADNEXT network of 30 facilities. Fragmented but not empty, and the upper rungs belong to well-capitalised component houses.
scored.end_state: Rad-hard electronics market is about $1.5-1.9B in 2025, growing to $1.8-2.9B by 2031-2034 (IMARC $1.5B, MarketsandMarkets $1.77B, Mordor $1.87B). No credible market size exists for test services; probably a few hundred $M (estimate). Adding qualified space avionics and power subsystems plus nuclear instrumentation gives maybe $5-10B (estimate). That falls short of the multi-$10B pool, and the top rung (a trusted rad-hard foundry) is a capex and accreditation wall that DoD controls.
scored.killer: Beam access is the bottleneck, and national labs, universities and well-funded TAU Systems own it; a founder-run lab only rents it. New capacity (Auburn 2027, TAU, RADNEXT) erodes the scarcity premium just as rung one ramps. The ML layer is weak: qualification standards and customers require measured lot data, because lot-to-lot variability is the whole reason testing exists, so predicted response cannot replace beam hours. The data is sparse and siloed, often under NDA or ITAR. Revenue concentrates in New Space startups that follow funding cycles. Climbing to owned components means competing with Frontgrade, Microchip and others on heritage, which takes years of flight history.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but small, crowded services niche (TAU Systems $35M, RTS/Cobham RAD, new Auburn proton line) where beam access sits with others, ML cannot replace measured qualification data, and the whole rad-hard chain is about $2B, not multi-$10B. About 14/30, versus the candidate's self-estimate of 22.

scored.name: Assay (waste characterization robot fleet climbing into decommissioning waste processing)
scored.industry: Nuclear decommissioning / low-level radioactive waste
scored.rung_one: An owned fleet of mobile characterization units (robotic gamma spectroscopy, free-release surface scanning, drum/box assay trailers) billed at $60-200k per unit-month to decommissioning contractors and licensees (Holtec, NorthStar, EnergySolutions, Westinghouse, DOE EM contractors) at Palisades, Indian Point, Pilgrim, Diablo Canyon, DOE sites, labs and hospitals; each cubic metre correctly classified as free-release or Class A saves $1-10k+. Incumbents: EnergySolutions, Perma-Fix, Veolia Nuclear Solutions, Mirion/Canberra (instruments), ORAU/ORISE; startups Gecko and Createc/H3D; no owned ML-driven characterization-to-processing ladder.
scored.ladder: 1) Characterization fleet. 2) Waste brokerage and segregation taking title to sorted waste per cubic metre. 3) Owned volume-reduction and free-release processing (metal decon, compaction, sorting). 4) Recycled free-released metal sales and a licensed processing network. 5) Turnkey decommissioning of research reactors, labs, cyclotrons and fuel-cycle facilities, then commercial units. US decommissioning plus DOE EM is $10B+ a year.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML on gamma spectra and scans (isotope ID, sub-surface activity, scaling factors) lowers detection limits and survey time, with robot-driven MARSSIM final-status surveys and auto-generated reports. Rung 2: a classification model predicting waste class from site history and sparse samples sets bid prices for taking title. Rung 3: sorting-line CV plus spectroscopy maximises free-release yield. Rung 4: a historical-site digital twin underpins fixed-price decommissioning bids.
scored.seed_plan: Build 2-3 units from COTS HPGe/NaI/LaBr3 detectors on quadruped or tracked robots plus trailer assay systems for about $1.5M, get a service licence, start with small-licensee decommissioning (university reactors, hospital cyclotrons, radiopharmacies, NORM sites) and subcontract final-status surveys to the big decommissioners. Kills: customer concentration in a few decommissioning firms; mitigate through DOE and small licensees. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: My estimates: a characterization unit costs about $250-600k (an HPGe or LaBr3 detector stack at $50-150k, plus a quadruped or tracked base at $75-250k, plus integration). A trailer assay system (ISOCS-class) is about $300-500k. The $1.5M seed build for 2-3 units is plausible. Billing is the weak part. Survey and characterization work in the US is priced by technician-hour and per survey unit, so $60-200k per unit-month only holds if a unit stays fully used on a big job. A realistic year-one estimate is 2-4 small-licensee jobs at $100-500k each, or $0.5-2M revenue, at a 30-45% gross margin after health-physics technician labour, travel and the instrument calibration/QA programme. You also need an NRC or Agreement State service licence and a 10 CFR 50 Appendix B / NQA-1 quality programme before a reactor decommissioner will accept your data, which is 6-12 months. For downstream value, Class A disposal at commercial sites runs about $35-222 per cubic foot, or about $1.2k-7.8k per cubic metre (NRC public comment citing WCS rates). That backs the claim that correct classification saves $1-10k per cubic metre at the low end. Commercial LLW volumes are small, though: the Appalachian Compact sent about 113k cubic feet (about 3,200 cubic metres) to Clive and WCS in all of 2025 (PA DEP). So the classification arbitrage pool is likely tens of millions of dollars a year nationally, not billions. Rungs 2-3, a licensed processing or volume-reduction facility, would cost an estimated $30-150M and take 3-5 years of licensing. That is far past seed money.
scored.buyers: Commercial decommissioners: Holtec (Indian Point, Pilgrim, Oyster Creek; note it is now restarting Palisades, not decommissioning it), NorthStar/Orano (Vermont Yankee, Crystal River), EnergySolutions (Zion, TMI-2, Kewaunee, SONGS with AECOM). DOE EM prime contractors (Amentum, BWXT, Fluor, Bechtel, UCOR, CPCCo). National labs, university research reactors, hospital cyclotrons and radiopharmacies, and NORM sites. These buyers are well capitalised and paid from decommissioning trusts or federal appropriations. But they are few, concentrated, and several do characterization in-house or through long-standing subcontractors.
scored.incumbents: Rung one is a crowded, mature services market. Health-physics and final-status-survey contractors include ORAU (DOE/NRC independent verification), Enercon, GEL Laboratories, Cabrera Services, Radiation Safety & Control Services, Ameriphysics and Perma-Fix Environmental Services. Mirion/Canberra (NYSE: MIR, about $1.7B market cap) sells ISOCS in-situ assay plus field services. EnergySolutions (private, owned by TriArtisan) is vertically integrated across characterization, processing (Bear Creek TN), decommissioning and the Clive disposal site. Veolia Nuclear Solutions (Kurion) is backed by Veolia. In robotics and imaging, H3D (Michigan, gamma imaging, revenue-funded plus SBIR), Createc (UK, N-Visage), and Boston Dynamics Spot radiological-arm integrations are in EU projects such as Garona, CLEANDEM (EUR 3.5M) and XS-ABILITY. CMU RadPiper has been deployed at Piketon. On the evidence available, no venture-backed ML-characterization startup holds rung one, but the work is already well supplied. The robot plus spectroscopy pieces are commoditising through public R&D programmes. My search budget ran out before I could confirm funding totals for H3D, Createc and the private survey firms.
scored.end_state: DOE Environmental Management is about $8.1-8.5B a year (FY2025 enacted $8.48B, FY2026 request $8.09B, FY2027 request $8.2B, per the DOE budget justification and ExchangeMonitor). Global nuclear decommissioning services are about $9.6-9.9B (2025-26), forecast at $13-19B by 2033-35 (GMInsights, Persistence; vendor estimates). US commercial reactor decommissioning is roughly $1-2B a year (my estimate) and the pipeline is shrinking: Palisades is restarting, Diablo Canyon is extended, and Pilgrim and Indian Point are well advanced. The total pool is about $10B+, but most of it is cost-plus federal M&O contracts held by large primes. Going end to end needs a licensed processing site, a disposal relationship (EnergySolutions controls Clive, WCS the other), and prime-contractor bonding. The candidate's own $10B+ figure is about right, but the "credible path end to end" part is weak.
scored.killer: Five problems, in order. (1) The commercial decommissioning pipeline is shrinking. The US now favours life extensions and restarts (Palisades is restarting; Diablo Canyon runs to 2030), so the flagship customers in the pitch disappear. (2) Rung four is mostly dead on regulation. There is no NRC volumetric clearance standard, and DOE has had a moratorium on releasing volumetrically contaminated metal since 2000, so free-released metal sales are politically and legally blocked. (3) Rungs two and three hit a capex and licensing wall ($30-150M and 3-5 years for a processing licence) and compete directly with EnergySolutions, which owns the disposal chokepoint. (4) MARSSIM and NRC acceptance cap the ML advantage. Regulators accept codified survey methods, so ML-lowered detection limits need years of regulatory buy-in before they change what a customer pays for. (5) Customer concentration among about 4 commercial decommissioners and a handful of DOE primes, several of whom are vertically integrated competitors.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but crowded, labour-priced health-physics services rung in a market where reactor decommissioning is shrinking, with incumbent-controlled disposal chokepoints and blocked metal-release regulation capping the climb; software helps at rung one but does not compound into a winnable chain.
sources: NOTE: the web search budget ran out after 3 searches; incumbent funding totals, characterization unit pricing and the NRC reactor-decommissioning count come from prior knowledge and are estimates.

scored.name: Revert Works (certified titanium revert and turnings to melt stock)
scored.industry: Specialty metals: Ti-6Al-4V recycling, melting and mill products for aerospace and defense
scored.rung_one: An owned turnings and solids processing plant (crush, degrease, magnetic and eddy separation, ML-verified chemistry, O/N and high-density-inclusion screening) turning contaminated Ti-6Al-4V chips from aerospace machine shops into certified revert for VAR/EB melters (ATI, Howmet/Timet, Perryman, Carpenter via Dynamet) at about $8-14/kg against $3-5/kg ferrotitanium downcycling; a 1,000 t/yr plant is about $10M revenue. The US has made no sponge since 2024 and ex-China sponge is forecast in deficit around 2028. IperionX is powder-focused; the bulk melt-revert rung is open.
scored.ladder: 1) Turnings-to-revert plant. 2) Compaction plus small cold-hearth (plasma or EB) melt selling 100%-revert slab and ingot. 3) Forging and rolling via contract, then an acquired mill. 4) Near-net preforms and powder for additive and defense (armor, hypersonics). 5) Closed-loop chip buy-back and ingot sale contracts. Part of a $30B+ titanium mill-product and forging pool.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: per-lot chemistry prediction from spectroscopy, images and source shop plus HDI/LDI risk models letting melters raise revert fraction. Rung 2: hearth-melt recipe optimisation from lot genealogy. Rung 3: process-structure-property models for forging and rolling yield. Rung 4: digital material certs with scrap-to-part traceability valued under DFARS specialty-metals rules.
scored.seed_plan: $2.5M: used crusher, degreaser, dryer, separation, LECO O/N and XRF ($1.2M) in leased space near Wichita, Phoenix or Connecticut; chip-buyback contracts with 15-25 machine shops; AS9100 and approval with one VAR melter in 12 months; 300-500 t/yr at 25% gross margin by month 18. Kills: aerospace build-rate dips and slow melter qualification. Rubric estimate about 22/30: L1 4, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: I could not run any live searches: the shared web-search budget for this turn was already used up. Every figure below is an estimate from prior knowledge and needs checking. Prices: Ti-6Al-4V turnings have historically traded at about $1.5-4/lb ($3-9/kg) and clean solids at about $3-7/lb, both swinging with sponge prices. Processed, certified revert usually sells for $1-3/kg more than the raw scrap cost. The pitch's $8-14/kg revert against $3-5/kg ferrotitanium compares a sale price with a price, not with the cost of buying chips. Chip buy-back costs eat most of that gap, so the real spread is roughly $1.5-4/kg (estimate). Cost per tonne: degreasing, drying, separation, LECO O/N and XRF testing, plus a 5-15% yield loss on contaminated chips. That gives a gross margin of about 15-25% on revenue (estimate). The pitch's 25% is at the optimistic end. Scale: a 1,000 t/yr plant at about $10/kg is $10M revenue but only about $2-3M gross profit. The $1.2M equipment figure is plausible with used kit. Real needs on top: working capital for chip inventory (aerospace pays 60-90 days, so about $1.5-2.5M), AS9100 certification, and a melter's qualification audit. The total need is about $3-4M, slightly above the seed. Rung 2 (an EB or plasma cold-hearth furnace) is a $30-100M+ capex wall.
scored.buyers: The buyers are capitalised and few: TIMET (PCC/Berkshire), ATI, Howmet, Perryman, VSMPO's ex-Russia substitutes, Carpenter/Dynamet, and the ferrotitanium producers (e.g. AMG, Global Titanium) at the low end. A handful of melters dominate demand. That is customer concentration, and they qualify scrap suppliers slowly. The EB cold-hearth melters (TIMET Morgantown, ATI) already take a large share of turnings directly, because the hearth itself removes HDIs. That lowers the premium for pre-screened revert.
scored.incumbents: Rung one is held, not open. The incumbents are established US titanium scrap processors and revert suppliers. ELG Utica Alloys (part of ELG Haniel, a multi-billion-euro group) is the largest titanium and superalloy revert processor, with US plants. Others are Supra Alloys (CA), Global Titanium (Detroit, which also makes ferrotitanium), TSI Titanium, and Universal Scrap Metals. PCC (Berkshire) owns its own revert operations, e.g. Caledonian Alloys, alongside TIMET. Closed-loop chip buy-back contracts already exist: TIMET with Boeing and Airbus tiers, and ATI with its customers. The best chip streams from large primes and Tier 1s are locked up. IperionX ($100M+ raised, DoD backed) and others such as Ti powder/HAMR players target the powder and sponge-free route, not bulk revert, but they could move in. Funding for the private processors is undisclosed; they are profitable family or PE-held businesses. These are from prior knowledge, not checked this round.
scored.end_state: Estimate, not checked. Global titanium mill products are about $8-12B a year, with aerospace-grade Ti forgings and castings adding several $B. The combined Ti mill, forging and casting pool is roughly $15-25B, not clearly $30B+. Even doing it end to end means competing with TIMET/PCC, ATI and Howmet. That needs $100M+ melt capacity, a $100M+ forge and rolling mill, and multi-year OEM qualification at every rung. The path is credible only on a decade-plus horizon with large capital.
scored.killer: The rung is already contested. Incumbent revert processors (ELG Utica, Supra, Global Titanium, PCC/TIMET in-house) and existing closed-loop OEM buy-back contracts squeeze both chip supply and the spread. Scrap prices are commodity and cyclical: Ti scrap collapses when sponge falls or aerospace build rates dip. Customers are highly concentrated (about 5 melters), and EB hearth melters need less pre-processing. Rung 2 is a $30-100M capex wall. The ML layer (lot chemistry prediction) is a modest gain over LECO/XRF testing every lot, which melters will insist on anyway.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but crowded scrap-processing business. The incumbents (ELG Utica Alloys, Supra, Global Titanium, PCC/TIMET closed loops) already hold the turnings-to-revert rung. The spread is a few dollars per kg of commodity margin, so ML adds little. Every rung above it is a $30-100M+ capex and qualification wall. About 14/30 against the pitched 22.
sources: No live sources: the web-search budget for this turn was already used up, so no searches ran and every figure is an estimate from prior knowledge that needs checking
Prior knowledge: ELG Utica Alloys (ELG Haniel) titanium and superalloy revert processing
Prior knowledge: Supra Alloys, Global Titanium, TSI Titanium as US Ti scrap processors
Prior knowledge: TIMET/PCC (Berkshire Hathaway) closed-loop scrap agreements with Boeing and Airbus; PCC's ownership of Caledonian Alloys
Prior knowledge: IperionX (Nasdaq IPX) Ti powder/HAMR funding and DoD support
Prior knowledge: historic Ti-6Al-4V turnings and solids scrap price ranges ($1.5-7/lb)

scored.name: Retrofit Halls (liquid-cooling upgrade then roll-up of legacy colos)
scored.industry: Data-centre real assets / cooling
scored.rung_one: An owned rear-door / direct-to-chip retrofit kit installed in a 1-5 MW legacy air-cooled colo hall (2008-2018 vintage), turning 6-8 kW/rack into 40-80 kW/rack inference zones; kit costs about $1-2M per MW, paid by monthly fee or rent-uplift split ($150-250/kW-month AI vs about $120 legacy). Incumbents: Vertiv, Schneider, USystems/Legrand sell kits; DataBank, Flexential and Cyxtera successors upgrade their own; nobody runs retrofit-then-acquire as a data-driven strategy.
scored.ladder: 1) Retrofit-as-a-service in third-party halls. 2) Master-lease retrofitted halls and sublease to inference neoclouds. 3) Acquire stranded legacy colos at distressed prices per MW. 4) Powered expansions on existing utility capacity. 5) A metro edge-AI colo portfolio with owned fibre interconnects.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: LIDAR plus BMS survey automation and a CFD/ML model predicting achievable density and retrofit cost in days. Rung 2: tenant placement and thermal-power co-optimisation. Rung 3: acquisition underwriting on the fleet's actual retrofit results to buy mispriced colos. Rung 4: capacity planning against grid headroom. Rung 5: portfolio energy and thermal OS.
scored.seed_plan: A 1 MW pilot in a regional colo with power headroom and empty halls: $1.5M on kit and install, about $1M on team and software, revenue share backed by a pre-signed inference tenant. Kills: floor-loading and plumbing limits, landlord concentration, AI rent compression as newbuild catches up. Rubric estimate about 19/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 4, L4 3, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Rung one is a 1 MW retrofit. The kit and install cost about $1.5M, per the candidate's own $1-2M/MW; my estimate for rear-door plus CDU plus secondary fluid loop is $1-2.5M/MW, and more if the hall has no chilled-water loop and needs one built. The core problem is the revenue side. A legacy hall's limit is its utility and UPS power, not its rack density. A retrofit packs the same ~1 MW into fewer, denser racks, so the operator still sells about the same kW. All the retrofit adds is the rent premium. CBRE H1 2025 puts primary-market pricing at $200+/kW-month and vacancy at a record-low 1.6%. Assume the legacy rate is ~$120-150/kW-month and the AI-ready rate ~$180-220 (estimate). That gives about $50-80/kW-month x 1,000 kW, or ~$0.6-1.0M a year of gross uplift. The landlord owns the power, building and tenant relationship and will keep at least half, so Retrofit Halls nets ~$0.3-0.5M a year on $1.5M of capex. That is a 3-5 year payback before O&M, fluid servicing and liability for leaks. Seed money (~$3M) covers one or two pilots. Getting to $5-10M ARR needs about $15-30M of project debt or equipment finance, which is available but thin when the counterparty is a single landlord.
scored.buyers: On rung one, the buyers are owners of legacy regional colos (independents and PE-backed regionals) who want AI-grade rent without spending their own capex. The other buyers are inference neoclouds (CoreWeave-tier down to small GPU clouds and Lambda-like firms) who need 40-80 kW racks quickly in metros. They are creditworthy only at the top end. On rungs 3-5, the counterparties for acquisitions and exits are infrastructure funds (DigitalBridge, Brookfield, KKR, Blackstone).
scored.incumbents: Kit and service vendors are already well capitalised and moving into turnkey retrofit: Vertiv (~$8B revenue), Schneider Electric (acquired Motivair, about $850M for 75%, 2024-25), nVent, CoolIT, USystems/Legrand, Motivair and Boyd. Operators retrofit their own halls: Digital Realty, Equinix, DataBank, Flexential, Cologix, QTS (Blackstone) and Evoque (Cyxtera assets went to Brookfield). Thermal software is held by Cadence (bought Future Facilities/6SigmaDC in 2022), EkkoSense and others. On the roll-up rung, PE and infra funds hold hundreds of billions of committed capital, and with vacancy at 1.6% (CBRE H1 2025) legacy colos are not distressed. These names and figures are from general knowledge; my search budget ran out, so they are not verified this round.
scored.end_state: The full chain is global colocation real estate and operations. I estimate it at roughly $70-100B a year of revenue, with the US ~$30-40B and growing more than 10%/yr. It is a real multi-$10B pool. The path to doing it end to end, however, means competing for assets against infrastructure funds with a much lower cost of capital, and that is not a software advantage.
scored.killer: Five problems, in order. (1) Power, not density, is the binding constraint, so a retrofit does not create sellable kW. (2) The landlord holds the power, the building and the tenant, and can bring retrofit in-house or cut Retrofit Halls out at renewal. (3) With record-low vacancy there are no distressed legacy colos, and infra funds outbid at low cost of capital, so the roll-up at rung 3 fails. (4) As GB200/Rubin racks go to 120-600 kW, 40-80 kW halls become tier-2, and rent compresses as newbuild arrives in 2027-28. (5) Vertiv and Schneider bundle turnkey retrofit with financing. The ML layer (CFD and density prediction) is commodity software, not a moat. Like powered brownfields, this is an execution and capital game run by a developer, not an ML company.
scored.one_line_reason: A retrofit doesn't create new power, and the landlord can take back the extra rent. With colos fully let and infra funds well funded, the roll-up has nothing cheap to buy. I score it about 14/30, below the candidate's own 19.
sources: https://www.cbre.com/insights/reports/north-america-data-center-trends-h1-2025 (primary-market vacancy at a record-low 1.6% in H1 2025; pricing forecast to stay at $200+/kW-month)

My own knowledge, unverified in this round because the web-search budget was used up: Schneider-Motivair deal (~$850M for 75%), Cadence acquisition of Future Facilities (2022), Vertiv revenue (~$8B), colo market size (~$70-100B global)
Estimates (my own): retrofit capex of $1-2.5M/MW, rent uplift of $50-80/kW-month, landlord split of at least 50%

scored.name: Fieldhouse Power (gas bridge-power fleet for AI campuses, crowded baseline)
scored.industry: Energy / behind-the-meter gas generation for data centers
scored.rung_one: An owned fleet of gas generation (2-5 MW recips with switchgear trailers, and refurbished 25-50 MW aeroderivatives bought from retiring peakers and overseas rental fleets) rented as bridge or prime power to data-centre developers and neoclouds awaiting energisation, at about $15-60/kW-month on 6-36 month rentals or 3-7 year PPAs (a 20 MW deployment is about $10M a year). Crowded: ProEnergy, VoltaGrid, Solaris, APR Energy, Aggreko, Caterpillar/Solar Turbines dealers, Enchanted Rock, Bloom, Crusoe in-house. Included as the comparison baseline.
scored.ladder: 1) Bridge-gen rentals. 2) Overhaul shop with hot-section parts remanufacturing, and permanent prime-power microgrids (gas plus BESS) sold as PPAs. 3) Gas supply and midstream laterals to campuses; on-campus behind-the-meter IPP. 4) Hot-section additive repair and own powered campuses where gas plus fleet make grid wait irrelevant. 5) Integrated power-plus-shell provider or gas generation packager. Large pool (AI campus power over $50B) but crowded.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: fleet health ML on vibration, oil and exhaust-temperature data for overhaul timing and allocation, plus emissions-permit compliance automation. Rung 2: CV borescope inspection for repair/replace, and microgrid control co-optimising AI training load transients with BESS buffering (a real compounding dataset). Rung 3: gas-nomination and price optimisation. Rung 4: site selection fusing pipeline capacity, permitting and fibre. Incumbents already hold OEM telemetry.
scored.seed_plan: Seed buys 2-3 used 2.5 MW recips (about $1.2M each, partly equipment-financed) plus permitting, landing one neocloud bridge contract; aeroderivatives ($10-20M each) only with structured financing against a signed PPA. Kills: capex wall, emissions permits, falling rental prices as fleets flood in. Rubric estimate about 15/30: L1 2, L2 4, L3 3, L4 4, L5 1, L6 1.
scored.rung_one_economics: Capex: reciprocating engines average about $1,248/kW (EIA benchmark, cited by a vendor). Fully installed island-mode systems with switchgear and emissions controls run about $1,400-1,800/kW (vendor blog). An unsourced guide gives $800-1,200/kW. On those numbers a 20 MW deployment needs about $25-36M of equipment, about 10x the seed. The seed plan's 2-3 used 2.5 MW recips (about $1.2M each, an estimate) gives only 5-7.5 MW. I found no public $/kW-month rental rate; rental prices come only as private quotes from Aggreko, Cat Rental and others. Taking the candidate's $15-60/kW-month as an estimate, 7.5 MW yields about $1.4-5.4M a year gross. Fuel pass-through, O&M (estimated $0.01-0.02/kWh), permitting and mobilisation come off that. Equipment payback is about 1-3 years if the fleet is fully used. Margins are good while capacity is short, but the advantage is buying equipment fast, not software. Solaris is the scale benchmark: about 760 MW earning revenue in Q3 2025, a 900 MW 7-year data-centre JV contract, and a fleet planned to reach about 2,200 MW by early 2028. Aeroderivatives at $10-20M each (estimate) need project finance against a signed PPA, which a seed-stage company with no track record will struggle to get.
scored.buyers: Hyperscalers and their developers (e.g. Stateline/Solaris-type JV customers), neoclouds (CoreWeave, Crusoe, Lambda, Nebius), and data-centre developers waiting years for grid interconnection. These buyers are well funded and pay for speed. But they want hundreds of MW with balance-sheet-backed availability guarantees. A 5-7 MW startup fleet only serves small edge or colo sites, and those buyers are weak and concentrated.
scored.incumbents: VoltaGrid: $1B equity from Blackstone and Halliburton (May 2026), about 7.5 GW order book through 2030, and it acquired its QPac supplier Propell to reach about 300 MW/month of manufacturing. Solaris Energy Infrastructure (NYSE: SEI): about 1,400 MW pro forma by H1 2027 and about 2,200 MW by early 2028, with a 900 MW 7-year data-centre contract. Also ProEnergy (private, aeroderivative refurbisher and packager, the closest match to the refurb-aero rung), APR Energy (Atlas Corp), Aggreko (TDR/I Squared), Caterpillar/Solar Turbines and their dealers, Enchanted Rock, Bloom Energy (fuel cells), Crusoe (builds its own), United Rentals and Cat Rental (mobile gen), Williams (BTM projects for Meta), and GE Vernova and Siemens Energy rental fleets. Rung one is already taken by players with billions in capital.
scored.end_state: Large. AI and data-centre power demand is often projected in the tens of GW of US load additions by 2030 (estimate). At about $100-150/MWh delivered, 10 GW of behind-the-meter generation is about $9-13B a year of revenue (estimate), and the full campus power plus fuel plus shell chain is a $50B+ pool (estimate, consistent with the candidate). VoltaGrid's 7.5 GW backlog and Solaris's ramp toward 2.2 GW confirm the demand is real. But the end-to-end path (gas laterals, IPP, packaging) is the same path VoltaGrid, Solaris and Williams already hold with far more capital.
scored.killer: Capital wall plus crowding. Rung one costs $1,400-1,800/kW installed, so seed money buys only about 5-7 MW. Meanwhile VoltaGrid ($1B raised, 300 MW/month manufacturing) and Solaris (2.2 GW) are flooding the segment, which will push rental prices down once turbine and engine backlogs clear and grid interconnections catch up in 2028-2030. The business is also exposed to emissions permitting (Title V/NSR for prime-power gas), customer concentration (one neocloud contract is the whole business), counterparty risk from neoclouds, and gas price pass-through risk. The ML layer does not differentiate: OEMs (Cat, GE, Solar) already own the fleet telemetry, and fleet-health ML is a feature every incumbent can add.
scored.one_line_reason: Real demand and a sellable rung, but rung one is a capital-heavy rental fleet already being won by VoltaGrid ($1B, 7.5 GW backlog) and Solaris (2.2 GW), and the software layer is a feature, not a moat. The baseline holds at about 13/30.

scored.name: Conduit Power (build, own and operate turbines inside water and irrigation pipes)
scored.industry: Energy / machines: in-conduit and canal hydro
scored.rung_one: Install 25-500 kW in-pipe turbines in place of pressure-reducing valves at municipal water utilities, or at irrigation-district canal drops, under 20-year build-own-operate contracts; the utility buys power or offsets pumping load at $80-150/MWh, plus pressure management. Units cost about $150k-1.5M, earn $40-400k a year, and qualify for the simplified FERC qualifying-conduit exemption. Competitors: Emrgy (canal hydro, VC-backed), InPipe Energy, Rentricity, Natel Energy; the water-utility BOO segment is thin.
scored.ladder: 1) Single valve or canal site. 2) Fleet of 100+ sites per state sold as aggregated low-carbon PPA. 3) Owned standardised turbine and generator line. 4) Pump-as-turbine plus storage flexibility, shifting pumping to cheap hours (the network as a battery). 5) Running utility pumping, pressure and energy operations on contract. 6) Owning or concessioning small water-energy infrastructure.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: siting over public hydraulic plans, SCADA disclosures, SRF filings and the Bureau of Reclamation canal inventory for head-flow pairs. Rung 2: remote dispatch and pressure-transient-safe fleet control. Rung 3: field data drive runner design per head-flow class. Rung 4: ML co-scheduling pumping, tanks and generation against prices. Rung 5: a hydraulic digital twin valuable when bidding to operate networks.
scored.seed_plan: Sign 3-4 BOO contracts with mid-size Western water utilities or irrigation districts, install off-the-shelf turbines with the team's control stack for $0.5-2M total using DOE and USBR WaterSMART grants; 2+ sites generating within 15 months. Kills: small per-site revenue, slow municipal procurement. Rubric estimate about 19/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 3, L4 3, L5 3, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Real sites are much smaller than the pitch assumes. InPipe's Hillsboro, OR PRV unit makes about 200 MWh/yr and EBMUD's about 130 MWh/yr (InPipe materials and Green Building Advisor). At $80-150/MWh that is roughly $10-30k a year per municipal PRV site, not $40-400k. Only large canal drops or transmission-main sites (several hundred kW at about 50% capacity factor, so 1-2 GWh/yr) reach $100-250k/yr (estimate). Capex is not published. InPipe claims its costs are 1/3 of conventional approaches and 3-5 c/kWh, with IRA ITC covering up to 50% of project cost. The candidate's $150k-1.5M per unit is plausible (estimate: $3-8k/kW installed at small scale). At $15-30k/yr against $150k+ capex, payback is 5-10+ years even with the ITC. Each project is far too small for tax equity or project finance on its own, so seed equity funds the assets. $0.5-2M buys 3-6 small sites making perhaps $0.1-0.5M/yr in total (estimate). ORNL also flags the diurnal flow swing (Homer, AK rejected in-main turbines because daytime flow far exceeds nighttime flow), which cuts the real capacity factor.
scored.buyers: Municipal water utilities and irrigation districts sign the offtake or net-metering deals, with IOUs and community choice aggregators as possible PPA buyers. A whole fleet could in principle be sold to an infrastructure fund or yieldco. At the realistic scale (tens of sites, a few MW), though, it is a sub-$20M asset that strategic buyers seldom pursue. Procurement is slow: council or board approval, SRF and grant cycles, and an RFP for each site.
scored.incumbents: Emrgy holds rung one in canal hydro: an $18.4M Series A in April 2023 led by Oval Park Capital with Fifth Wall, Blitzscaling, Overlay and Veriten, a Colorado turbine assembly plant, and customers including Denver Water and Davis and Weber Counties Canal Co. InPipe Energy (HydroXS / In-PRV) offers turnkey municipal PRV recovery projects with financing support, which is effectively BOO-adjacent. Rentricity (PRV energy recovery), Natel Energy (VC-backed, restoration hydro) and Canyon Hydro / Cornell Pump PAT vendors are also active. Lucid Energy, the earlier in-pipe startup, struggled, which is a cautionary precedent. The water-utility BOO niche is thin because its unit economics are poor, not because nobody has noticed it.
scored.end_state: The end state is small. ORNL's 2022 assessment puts new US conduit potential at about 1.41 GW in total (374 MW municipal, 662 MW agricultural, 378 MW industrial; Colorado 154 MW; California municipal 109 MW), against about 512 MW already installed. At roughly 50% capacity factor and $100/MWh, the whole new US conduit resource is about 6 TWh/yr, roughly $0.6B/yr of revenue if 100% captured (estimate). Rungs 4-6 (pumping flexibility, contract O&M, water concessions) reach a larger pool, the US water/wastewater O&M and energy spend in the tens of $B. That pool is held by Veolia, Jacobs, Suez/American Water and others, and winning it rests on public-procurement relationships, not on owning turbines. The credible end-to-end path is weak.
scored.killer: The resource ceiling and per-site size kill it. About 1.4 GW of total new US potential and $10-30k/yr per typical PRV site mean the business never compounds into a large asset base. Per-site municipal procurement (council votes, 6-18 month cycles), diurnal flow variability, and dependence on ITC and WaterSMART grants make it worse. The later rungs (utility operations and concessions) are a different business held by entrenched operators.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but tiny resource: ORNL counts about 1.4 GW (about $0.6B/yr) of new US conduit potential in total, and typical PRV sites earn about $20k/yr. Emrgy ($18.4M) and InPipe already work the niche, and the climb to water operations runs into Veolia-class incumbents. About 13/30.

scored.name: Lasergraft (industrial fiber-laser remanufacturing climbing to laser sources and cells)
scored.industry: Machines / photonics (industrial lasers)
scored.rung_one: A remanufacturing depot (about 8,000 sq ft, clean bench, splicers, burn-in rack) repairing and reselling out-of-warranty 1-20 kW industrial fiber laser sources (IPG, Raycus, nLight, Max). Repairs, swapped pump-diode modules or refurbished sources sell for $8-60k to job shops, sheet-metal fabricators and cutting-system integrators facing 8-16 week OEM repair quotes; tens of thousands of installed sources in North America.
scored.ladder: 1) Repair and refurbishment depot. 2) Remanufactured pump-module and combiner line sold as second source to integrators. 3) Own laser source designed from fleet failure data. 4) Laser processing cells (cutting, welding, cladding) sold or leased per spindle-hour. 5) Laser-as-a-service contract manufacturing; the chain is a $20B+ industrial laser market.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: labelled failure data from each repair (back-reflection events, pump degradation, fiber burns) trains a diagnostic triaging units from customer telemetry. Rung 2: the dataset sets derating and binning for reman modules. Rung 3: source design optimised against cross-brand field failures, with an embedded health monitor. Rung 4: ML process tuning per material and thickness from operated cells. Rung 5: fleet predictive maintenance for multi-brand uptime guarantees.
scored.seed_plan: About $1.5M for depot, test equipment, distressed/used source spares inventory and two laser technicians; direct outreach to fabricators around Chicago, Ohio and Texas plus wholesale to used-machine dealers; target $3-5M a year by month 15, with a telemetry dongle sold with each repair. Kills: OEM firmware lock-out and falling Chinese source prices; mitigate by building rung 2 early. Rubric estimate about 19/30: L1 5, L2 4, L3 3, L4 3, L5 3, L6 1.
scored.rung_one_economics: The pitch's $8-60k ticket doesn't hold up against current Chinese pricing. Complete Raycus 3 kW handheld weld/cut/clean systems, with chiller and a 5-year warranty, sell retail in the US for about $5,000-6,650 (eBay listings, 2024-25). A 2-3 kW Chinese source on its own is therefore probably about $2-4k (estimate). Repairing a Raycus or Max source below about 6 kW is worth less than replacing it, so the tickets that justify a depot are mostly legacy IPG YLS/YLR units of 6-20 kW. Those top out around $15-60k (estimate), and they shrink every year as Chinese sources replace them. The parts are also a problem. Pump diodes, combiners and active fiber are OEM-vertical: IPG makes its own diodes and won't sell spares. That leaves distressed and used donor units or Chinese diode suppliers as the only supply. Depot capex is about $1-1.5M (splicers about $50-100k each, power meters, burn-in rack with chillers and power, clean bench, donor inventory). That part is plausible with seed money. Revenue: maybe $1.5-3M a year at 30-45% gross margin is realistic for a two-technician depot by month 15 (estimate). $3-5M looks optimistic because high-value tickets are scarce and certified high-power fiber laser technicians are hard to hire. IPG FY2025 revenue was about $1.0B, so there is a large aging IPG fleet. IPG's standard warranty is 3 years.
scored.buyers: Job shops and sheet-metal fabricators. They are mostly small, thinly capitalised and price-driven, and they can buy a new Chinese source for less than most repairs. Cutting-system integrators and OEM machine builders (Trumpf, Bystronic, Amada, Mazak) mostly use their own or captive OEM service. Used-machine dealers buy wholesale. Larger automotive and battery welding lines will pay for uptime, but they demand OEM-certified service. Few buyers are capitalised, and the ones that are prefer OEM paper.
scored.incumbents: The OEM depots hold rung one. IPG runs an in-house repair depot (Marlborough MA HQ; about $1.0B FY2025 revenue; Oxford MA depot technician postings) and offers retrofit services. nLight designs its sources for on-site service and trains integrators to do their own repairs. Raycus (Wuhan Raycus, listed, the price leader in China) and Max Photonics ship cheap replacement modules through distributors. Independents are small, fragmented and unfunded: Synchronics in India for IPG YLS/YLR, plus Chinese and Indian all-brand repairers. In the US the space is a scatter of small laser-service shops. No venture-funded independent fiber-laser reman player was found, so the rung is open, but probably because the economics are thin rather than because nobody has noticed.
scored.end_state: Fiber laser sources alone are about $4.3B in 2025, projected to reach about $12.8B by 2035 (single consultancy estimate, rough). The broader industrial laser plus laser systems pool is about $20B+, which is the candidate's own claim and is roughly consistent with system-level market reports (estimate). Doing it end to end means competing with IPG ($1B revenue, falling margins: net income $31M in 2025) and Raycus/Max, who have pushed source prices down sharply. Then come cell/system makers Trumpf, Han's Laser and Bodor. The value pool is large, but the vertically integrated incumbents' own margins are being crushed, so climbing the chain means climbing into a deflationary price war.
scored.killer: Commodity deflation of Chinese fiber laser sources. A complete Raycus 3 kW system now sells for about $6k, so repair loses to replacement for most of the installed base, and the high-value IPG legacy fleet that justifies the depot shrinks every year. Secondary killers: OEM parts lock-out (vertically integrated diodes and fiber, firmware/serial lock-outs, warranty voiding), scarcity of high-power laser technicians, and the fact that rungs 3-5 (own source, cells, laser-as-a-service) mean head-on competition with IPG, Raycus, Trumpf and Han's in a market where even IPG earns about 3% net margin.
scored.one_line_reason: The depot can be built with seed money, but its value is shrinking: Chinese sources at a few thousand dollars make repair uneconomic for most units. Repair data alone doesn't give the company an edge when it tries to build its own laser source. And the end state is a deflationary commodity market where IPG nets about 3%, so this scores about 13/30, not 19.

scored.name: Chiplet Foundry Express (quick-turn advanced-packaging line for chip startups and defense)
scored.industry: Semiconductors / advanced packaging
scored.rung_one: A low-volume advanced-packaging line (flip-chip and thermocompression bonding, interposer rework, underfill, X-ray, CSAM) assembling prototype and pilot multi-die chiplet lots at $25-250k per lot with 3-6 week turns instead of 4-6 month OSAT queues, for funded AI-chip and photonics startups, DARPA/university programs and defense primes. Competitors: Amkor, ASE, SkyWater/Fraunhofer, Promex, Quik-Pak, Micross, NAPMP pilot lines, Chipletz, Silicon Box.
scored.ladder: 1) Quick-turn prototype packaging. 2) Low-volume trusted US-only production for defense and space. 3) Co-packaged optics assembly. 4) A US chiplet-integration fab with standard interposers and a chiplet library. 5) Own integrated compute/memory/optics modules. Pool $50B+.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: recipe and warpage models from every lot predict bond-yield and underfill voids before first article. Rung 2: per-part traceability and yield graph for defense. Rung 3: active fiber-alignment ML cutting CPO attach time. Rung 4: package co-design copilot from a cross-stack dataset. Rung 5: system test data feeds chiplet selection.
scored.seed_plan: About $3M (tight): used Finetech/Besi/ASMPT bonders plus metrology co-located in a university or state cleanroom (NY CREATES, Arizona, Texas) to avoid fab capex; pre-sell lots to 5-6 startups and one DARPA program for $2-3M revenue by month 18. Kills: CHIPS-funded public pilot lines giving away capacity and startup funding cycles. Rubric estimate about 18/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 4, L4 3, L5 2, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: Lot price: $25-250k per lot (candidate's assumption, not verified). Capital: one new die-to-wafer TCB tool costs about $4M (Besi's 2025 order was 5 TCB Next systems for about $20M). A 2015 Besi order worked out to about $0.9M per bonder, so used or older TCB tools probably cost $0.5-1M (estimate). Used Finetech-class flip-chip bonders cost roughly $0.2-0.5M (estimate). X-ray plus CSAM is roughly $0.5-1M (estimate). Underfill, dispense, plasma and reflow are roughly $0.3-0.5M (estimate). A credible minimum line with used tools in a shared cleanroom is therefore about $1.5-3M of tools before payroll. That uses the whole $3M seed, or needs equipment leases or venture debt. Revenue (estimate): about 15-25 lots a year at about $80k average gives $1.2-2M a year. Gross margin is probably 30-50% at low volume, because yield losses on customers' scarce known-good die can wipe out a lot's margin. Making $2-3M by month 18 is plausible but tight, and there is little left for rungs 2-4. Moving to production (rung 4) means $100M+ fab capex.
scored.buyers: Funded AI-accelerator and photonics/CPO startups needing prototype multi-die builds. DARPA, AFRL and university programs. Defense primes and space companies needing trusted US-only low-volume assembly (Lockheed, Northrop, RTX, BAE). Buyers have money but order in small, irregular lots. Startup demand rises and falls with funding cycles, and DARPA work follows program timelines.
scored.incumbents: The rung is crowded and heavily subsidised. Natcast received $1.1B of CHIPS NAPMP money to run an advanced-packaging prototyping facility and baseline pilot line in Tempe, AZ, for exactly this user base. Absolics, Applied Materials and ASU shared $300M under NAPMP for substrates and materials. Promex plus QP Technologies (ex-Quik-Pak) is a Silicon Valley and San Diego quick-turn assembly house adding chiplet-oriented tools in 2025. Other players: Micross (trusted/DMEA), SkyWater (Florida packaging), Fraunhofer IZM, imec, NY CREATES, Applied Materials' META Center, and Intel Foundry and Amkor Arizona offering packaging. Silicon Box raised about $200M Series B (valued at over $1B) and S$100M of debt, and is building chiplet packaging plants in Singapore and Italy. Chipletz is developing Smart Substrate packaging (funding about $30M, unverified). On both price and turn time, subsidised public pilot lines can undercut a seed-funded startup.
scored.end_state: Yole forecasts advanced packaging revenue rising from $46.1B (2024) to $79.4B (2030), about 9.5% a year. Grand View and ResearchAndMarkets put 2030 at about $55B. Integrated compute/optics modules (rung 5) would add a multi-$10B pool on top. The pool is large, but going end to end means a US chiplet-integration fab competing with TSMC CoWoS, Intel and Amkor at billions of capex. No seed-to-Series-B path reaches that without something like a CHIPS-scale award.
scored.killer: Subsidised competition plus capex. Natcast's $1.1B Tempe prototyping line and the state cleanrooms (NY CREATES, ASU, Texas) offer the same quick-turn prototype service to the same startups and DARPA programs. Natcast's funding is politically uncertain, but government-backed capacity remains either way. Other problems: tight tool capex and leases, liability for yield loss on customers' scarce known-good die, small lumpy lots with demand tied to startup funding cycles, and too few lots for the ML yield/warpage models to compound (tens of lots a year is a weak data flywheel). In practice it is a job shop with good process engineers, not an ML company.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but crowded, subsidised job-shop rung: Natcast's $1.1B CHIPS prototyping line, Promex/QP, Micross, Fraunhofer and imec already hold it. Lot volumes are too small for an ML flywheel, and the higher rungs need fab-scale capex, so it scores about 13/30.

scored.name: GaGe Reclaim (gallium and germanium from fab and optics scrap)
scored.industry: Critical-material recycling for compound semiconductors, IR optics and fiber
scored.rung_one: An owned toll-recovery cell (hydrometallurgy, fractional crystallisation, zone refining) on long-term contracts with GaAs/GaN RF fabs (Qorvo, Skyworks, Wolfspeed, Win Semi US), LED and laser makers and germanium IR-optics grinders, recovering 4N-6N Ga and GeO2/Ge from kerf, sludge, broken wafers and lapping slurry now stockpiled or shipped to Asia. Ex-China Ga trades around $700-1,500/kg since the 2023-24 controls, Ge around $2,500-3,500/kg; a 5-10 t Ga plus 3 t Ge cell is about $10-20M revenue. Incumbents (Umicore, 5N Plus, Indium Corp, Nyrstar, Trafigura plans) are refinery or mining-adjacent; none is a fab-scrap-native US recycler.
scored.ladder: 1) Scrap tolling and recovery. 2) 7N refining and TMGa/GeCl4 precursors. 3) Ge and GaAs VGF substrate crystal growth. 4) Epi wafers and GaN-on-SiC substrates for defense RF and power. 5) Contract by-product recovery from existing US alumina and zinc refinery liquors (processing others' streams, not mining). Pool: $3-5B of materials plus a $10B+ substrate and epi market.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: assay and recovery-yield prediction per scrap stream and contract pricing from fab process data. Rung 2: impurity-fingerprint models tuning zone-refining passes. Rung 3: crystal-growth ML (thermal field, defect prediction) on purity genealogy. Rung 4: substrate defect maps feed back to blending; fab scrap contracts also give a live view of US compound-semi utilisation for offtake and hedging.
scored.seed_plan: $2M: lab-plus-pilot unit in North Carolina or Texas, a 1 t/yr-feed pilot (leach, SX, electrowinning, zone refiner) for about $800k, two fab scrap MOUs, DoD DPA Title III and IBAS applications, 5N Ga qualification at one customer by month 15. Kills: Chinese policy reversal collapsing prices (DoD offtake floors and tolling fees) and small absolute volumes requiring the climb to substrates. Rubric estimate about 21/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 4, L4 4, L5 4, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: The volume premise does not hold. USGS MCS 2025: total reported US gallium consumption is about 19 t/yr (19,000 kg in 2024e), US gallium metal imports were about 11 t, and the value of those imports was only about $4M in 2024, against about $140M of GaAs wafer imports. World refined high-purity Ga is about 320 t/yr, and world secondary (scrap) refining capacity is already about 280 t/yr. A 5-10 t Ga cell would therefore be 25-50% of all US consumption. That is implausible from US fab back-end scrap: most Ga loss happens at crystal growth and wafering (AXT in China, Freiberger, Sumitomo), not at Qorvo or Skyworks device fabs. Realistic US fab-scrap feed is my estimate of 1-3 t Ga/yr. Prices: China low-purity 4N Ga was $380-420/kg in 2024 (USGS). Ex-China high-purity runs about $700-1,500/kg (estimate, consistent with the candidate). Ge is about $2,500-3,500/kg (estimate; no source fetched). So rung-one revenue on metal value is about $2-6M/yr, and lower as a toll fee (typically a share of contained value; estimate 20-40%). Capex: the roughly $800k pilot is plausible. But GaAs scrap carries arsenic, so a production cell needs RCRA hazardous-waste handling and air permits (estimate $5-15M and 18-30 months for a commercial cell). 5N/6N qualification at an RF fab typically takes 12-24 months. Gross margin on toll recovery is thin unless prices stay elevated.
scored.buyers: Same-party closed loop: GaAs/GaN RF fabs (Qorvo, Skyworks, Wolfspeed, MACOM, Win Semi US) sell scrap and buy back refined Ga or precursors. Also MOCVD precursor makers (Nouryon, Dockweiler, Entegris), substrate growers (AXT, Freiberger, Sumitomo Electric, Coherent), IR-optics makers (Coherent, LightPath, Umicore), and DoD (DPA Title III, DLA stockpile) as a price-floor offtaker. These buyers are well capitalised, but each one's volume is tiny and they already have scrap-return contracts with existing refiners.
scored.incumbents: Rung one is not open, though there is no single dominant US-native fab-scrap player. USGS confirms that one New York facility already reprocesses "substantial quantities of new scrap" from GaAs manufacture into high-purity Ga, and that "an Australian company plans to open an industrial electronic scrap recycling plant in the United States with an initial focus on gallium recovery." From memory, that is very likely MTM Critical Metals, ASX-listed, with a Flash Joule Heating plant in Texas. Other incumbents: 5N Plus (TSX, about C$300M+ revenue, formerly Recapture Metals in Utah, does GaAs scrap tolling), Umicore (Ge optics and scrap closed loop, a multi-$B group), Dowa and Mitsubishi Materials in Japan (internal Ga scrap loops), PPM Pure Metals in Germany, Indium Corporation, and Teck (Ge). Primary Ga ex-China (outside rung one but a cap on prices): Nyrstar/Trafigura Clarksville TN (Ga/Ge with US government support), Atalco/ElementUSA in Louisiana, Alcoa with Japan/US at Wagerup, and Rio Tinto/Indium Corp in Quebec. These also take rung 5, the by-product liquors.
scored.end_state: Much smaller than claimed. The refined Ga metal pool is about 320 t x $500-1,000/kg, roughly $0.2-0.4B/yr globally (USGS volume; price is my estimate). The Ge pool is about 140 t x ~$3,000/kg, roughly $0.4B (estimate). The GaAs substrate market is about $1-1.5B, and the GaN-on-SiC/GaN epi and substrate market a few $B (estimates). An end-to-end Ga/Ge materials, substrate and epi chain is about $3-6B total, not $10B+. The device market above that (RF front-ends, power GaN) is large, but climbing into devices is a fab business competing with Qorvo, Wolfspeed and Infineon, with a capex wall of $100M-$1B+. VGF crystal growth (rung 3) is a mature, capex-heavy, yield-know-how business held by AXT, Freiberger and Sumitomo.
scored.killer: 1) Price and policy reversal. China's Ga/Ge export restrictions are a political lever; the Dec 2024 ban on US exports was, as I recall, suspended in the Nov 2025 US-China truce, and the premium can collapse at any time. Recovery economics at about $2-6M revenue do not survive Ga back near $300/kg. 2) Tiny absolute volume. US consumption is only about 19 t/yr, so even a dominant US scrap share stays a sub-$10M business, and climbing needs crystal-growth and epi capex far beyond seed. 3) Arsenic-bearing hazardous-waste permitting. 4) Customer concentration: about five RF fabs. 5) Incumbent closed-loop contracts (5N Plus, Umicore, Dowa). 6) ML is not decisive: assay and yield prediction on a handful of scrap streams is a spreadsheet problem, and zone-refining tuning gives marginal gains.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a strategically sympathetic DoD story with no real ML moat. US Ga demand is only about 19 t/yr, so rung one is a $2-6M toll business already contested by 5N Plus, a New York recycler and MTM, and it hinges on a reversible Chinese price premium; climbing to substrates and epi means fighting AXT, Freiberger and Wolfspeed with capex far beyond seed. Score: 13/30, not the 21 estimated.
sources: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Gallium: https://pubs.usgs.gov/periodicals/mcs2025/mcs2025-gallium.pdf (US consumption ~19,000 kg/yr; metal imports ~$4M; GaAs wafer imports ~$140M; China 4N Ga $380-420/kg in 2024; world refined 320 t, secondary capacity 280 t/yr; one NY scrap recycler; Australian e-scrap Ga plant planned in US; Dec 2024 China ban on Ga exports to US)

Note: the shared web-search budget was exhausted, so only one primary source could be fetched. Ex-China Ga/Ge prices, incumbent revenues, MTM Critical Metals identification, the Nov 2025 suspension of China's ban, and substrate/epi market sizes are from model knowledge and marked as estimates.

scored.name: Brightline (X-ray sterilization sites that climb to photonuclear isotopes)
scored.industry: Accelerator-based irradiation (medical device sterilization, food irradiation, isotopes)
scored.rung_one: One electron-beam or X-ray irradiation line in a leased shielded building (refurbished 5-10 MeV e-beam/X-ray converter or capacity lease, $2-4M with equipment financing) selling contract sterilization to mid-size device and pharma packaging makers displaced from EtO (EPA 2024 rule) and Co-60 gamma (cobalt squeeze), at $0.10-1.00 per cubic foot or $0.5-3M a year contracts. Incumbents: Steris AST, Sotera (Sterigenics/Nordion), E-BEAM Services, Mevex, Steri-Tek, NextBeam; isotope side NorthStar, SHINE, Niowave, IBA. The mid-market capacity shortfall is open.
scored.ladder: 1) Single sterilization site. 2) Regional network near device clusters (Minneapolis, Costa Rica, Ireland, Puerto Rico). 3) Photonuclear isotope production on the same accelerators (Mo-99/Tc-99m, Cu-67, Sc-47, Ac-225). 4) In-house high-power electron linac manufacturing. 5) Fully integrated irradiation (sterilization, phytosanitary, crosslinking, isotopes); sterilization alone is $5B+.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: ML dose mapping and load-pattern optimisation cut validation runs and raise throughput per beam-kW, with an AI-assisted ISO 11137 validation package as the wedge. Rung 2: network scheduling, dynamic pricing and a cross-site validation library. Rung 3: target-design surrogates and decay-aware beam time-sharing between sterilization and isotopes. Rung 4: klystron/modulator health data feeds in-house accelerator design.
scored.seed_plan: Use a refurbished linac or vendor deferred payment (IBA, Mevex, L3), site next to a device cluster, and pre-sell capacity through 3-5 LOIs from EtO-displaced device makers before buying; seed covers fit-out and validation. Kills: per-site capex and incumbents' validation lock-in. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 4, L4 4, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: The pitch's $2-4M cost for rung one is off by about 5x. Real reference points: NextBeam describes its single e-beam site in North Sioux City as a $20M facility (mtec-sc.org profile). IBA's Be Wide X-ray system alone lists at EUR 16-19M with customisation, before the building (IBA/Steri-Tek June 2025 release). Steri-Tek's expansion of an existing site needed a $12.8M BARDA/ASPR base award to reach 3.5M cubic feet a year (ASPR, March 2025). My estimate: a refurbished 10 MeV linac costs $3-6M, a shielded vault or concrete fit-out $4-10M, and dosimetry, conveyor and QA staff $1-2M, so the minimum credible site is about $10-20M (estimate). Revenue: at 3.5M cu ft a year and $0.30-1.00 per cu ft, a site earns about $1-3.5M a year (estimate), which gives a payback of 5-10 years at high utilisation. Ramp is slow because each customer's product must go through ISO 11137 dose-setting and revalidation, and an FDA 510(k)/PMA supplement is often needed to switch modality, which takes 6-24 months per customer before revenue arrives. Margins at scaled incumbents are attractive: Sotera and Steris AST run about 50% segment EBITDA (from memory, not verified this round). A single subscale site would run well below that until it is full.
scored.buyers: Mid-size medical device makers, contract manufacturers and pharma packaging firms that are losing EtO capacity under the 2024 EPA NESHAP rule or cannot get Co-60 gamma time. These are capitalised buyers, but each one has to revalidate its products (ISO 11137 dose audits, a regulatory filing for the modality change) before switching, so procurement is slow and conservative. Secondary buyers: polymer crosslinking (wire, cable, tubing) and phytosanitary food irradiation.
scored.incumbents: Rung one is crowded and well capitalised. Steris (more than $5.1-5.5B total revenue in FY24/25, with AST running 50+ contract sterilization sites in EtO, gamma, e-beam and X-ray). Sotera Health/Sterigenics, the #2 globally; it opened a new X-ray site in Haw River, NC in March 2026. Steri-Tek is adding an IBA X-ray line in Texas with $12.8M of BARDA money. NextBeam runs a $20M e-beam site in South Dakota. BGS opened a US e-beam site in Pennsylvania. E-BEAM Services, Mevex and Ion Beam Applications (IBA, which both sells and partners) are also active. The US government (BARDA/ASPR) is directly paying for capacity growth among existing players, which removes much of the 'mid-market capacity shortfall'. Isotope rung: SHINE (more than $1B raised, from memory), NorthStar (accelerator Mo-99, troubled and restructured, from memory, not verified this round), Niowave, and IBA. Capacity there is already funded.
scored.end_state: Global sterilization services are about $3.75B in 2025, rising to $5.49B by 2030 (MarketsandMarkets). The US market is $2.71B by 2030, with contract work at 70.6% share (Grand View). Adding crosslinking, food irradiation and medical isotopes (Mo-99 about $0.5-1B, plus a speculative Ac-225/Cu-67 therapeutic pipeline; estimates) gives a total pool of perhaps $8-15B (estimate). That is below the multi-$10B bar. Accelerator manufacturing (IBA, L3/Mevex) is a small, lumpy capital-equipment market. Doing the whole chain end to end is technically coherent, but each rung is capital-heavy and the isotope step means a different regulatory regime (NRC/FDA drug master files).
scored.killer: The killers compound: (1) a capex wall of $10-20M per site, not $2-4M, so seed money cannot buy rung one, and leasing capacity means the company does not own the rung. (2) Validation lock-in: customers switch only after slow ISO 11137 revalidation and regulatory filings, so a new entrant needs years to fill a beam. (3) Incumbents and BARDA-funded players (Steris, Sterigenics' new X-ray site, Steri-Tek's IBA line) are already adding the X-ray/e-beam capacity that EtO displacement creates. (4) Thin software leverage: dose mapping is a small efficiency gain, already done in-house with Monte Carlo codes, and it is no moat. (5) The step up to isotopes is a separate capex and regulatory chasm where well-funded players (SHINE, NorthStar) have struggled.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but capital-heavy, validation-gated service business. Rung one costs about $10-20M (NextBeam $20M; IBA X-ray EUR 16-19M for equipment alone), not $2-4M. Steris, Sotera and BARDA-funded Steri-Tek already hold the capacity build-out, and ML dose mapping is a marginal optimisation rather than a compounding moat. About 12/30.

scored.name: Switchyard (battery-electric conversion of switcher locomotives for industrial and short-line rail)
scored.industry: Machines / rail transport
scored.rung_one: Remanufactured diesel switchers (EMD SW/GP cores bought at $100-300k) converted to battery-electric or hybrid and sold ($1.5-3M) or leased ($15-30k per month, 60-80% fuel savings) to industrial yards (steel, grain, chemicals, ports) and short lines facing CARB/EPA and port emissions rules. Incumbents: Progress Rail and Wabtec (mainline-focused), Knoxville Locomotive Works, OptiFuel, Parallel Systems (autonomous railcars, not switchers).
scored.ladder: 1) Converted switchers. 2) Leased fleet with bundled energy and maintenance and yard autonomy (remote control, then autonomous switching). 3) Switching-as-a-service yard operations contracts. 4) New-build battery locomotives on own platform. 5) Short-line ownership/operation and port rail drayage. 6) Zero-emission rail equipment and operations across 600+ US short lines and thousands of industrial yards.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: telematics duty-cycle modelling sizes the battery per customer. Rung 2: fleet energy and charging optimisation, predictive maintenance and remote-control autonomy trained on yard video and telemetry. Rung 3: yard scheduling and railcar-movement optimisation with performance pricing. Rung 4: design from fleet duty data. Rung 5: network planning.
scored.seed_plan: $3M: buy 2 cores, convert the first unit in a leased shop with an off-the-shelf battery/traction stack, first customer a California port or industrial yard under CARB in-use locomotive pressure with HVIP/Carl Moyer grants. Kills: CARB rule litigation or rollback, battery cost, FRA approval; hedged by fuel savings at high-duty yards. Rubric estimate about 20/30: L1 3, L2 4, L3 3, L4 3, L5 4, L6 3.
scored.rung_one_economics: Search caveat: the shared web-search budget was used up before this candidate ran, and the CARB and Wikipedia fetches returned nothing usable. All numbers below are ESTIMATES from prior knowledge, not checked this round. Core: an EMD SW/GP core costs about $100-300k (the candidate's figure; plausible). Conversion cost (estimate): a 1-2 MWh rail-grade LFP pack, installed at about $400-600/kWh, comes to roughly $0.5-1.2M. Add traction and controls rework, a charger with utility work ($150-400k) and engineering plus FRA (Federal Railroad Administration) compliance. The first unit lands at roughly $1.5-2.5M all-in, plus heavy one-off engineering cost. OEM battery yard units have reportedly been grant-funded at about $3-5M each (estimate). Selling conversions at $1.5-3M would give perhaps 15-30% gross margin after unit 3-5; units 1-2 make no margin or lose money. Customer side: a yard switcher burns about 20-60k gal of diesel a year (estimate), worth about $70-250k/yr, plus maintenance savings. Unsubsidised payback is about 8-15 years, so nearly every deal depends on grants (Carl Moyer, CRISI, DERA). $3M seed buys 1-2 units and a leased shop. The leasing rung needs asset debt at $2M+ per unit, which seed cannot carry.
scored.buyers: Buyers would be captive industrial yards (steel, grain, chemicals, refineries, auto plants), port terminal railroads (LA/Long Beach, Oakland), short-line holding companies (Genesee & Wyoming, Watco, OmniTRAX, RailUSA) and Class I railroads buying yard units. From memory, Union Pacific ordered about 20 battery locomotives from Wabtec and Progress Rail in 2022. These buyers have capital, but they buy battery units only when a grant or a rule forces it. Industrial yards each run 1-3 locomotives, so sales are lumpy, slow and procurement-heavy.
scored.incumbents: Rung one is crowded. From memory, unverified this round: Progress Rail/Caterpillar (EMD Joule battery locomotives); Wabtec (FLXdrive, plus a battery switcher line); Knoxville Locomotive Works (battery and Tier 4 genset switchers for industrial yards); OptiFuel Systems (zero-emission switchers, RNG and battery); Rail Propulsion Systems (California battery switcher conversions, CARB-grant funded); Cummins and Sierra Northern (hydrogen switcher, CA grant); Brookville; and the National Railway Equipment/Motive Power rebuilders. Watco, OmniTRAX and others already sell switching-as-a-service (rung 3). Remote control is standard and commoditised (Cattron, Wabtec). Parallel Systems (about $100M+ raised, estimate) works on autonomous rail but not switchers.
scored.end_state: End state is modest (all ESTIMATES, not verified this round). US short-line revenue is roughly $5-7B across about 600 Class II/III railroads. Industrial in-plant switching services are perhaps $1-3B. The new and rebuilt switcher equipment market is a few hundred million to about $1B a year in North America. The whole chain (equipment, yard operations, short lines, port drayage) is perhaps a $10-15B revenue pool, mostly low-margin operations held by entrenched consolidators (G&W is Brookfield/GIC owned; Watco). Doing it end to end means becoming a Watco-like operator, which is a roll-up and asset business, not an ML company.
scored.killer: The demand driver is gone, and nothing compounds. To my knowledge, CARB withdrew its EPA authorisation request for the In-Use Locomotive Regulation in January 2025 and moved to repeal it, so the regulatory forcing function behind rung one no longer exists. I could not re-check this here because the CARB page came back empty. Without the rule, unsubsidised payback is 8-15 years and diesel is cheap, so sales are grant-gated and lumpy. At least six funded or established players already make battery and zero-emission switchers. FRA and AAR (Association of American Railroads) qualification and battery fire-safety add time. Software is thin: duty-cycle sizing is a spreadsheet, remote control is commoditised, and railroads with small fleets produce little data.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one can be sold but is crowded and grant-dependent, and its regulatory driver (CARB in-use locomotive rule) was withdrawn. The software is thin and does not compound, and the end state is a low-margin short-line roll-up. About 12/30, against the candidate's 20.

scored.name: Loopkeeper (coolant-as-a-service for liquid-cooled AI halls)
scored.industry: Cooling / thermal infrastructure
scored.rung_one: Owned coolant inventory, filtration and sensor skids on the secondary loops of direct-to-chip liquid-cooled racks at neoclouds and colos, sold per rack or per MW (fluid supply, chemistry monitoring, filter changes, contamination response, SLA-backed uptime) at about $15-40k per MW per year (a 20 MW customer is roughly $0.5M ARR). Incumbents: Vertiv/CoolIT, Schneider (Motivair), nVent, and water treaters Ecolab/Nalco, ChemTreat and Veolia, which do facility water rather than secondary-loop GPU chemistry as an owned-asset SLA.
scored.ladder: 1) Fluid and loop-chemistry service contracts. 2) Owned and operated CDUs under the same contract. 3) Own CDU and manifold manufacture. 4) Facility-water and dry-cooler plant as a service. 5) Selling recovered heat to district heating or industry, a thermal utility owned end to end.
scored.software_layer: Rung 1: inline sensors (conductivity, particulates, pH, inhibitor depletion) plus ML predicting corrosion, biofouling and cold-plate clogging before GPU throttling, a unique cross-site dataset. Rung 2: closed-loop CDU flow and temperature control against GPU telemetry, raising inlet setpoints. Rung 3: designs tuned from field failures. Rung 4: plant-level free-cooling and dry-cooler optimisation. Rung 5: heat dispatch forecasting.
scored.seed_plan: Build the skid (about $25k BOM) and an incident playbook, sign 2-3 neoclouds running GB200/GB300 halls that have had contamination incidents; about $1M on hardware fleet and $1M on field techs across two metros. Kills: OEMs bundling fluid service into CDU warranties and low-margin consumables if software value is unproven. Rubric estimate about 19/30: L1 4, L2 3, L3 4, L4 3, L5 3, L6 2.
scored.rung_one_economics: The web search budget ran out before this run made any searches, so every figure here comes from prior knowledge and should be treated as an estimate. Proposed price: $15-40k per MW per year. A 20 MW neocloud hall would therefore pay about $0.3-0.8M a year (estimate). The coolant itself is a small, one-off purchase. A 1 MW direct-to-chip secondary loop holds only a few thousand litres of PG25, roughly $10-30k of fluid (estimate), so recurring revenue would have to come from monitoring, filter changes and response SLAs. Field-service labour margins typically run 25-40% (estimate). The software only earns a premium if it demonstrably prevents GPU throttling or cold-plate failures, and once a loop is commissioned and stable those events are rare. Capital: a skid costs about $25k in parts, so 40-80 deployed skids is $1-2M, plus field technicians in two metros. That fits inside $3M. Scale problem: about $0.5M ARR per 20 MW customer means reaching $10M ARR needs 400+ MW under contract. That is roughly 5-10% of all neocloud direct-to-chip capacity built in 2026 (estimate), from a very concentrated buyer set.
scored.buyers: Neoclouds and GPU colos running GB200/GB300 direct-to-chip halls: CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe, Nebius, Together, Voltage Park, Applied Digital, plus retail colos such as Equinix and Digital Realty. Hyperscalers run their own loops. The buyers are capitalised but few and concentrated. They usually take fluid and commissioning services bundled with the CDU or the facility-build contract, and their facilities teams prefer one throat to choke (the OEM).
scored.incumbents: From memory, not re-verified this run. Vertiv: acquired CoolTera (2023, coolant distribution), CoolIT's partner channel and PurgeRite (announced 2025, about $1B). PurgeRite does exactly this work: flushing, filtration, fluid management and commissioning of mission-critical liquid-cooling loops. Ecolab: launched 3D TRASAR monitoring for direct-to-chip liquid cooling (2025), which is inline secondary-loop chemistry monitoring sold as a service. Schneider Electric: bought 75% of Motivair for about $850M (2024) and bundles CDUs with service. Eaton: buying Boyd Thermal for about $9.5B (2025). nVent, Nalco Water/ChemTreat and Veolia sell facility-water treatment. CDU makers (CoolIT, Motivair, LiquidStack, Chilldyne, JetCool/Flex) offer fluid and service packages under their warranties. Rung one is already held by a $1B Vertiv-owned specialist and by Ecolab's monitoring product.
scored.end_state: The end state the candidate describes: rung 3 is CDU and manifold manufacture, rungs 4-5 are cooling plant as a service and selling heat. The data-centre liquid-cooling equipment market is roughly $5-6B (2025) heading to about $15-25B by 2030 (estimate, consensus range of analyst reports such as Dell'Oro and MarketsandMarkets). Total data-centre thermal management, including chillers and dry coolers, is about $20-30B (estimate). Selling recovered heat is a low-grade product worth very little: 30-45C water mostly earns cents per kWh-thermal, and only where a district heating network exists. That is meaningful in the Nordics and Germany, not in US neocloud metros. The pool is large, but the steps from rung 3 onward run head-on into Vertiv, Schneider and Eaton, who have just spent $1-10B each to own exactly this chain.
scored.killer: Incumbent bundling. Vertiv (PurgeRite), Schneider (Motivair) and Eaton (Boyd) sell CDU, fluid, commissioning and lifecycle service as one warranty-backed package. Neoclouds will not let a third party touch the loop chemistry on a CDU whose warranty depends on the OEM's approved fluid. Ecolab already sells inline monitoring. The other killers: secondary-loop service is a small slice of each contract (tens of $k per MW per year against a $1-3M+ per MW build), there are only about 10 buyers, and the ML loses its edge because closed loops with filtration and PG25 inhibitors fail rarely, so the data flywheel is thin.
scored.one_line_reason: Rung one is already held: Vertiv's roughly $1B PurgeRite deal and Ecolab's 3D TRASAR for direct-to-chip cover owned secondary-loop fluid service and monitoring. The service is a low-value consumable that CDU warranties absorb, sold to about 10 concentrated buyers, and each higher rung runs into Vertiv, Schneider and Eaton. About 12/30.
