deep.memo:
# Recast: feasibility deep-dive

*Evidence caveat: the shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn) ran out before this agent started, so no new searches ran. Numbers come from direct fetches of known URLs or are marked ESTIMATE. A follow-up turn could run the searches still needed: transit agency bids, DLA reverse-engineering volumes, and the US hydro fleet's age.*

## Rung one
- **What is owned:** a qualified metrology, reverse-engineering and production cell, plus a growing library of part files with qualification packages for obsolete or long-lead non-hot-section parts: pump impellers, valve trim, gears, seals, breaker linkages, hydro wicket-gate bushings, and transit parts.
- **Buyers:** hydro and municipal utilities, IPPs with legacy frames, refiners and mills, transit agencies, and DLA.
- **Unit price:** about $2-50k per part in the band a seed company can make (ESTIMATE). Parts at $100-500k are hot-section and out of reach.
- **Gross margin:** 40-60% before engineering hours (ESTIMATE).
- **Year-one revenue:** $0.5-1.5M (ESTIMATE).
- **Why the window exists:** Chromalloy, quoted in Turbomachinery Magazine, sizes gas-turbine services at $16-17B a year, or about $20B with upgrades. It advises OEM parts for designs under 10 years old and says Frame 5 through E-class have "plenty of spare parts choices". So the legacy fleet is already a buyer of non-OEM parts ([Turbomachinery](https://turbomachinerymag.com/view/aftermarket-parts-is-there-life-after-oem)).
- **Hydro:** facilities last 65-85 years ([DOE](https://www.energy.gov/eere/water/hydropower-basics)), and the US had 80.25 GW of hydro in 2019 ([DOE market reports](https://www.energy.gov/eere/water/hydropower-market-reports)). That is a large, aging base of orphaned mechanical parts.

## How two founders win it with seed money
About $2.5M (ESTIMATE):
- **Kit:** a 5-axis CNC ($0.3-0.8M), blue-light scanners ($50-150k) and a handheld XRF/OES for material ID ($30-80k). Rent CT time and outsource casting and AM. All figures ESTIMATE.
- **Certification:** ISO 9001 in about 6 months; AS9100 in 9-12 months, only if the company goes after defense work (ESTIMATE).
- **Wedge:** municipal hydro and public-power utilities plus transit agencies. Both post obsolete-part bids publicly and have weaker OEM lock-in than gas-turbine LTSAs.
- **Exclusions:** nuclear is out (10 CFR 50 Appendix B). DLA is a year-2 channel, because Source Approval Requests take a year or more per part family (ESTIMATE).
- **The bar:** 40-80 paid jobs and 3-5 approved-vendor listings in 18 months is ambitious but doable. AddParts in Sheffield shows the shape: founded 2024, ISO 9001, a $570k pre-seed led by SFC Capital in April 2026 ([Caplight](https://www.caplight.com/company/addparts-co)).

## The ladder (each rung, capital and buyer)
All capital figures are ESTIMATES.

| Rung | What it is | Capital | Buyer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Per-part reverse engineering and fulfilment | $2-3M | Plant maintenance or emergency budgets |
| 2 | Pre-qualified digital catalogue, resold across fleets with the same equipment | $5-10M | Utility supply chain and stores |
| 3 | Non-hot-section repair and remanufacture: pumps, valves, gearboxes, breakers | $10-20M | Same buyers, through repair contracts |
| 3b | Hot-section repair and coating | $30-50M+ | Gas-turbine fleets |
| 4 | Multi-year sustainment and parts-supply agreements for orphaned fleets | Working capital | Utility and transit procurement |
| 5 | Buy orphaned OEM product lines, IP and drawings | M&A (debt or PE) | Owners of those fleets |
| 6 | Independent aftermarket OEM-equivalent and roll-up | Buyout-scale capital | Whole legacy fleet |

## What software/ML compounds at each rung
- **Rung 1:** scan-to-CAD, material ID and quote/lead-time prediction. This is commoditising. Novineer's NoviVision makes an editable STEP file from 1-4 phone photos in about 2 minutes, claims an average error of 0.72mm, and has US Army agreements and Stratasys integration (sponsored article, so the claims are the company's own: [Defense Post](https://thedefensepost.com/2026/06/30/novineer-ai-reverse-engineering-sustainment/)). Its value is lower engineering hours per part, not a moat.
- **Rung 2:** a part-identity graph across equipment families. It compounds only if parts repeat across sites, which is unproven. It is the key thing to test.
- **Rung 3:** repair-vs-replace models from returned-part wear. This is real, but the scale players (PSM, EthosEnergy, the OEMs) have far more data.
- **Rungs 4-5:** pricing outage risk, and choosing which orphaned lines to buy using installed-base data.
- **Conclusion:** the qualified library and qualification records compound. The ML mostly cuts cost.

## Who holds rung one today
- **OEM aftermarket arms:** GE Vernova holds over 14.5% of gas-turbine services, and the top five hold 41.5% ([GMI](https://www.gminsights.com/industry-analysis/gas-turbine-service-market)).
- **Independents:** PSM (Hanwha), EthosEnergy, Chromalloy, MD&A, Sulzer.
- **Nuclear:** Curtiss-Wright Nuclear (commercial-grade dedication).
- **Startups:** AddParts (closest analogue), Intropy ($11M seed on 30 Jul 2026, software only: [aifunding](https://aifunding.me/companies/intropy)), Novineer, DISCUS, Replique, Ivaldi.
- **The long tail:** thousands of local reverse-engineering and machine shops.
- **Re:Build** is contract design and manufacturing; its site does not mention reverse engineering or spares ([Re:Build](https://www.rebuildmanufacturing.com/)), so it is adjacent rather than a direct holder.
- **Overall:** fragmented but occupied. The open slot is "owned production plus a cross-fleet library" in hydro and transit.

## End-state size
- Gas-turbine services: $27.1B in 2025, growing to $78.7B by 2035; the US was about $4.5B ([GMI](https://www.gminsights.com/industry-analysis/gas-turbine-service-market)). Chromalloy's estimate is $16-20B ([Turbomachinery](https://turbomachinerymag.com/view/aftermarket-parts-is-there-life-after-oem)).
- Adding hydro, steam, switchgear, rail and DoD sustainment gives $50B+ (ESTIMATE).
- The part a newcomer can reach (legacy and orphaned equipment, excluding hot sections) is perhaps $5-10B (ESTIMATE), and it shrinks as plants retire. Hydro and transit are the exception: those assets are not retiring.

## What kills it
1. **Job-shop economics.** Revenue scales with engineers if parts don't repeat across sites.
2. **Liability and qualification.** One failed rotating part can end the company. Each utility qualifies vendors separately.
3. **OEM LTSA penalties and IP litigation** on current frames.
4. **Commoditised ML,** as Novineer shows.
5. **Capex wall.** Hot-section work needs $30-50M+ (ESTIMATE).
6. **Customer concentration** is low, so it is not a killer.

## Smallest 2-week feasibility test
1. Pull every obsolete or "no longer available" part solicitation from the last 12 months: 10 large transit agencies, 10 public-power or hydro utilities, and DLA DIBBS. Log the part type, material, price and repeats.
2. Interview 15 hydro, municipal and transit maintenance leads. Ask:
   - How many orphaned parts they need a year.
   - What they paid last time.
   - What vendor qualification takes.
   - Whether a pre-qualified catalogue would change how they buy.
3. Quote 3 real parts end to end with a rented scanner and a partner machine shop. Log the engineering hours.

**Pass if:** at least 30% of parts recur across two or more owners; the cost per part shows at least 50% gross margin; and two buyers commit to a paid first article.

## Verdict
**L1 3, L2 3, L3 2, L4 3, L5 2, L6 3 = 16/30.** Rung one is fundable and sellable, but it behaves like a qualified services job shop:
- The software adds efficiency, not a flywheel, unless the test shows parts repeat across fleets.
- The rung is crowded.
- The ladder hits a wall at rung 3b (hot sections), and rungs 5-6 need M&A capital.

It is only worth pursuing if the 2-week test shows strong repeat rates in hydro and transit. Otherwise drop it.

theses:
**Note on sources:** the shared web-search budget for this run ran out before my first query, and the four primary-source pages I tried to fetch directly returned 404, 403 or a redirect. I have no verified URLs. Every number and date below comes from my own knowledge (cutoff mid-2026) and is marked **(est.)** or **(unverified)**. Each thesis ends with "Verify first" items to check before this goes to Dhruv and Charlie.

# New-thesis option: three ladder-first companies

All 25 scored candidates finished between 15 and 19 out of 30, and all failed the same way: rung one was a services shop that private equity is already rolling up, with too little data to compound. The three theses below each start on a rung that a recent rule or market change created. In each, the company's own operations generate the labelled data that the next rung needs.

## 1. Nodal: an integrated Texas power company, starting with distressed batteries it owns

**Pitch:** Buy small, underperforming batteries on the Texas grid (ERCOT) and trade them with our own ML. Then use that fleet as a physical hedge to sell retail power to large customers. The model is Octopus Energy's own-and-supply approach, applied to Texas.

**Why now:**
- ERCOT battery revenue per kW fell steeply between 2023 and 2025 because the market became saturated (unverified; Modo/ERCOT data). That puts pressure on small developers holding batteries built in 2020-22.
- ERCOT's new market design (RTC+B), live around Dec 2025 (unverified), reset how batteries earn money. Operators running old bidding playbooks are losing.

**Rung one and buyer:**
- Buy 1-3 operating batteries of 10-20 MW at a distressed price, estimated $2-6M each with asset debt.
- They earn from energy arbitrage and ancillary services. Operating batteries sell readily to infrastructure funds and IPPs (Jupiter, Plus Power, Spearmint, infra funds), so rung one has an exit on its own.

**Ladder:**
1. Own and trade the batteries.
2. Operate other owners' batteries on revenue-share or toll deals, which broadens the data.
3. Become a licensed retail provider (REP) serving commercial customers and data centres that can flex their load, hedged by our own fleet.
4. Build new storage at the grid nodes the model ranks highest.
5. Become an integrated Texas utility.

End state: Texas retail power is about $50B a year (est.).

**How the software compounds:**
- Forecasts of price and grid congestion improve with every MW we dispatch.
- Retail customers' load data improves the hedging.
- Dispatch history improves where we site new batteries.

**Unfair advantage:** ERCOT's 60-day disclosure and dispatch (SCED) data is public but hard to read. That is the same kind of problem as Terranox's assessment files, and Dhruv has solved it once.

**Biggest risk:** Battery margins keep falling as storage saturates. A 2021-style Winter Storm Uri event would hit the retail rung hard (Griddy went under in 2021). Gridmatic, an ML trader that also sells retail power, and Tesla Autobidder are the closest competitors.

**First 2-week test:**
- Rank every ERCOT battery under 20 MW by revenue per MW using the 60-day data.
- Backtest our bidding policy on 2025 and show at least 20% uplift (target, est.).
- Call the owners of the bottom 10 batteries for indicative prices.
- **Kill it if** no seller will go below about 50% of replacement cost (est.).

**Verify first:** the RTC+B go-live date, and Modo's ERCOT revenue figures for 2023-25.

## 2. Loopworks: test loops for advanced reactors, climbing to qualified components

**Pitch:** A private, non-nuclear test facility that runs helium, molten-salt and sodium loops for advanced-reactor developers. It sells test campaigns first. The degradation data it gathers then turns it into a supplier of qualified components for those reactors.

**Why now:**
- On May 23, 2025, four nuclear executive orders called for faster reactor testing and for NRC decisions within 18 months (unverified).
- In Aug 2025, DOE's Reactor Pilot Program selected about 11 projects aiming for criticality by July 4, 2026 (unverified).
- National-lab test queues are the bottleneck.

**Rung one and buyer:**
- Rung one is 1-2 loops, estimated at $1-3M each, sold as campaigns at about $0.3-2M each (est.).
- Buyers are well-funded developers: TerraPower, X-energy, Kairos, Oklo, Natura, Aalo, Radiant, Valar, Terrestrial.

**Ladder:**
1. Run test campaigns.
2. Sell ML models of corrosion, creep and wear, which shorten qualification for the next customer.
3. Make ASME III (N-stamp) qualified valves, pumps, heat exchangers and instruments for salt and helium service.
4. Build balance-of-plant skids and modules.
5. Supply the full non-fuel heat-transport package.

End state: about $10B+ a year in components (est.), but only if advanced reactors actually get built.

**How the software compounds:** every campaign's results label the materials model. Once the model is good enough, data and component sales become cheaper to win.

**Unfair advantage:** Dhruv's nuclear background plus ML. The rung is physical and owned, which keeps it clear of the excluded AI-engineering firm (Margin).

**Biggest risk:**
- Only about 15 customers, and some (Kairos, for example) test in-house.
- National labs (INL, ORNL, Argonne) are subsidised by DOE's GAIN vouchers.
- Regulators are conservative about ML extrapolation.
- Alpha Tech Research and Curtiss-Wright already run some of these loops.

**First 2-week test:**
- Interview the component-qualification leads at 10 developers.
- Get the current national-lab queue lengths.
- Ask for 2027 test-slot letters of intent backed by deposits. Target: 3 or more.

**Verify first:** the pilot-program status, including whether any reactor reached criticality, and Alpha Tech's offerings.

## 3. Overwatch: a beyond-line-of-sight drone network over the grid, climbing to grid maintenance

**Pitch:** Own docked drone networks that fly beyond the operator's line of sight (BVLOS) to patrol, inspect and respond to intrusions across utilities and solar or battery sites. Then use the labelled condition data to take over the maintenance work itself.

**Why now:**
- The June 6, 2025 executive order on drones and the FAA's proposed Part 108 BVLOS rule (Aug 2025) are making routine flights without an observer on site legal (unverified; check whether the rule is final).
- Physical attacks on grid assets have grown since the Moore County substation attack on Dec 3, 2022. Copper theft at solar farms is rising.

**Rung one and buyer:**
- About 20-40 docks over one rural electric co-op's territory or one cluster of solar and battery sites, sold as a subscription at roughly $2-6k per dock per month (est.).
- Buyers are co-ops, municipal utilities and IPPs.
- The subscription book is sellable to an inspection company or an infrastructure fund.

**Ladder:**
1. Dock-network subscriptions.
2. A condition record for every pole and span, labelled by our flights and by later outages.
3. Our own vegetation-management and minor-repair crews, dispatched by ML on contracts paid for outage minutes avoided.
4. Wildfire and storm contracts where we bear the risk.
5. Operating municipal distribution systems under concession.

End state: US vegetation management plus T&D inspection is about $10B+ a year (est.).

**How the software compounds:**
- Every flight adds labels to the models.
- Outage outcomes label the risk models.
- Better risk models cut crew hours per mile.

**Unfair advantage:** Dhruv's ML on imagery and public data, combined with Charlie's vertical integration into crews and assets.

**Biggest risk:**
- Part 108 could slip.
- Utility procurement is slow.
- Percepto, Skydio and Flock could move down into operations.
- Asplundh and Davey hold the crew relationships.
- Drone supply is constrained by the NDAA rules.

**First 2-week test:**
- Price one co-op's helicopter and foot-patrol cycle against a modelled dock network.
- Get one paid pilot letter of intent.
- Map co-op territories with 10 or more spans per square mile (est.) to size the first market.

**Verify first:** the Part 108 status, and co-ops' inspection spend.

## Self-scores (rough, before verification)

| Thesis | L1 | L2 | L3 | L4 | L5 | L6 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nodal | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 2 | **21** |
| Loopworks | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 2 | **18** |
| Overwatch | 4 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 | **20** |

These are my own unverified scores, not the verifier panel's. Treat them as at least 2 points too high: the panel cut most candidates' self-scores by 3-8 points. On these numbers Nodal fits Dhruv and Charlie best. Its software layer is the real moat, it has a sellable asset from day one, and every rung up the ladder is a physical one.
